CIA warned of threat of 'explosive airplane' years before 9/11, documents show

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:53:54 GMT

Newly declassified documents show that three years before 9/11, US intelligence officials were discussing the possibility that al-Qaeda "may fly an explosive airplane into a US city".

On Friday, the 25th anniversary of hijacked planes being crashed into the World Trade Center, Pentagon and a Pennsylvania field, the CIA released 71 daily presidential briefs spanning from early 1998 to the day after the attacks.

Another document, dated 12 September 2001, said the plot's existence was "widely known" in extremist circles.

President's Daily Briefs are among the most secretive intelligence analyses in the US government, and typically remain classified for 40 or 50 years after publication.

"Twenty-five years ago, the 9/11 attacks struck a blow to our nation, but they did not break us," CIA Director John Ratlcliffe said in a statement

"Generations of C. I. A. officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring Al Qaeda would never again harm our country," he added.

Of the 71 documents published by the CIA, 69 have never been seen by the public.

The briefs - many still heavily redacted - were created during both the Clinton and Bush administrations.

They show increasing alarm over the al-Qaeda network and its leader, Osama Bin Laden. They also echo the assessment of the official commission that reviewed what happened that day that US intelligence repeatedly warned of a potential attack, but had few details or sense of the scale of what was coming.

One briefing document, dated 10 September 1998, reported Bin Laden's preferred location for a strike was within the US, with Washington a prime target.

The group, a CIA analyst wrote, "may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city".

While the 9/11 Commission's 2004 report noted US intelligence believed al-Qaeda was considering using an airplane in the attack, it was never clear that the warning reached then-President Bill Clinton.

Bin Laden and al-Qaeda were already well-known to the US intelligence community in1998.

In August that year, they attacked US embassies in both Kenya and Tanzania, killing 224 people and prompting the US to strike targets in Afghanistan and Sudan with cruise missiles.

One document written on 28 August 1998 - 21 days after the embassy attacks and eight days after the US retaliation - warned that the network remained intact and that Bin Laden was actively "considering attacks in the US".

Only one of the presidential briefings in the release comes from after the attacks. It was sent to the White House 0400 on 12 September, just under 20 hours from when the first aircraft struck the World Trade Center in New York.

The report noted that "mounting evidence" suggested extremists in Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf "were aware" the attack had been imminent.

Another partially redacted sentence said the plot was "widely known" among extremists and that Bin Laden may have relocated to Kabul, in Afghanistan, to avoid conflict with the country's Taliban rulers with whom he had "clashed" over the plan.

The then-head of the Taliban, Mullah Omar, was reported to have been evacuated with his family from the southern Afghan city of Kandahar immediately following the attacks. Less than a month later, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan, seeking to destroy al-Qaeda.

England had "no plan" and were "out of control" in the face of Razaullah's stunning hitting on the third day of the final Test against Pakistan, according to former captain Alastair Cook.

Razaullah, the 21-year-old batting at number nine on Test debut, clobbered 81 from 63 balls at Edgbaston.

"You can get done by the tail - it's very hard when people have the license and ability to hit sixes," Cook told Test Match Special. "What I saw was no plan, it got out of control.

England need 130 after thrilling Razaullah hitting

England are currently led by interim head coach Marcus Trescothick, with New Zealander Stephen Fleming due to take on the role from December's tour of South Africa.

Trescothick is assisted by bowling coach Tim Southee, who was seen on the boundary rope at times during the partnership.

England's tactics were curious throughout the Razaullah-Abbas partnership. The seamers often stuck to a short-ball plan, with fielders back on the boundary. When their pace bowlers tried to hit the stumps, they could not find the target.

More bizarre was Root giving the second new-ball to part-time off-spinner Dan Lawrence, who had barely bowled in the series to that point. In doing so, Root bowled Lawrence in front of seamer Ollie Robinson, who has had a sensational summer as England's attack leader.

Jonathan Agnew, the former England fast bowler and the BBC's chief cricket commentator, called the tactics "appalling".

"You cannot and should not bowl like that to tailenders as soon as they come in," he said.

"You have to set the tone when you're bowling against tailenders. Yes, you bowl aggressively, but in a controlled way. They are numbers nine and 10 for a reason. It was bitterly disappointing.

"Dan Lawrence is a part-time off-spinner and he took the second new-ball. If you're looking for any aspect of the day that is utterly bonkers, that is it."

Only six of the 63 balls England bowled at Razaullah would have hit his stumps

Razaullah's thrilling knock included nine sixes, tying the record for the most maximums in an innings by a batter on Test debut.

He also equalled Stokes' record for the most sixes in a Test played in England.

There were times when Root looked devoid of ideas, while the energy was sapped from his team. Jofra Archer cut a frustrated figure when Razaullah hit him for successive straight sixes and at one point Gus Atkinson was asked to bowl bouncers with eight fielders on the boundary.

"We shouldn't be surprised by England, they've delivered tactically like this on a regular basis," said ex-England captain Michael Vaughan.

"I think they'll win this game but they can't keep making mistakes like that. The basics of Test cricket generally work and that's to hit the top of the stumps. It's a bit of a warning sign that this attack is very good but they aren't the finished article just yet.

"Who are the characters in the team who are going got grab a hold of everyone and say, 'right, I'm going to make a moment'. I didn't see it from anyone today."

At one stage Root left the field for an opportunity to consult with the England backroom staff, although it did little to alter the course of the evening.

Eventually, Abbas poked the pace of Josh Tongue to point before Razaullah was stumped off Lawrence from the final ball of the day to leave Pakistan 453 all out.

"I'm disappointed, of course," said Trescothick. "We were in a position where they were eight down and the scores were level. We were hoping to go through them pretty quickly.

"We tried many different things. You have variations of plans. We bowled the short ball for a period of time, then length for a period of time, then a bit of spin. You're always chopping and changing, with various ideas.

"You'd always like to think you can do it better and you analyse it afterwards saying, 'right, was there an area or tactic we missed to get it right?' You hope in those situations when you bowl it in the right place, which we did on many occasions, that you get the nick or bowl them. Fair play, they played pretty well."

Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:44:58 GMT

The Houthis' lightning advance across the southern reaches of the Tihamah – Yemen's arid coastal plain – appears to have taken most observers by surprise.

Until recently, the anti-Houthi coalition known as the National Resistance held significant territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast. In a matter of days, much of this has fallen to the Houthis.

According to some estimates, the Iranian-backed rebels have captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's strategically important coastline.

It's the group's most impressive military coup for several years, proving that despite a civil war that has lasted 12 years, devastating Saudi air raids and attacks by American, Israeli and British forces, the Houthis remain a force to be reckoned with.

With their opponents stunned and demoralised, it's unlikely the Houthis will be dislodged any time soon.

"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" – Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

If the Houthis have also taken control of several key islands in the Red Sea, including Perim - which sits in the middle of the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab - then the group's ability to interfere with international shipping will be greatly enhanced.

As the group's actions in the wake of Israel's war on Gaza proved, shipping in the Red Sea is highly vulnerable to Houthi missiles, drones and small attack boats.

"They were able to control what was going in and out of the Bab al-Mandab and up towards Suez without having these territorial gains," Yemen expert Iona Craig told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"But of course now they're controlling the area immediately overlooking the Bab al-Mandab, and this gives them far more leverage."

Shipping companies are likely to be sceptical about the sincerity of a statement released on Friday afternoon, in which the Houthi military said that maritime navigation was "safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels, which have already been subject to a blockade".

In their earlier attacks, the Houthis said they were only targeting vessels linked to Israel, but in fact hit ships with no such connection, including a Norwegian-flagged tanker.

Craig said the Houthis may nevertheless refrain from indiscriminate attacks, fearing a repeat of Operation Rough Rider - six weeks of major US air and naval strikes in the spring of 2025.

"They've already felt the wrath of the US," she said.

But would the US want to get involved anyway?

President Donald Trump's war with Iran is already unpopular. With oil prices creeping back up, it's doubtful that a new front would do much to enhance his approval ratings or his Republican party's chances in November's midterm US elections.

According to the Axios website, appeals for US intervention from the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman have so far gone unanswered.

Axios writes that the US "is increasingly concerned about the escalating conflict in Yemen and is working to intensify its support for the kingdom while simultaneously seeking to avoid direct military involvement".

But it's not just the potential threat to the Bab al-Mandab that's causing fear in Saudi Arabia.

Satellite images of an apparent Houthi missile-and-drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline – a vital alternative route for oil exports following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year – point to an effort by Iran's Yemeni allies to add to the economic pressures generated by the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Even if Iran did not directly order the attack, it clearly stands to benefit.

Baraa Shaiban, a researcher and analyst at the London-based Royal United Services Institute, says the origins of the latest upsurge in fighting – the worst since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 - can be traced back to July, when a Houthi delegation returned from the state funeral of Iran's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

"Immediately after, the escalation started," he says, "and it looked very clearly that [Iran was] determined to now have a bigger foothold on the Red Sea".

With Yemen teetering on the edge of a return to all-out war, Saudi Arabia anxious about preserving its economic lifeline to the Red Sea and Donald Trump apparently reluctant to get involved, America's conflict with Iran just took on a new and potentially dangerous dimension.

For the people of Yemen, displaced, bombed, starved and impoverished by a dozen years of civil war, recent developments can only make their lives worse.

Razaullah introduces himself as Pakistan thrive in chaos

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:35:07 GMT

This video can not be played

'He's become a star' - watch the best shots of Razaullah's stunning innings

Cancel the tee time at the Belfry, rearrange the trip to Cadbury World and abort the shopping jolly to the Bullring.

The reason? Pakistan's new star Razaullah and 'Razball'.

England's bowlers were thwarted by a Pakistan side who mixed batting belligerence with brilliance and instead of a Saturday off must reconvene at Edgbaston for day four.

The brilliance was provided by Razaullah, who produced a dizzying knock to breathe life into the third Test and lift the spirits of Pakistan supporters everywhere. A new hero, a new hope.

Bazball might be on its way out, but Birmingham might just have witnessed the birth of a new phenomenon during two hours of unbridled chaos where the Test debutant made a stunning 81 off 63 balls coming in at number nine.

A raw 21-year-old with just eight first-class matches to his name, selected more as a tearaway fast bowler reminiscent of Waqar Younis, Razaullah was probably not a name on the radar of England's bowlers when he was called up amid wholesale changes made by Pakistan before the final Test.

After some blistering strokeplay when he took down the home side's attack, they certainly know who he is now.

There were shades of Shahid Afridi or Abdul Razzaq in the flamboyant nature of the way Razaullah flayed England to all parts.

He took three bats to the crease but broke two with his explosive hitting.

"It's the first time he's been out there for Pakistan ever, and he absolutely lights up the show. This is the attitude that was needed," said former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja on BBC Test Match Special.

"Someone with a strong body language and who believes in himself. They'll want him playing all formats because he's a natural in mind, body language and attitude. It was a tremendous fightback."

This video can not be played

Highlights: Razaullah stars as Pakistan fight back against England

'Out of control' - Cook questions England tactics

England need 130 after thrilling Razaullah hitting

At times when Razaullah - who has one first-class century - was teeing off, England captain Joe Root wore the expression of a chess player waiting for someone to tell him it was his move.

Root stationed eight fielders on the boundary at one point - but it did not deter Razaullah as he brashly swaggered at the crease with the arrogance of youth.

This was a special innings.

Razaullah's nine sixes is the joint-most ever in a Test innings in England. The other is Ben Stokes' famous 155 with nine against Australia in the Ashes Test in 2023.

He hit as many sixes as Sir Geoffrey Boycott did in his 108-Test career.

Perhaps being so far behind, and expected to capitulate, liberated Pakistan. There was a freedom to their batting hitherto unseen in this series so far.

Shan Masood played with admirable application with a stoic 95 while captain Babar Azam, a weight lifted off his shoulders, made 76.

Yet it was the swashbuckling Razaullah who really captured the imagination.

"England are going to win this Test match, I'm sure," said former England captain Michael Vaughan.

"But Razaullah has given Pakistan cricket some hope. They've unearthed a gem and he will be a superstar for many years."

Even Razaullah's dismissal was pure theatre lapped up by the crowd. Reprieved lbw to Dan Lawrence he danced down the pitch and was stumped next ball.

The young Pakastani left the field to the warmest ovation.

In another world he might have been playing for Cleethorpes in the Yorkshire Cricket Southern Premier League, having signed for the 2026 season only to be called up to a national training camp in May.

Those with tickets for Saturday must have thought the prospect of seeing any play was remote when Pakistan offered a meek surrender on day one.

Steamrolled for 133 just after lunch in Birmingham on Wednesday they looked rudderless against opponents who were ruthless.

Doubtless many punters will have started to make other plans in the expectation this would all be over swiftly, especially when England racked up 453.

Yet with 129 to defend, Pakistan have an outside chance of what would be the most famous of victories.

It's tempting to look at Pakistan cricket through a certain prism, but when moments like these arrive it's impossible not to. Through the emotional wringer again - despair to hope in the space of three days.

"There wouldn't be any person in the world that would've thought we'd go to day four," added Vaughan.

"That is what Pakistan cricket is. They have had a difficult few weeks. The team has been in turmoil. That is why I love Pakistan cricket.

"England will look back at a lot of the tactics and realise they got it wrong. The short stuff, one over of spin, the second new ball with the spinner.

"That day today will make the England team realise there is a long way to go to be world class."

Ciganda's late sparkle lifts Europe on dramatic opening day of Solheim Cup

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 18:26:09 GMT

Europe's Ciganda rescues half after dramatic final hole

Carlota Ciganda once again stole the show after Europe's top pairing of Charley Hull and Lottie Woad failed to ignite against the USA on the opening day of the Solheim Cup.

The 36-year-old Spaniard - the oldest player competing this weekend - let out a roar after holing a 15-foot putt to earn Europe an unlikely half point in the final fourball match of the day and ensure honours are even at 4-4.

Ciganda's celebration evoked memories of the nerve-shredding finale at Finca Cortesin in 2023, when her putt allowed Europe to retain the trophy with a 14-14 tie.

And once again Nelly Korda, beaten by Ciganda in Spain three years ago, was on the receiving end.

The world number one and her playing partner Lauren Coughlin both left match-winning putts short to allow Ciganda, who had crucially won the 16th hole with an eagle, to deliver a stunning reprieve for Anna Nordqvist's team at Bernardus Golf Club in the Netherlands.

"I love this week. I just love playing for the team, for my team-mates. We fought hard and we got half a point, which is important," said Ciganda, who is playing in her eighth Solheim Cup.

"It gives us big momentum and hopefully we can take that into and win both [of Saturday's] morning and afternoon sessions."

This video can not be played

Woad & Korda lead best shots from Solheim Cup day one

European hopes of parity had begun to fade into the shadows of the evening sunshine, with Angela Stanford's visitors seemingly assuming control of the 20th edition of the biggest team competition in women's golf.

It proved to be a hard-fought opening day between Europe and a US team looking to retain the trophy following their 15½-12½ victory in Virginia two years ago.

However, despite Ciganda's heroics, there was also a sense of what might have been for the hosts, who found themselves 6-2 behind at this stage two years ago at the Robert Trent Jones Golf Club.

History has shown a good start to be essential in this competition, with the team holding the advantage after the opening day taking home the trophy 14 out of 19 times.

And the decision to send out Hull and Woad first in both the morning foursomes and the afternoon fourballs failed to deliver the impetus Europe's captain Nordqvist would have hoped for.

When Hull and rookie Woad emerged on the raucous opening tee with daylight barely breaking through at 06:40 BST, they did so as the two highest-ranked players in the European side at eight and seven respectively.

Yet despite winning the opening hole, Nordqvist's gamble never looked like paying off against the formidable pairing of Korda and Allisen Corpuz.

The American duo won all four of their foursomes matches across the previous two editions of this contest and became the first to make it five on the spin with a comfortable 4&3 victory.

Disappointingly for Europe, Hull and Woad then let a three-hole advantage slip on the back nine on Friday afternoon against Yealimi Noh and Angel Yin, who was playing only her third competitive round since June.

They did at least scramble a half point despite loud music being played by an on-course DJ clearly distracting Woad and Noh as they lined up their final putts. BBC Sport has contacted the Ladies European Tour about the incident which clouded the end of a pulsating match.

In contrast Europe's three other debutants, Julia Lopez Ramirez, Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud, delivered in style.

England's Rhodes and France's Nadaud produced a superb performance to defeat Corpuz and Auston Kim 2&1, while the big-hitting Lopez Ramirez teamed up with her compatriot Ciganda in that final match against Korda and Lauren Coughlin.

"There's another 36 holes [on Saturday], so not every player's going to play five matches," said Nordqvist of her plans.

"Sometimes you've got to sit out someone, and for me, it was important to play all 12 players [on Friday], and the way the pairings worked out, that's how I had to play it."

During the build-up Nordqvist and Stanford both spoke of using the Solheim Cup as an advertisement for women's golf.

And the levels of skill, drama and grit on display only served to underline those comments, with the American players also poignantly wearing custom pins to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

"I just told them that I was proud of them again," said Stanford after the conclusion of play.

"We took a big swing from them. When you send Charley and Lottie out first, both sessions, we took some of their best body blows today.

"I'm excited because I feel like we're a heavyweight fighter. We fight with our mentality and we're just going to see how long we can last, and I feel pretty good about how long we can go."

Korda in particular set the tone early on Friday with her fifth win with Corpuz, equalling the points record for pairings set by Europe's Alison Nicholas and Laura Davies.

The US pairing of Alison Lee and Coughlin were always in control against Nanna Koerstz Madsen and Celine Boutier, taking their foursomes match 3&2 as the US opened a 2-0 lead.

An out of sorts Koerstz Madsen, who talked to her coach between sessions about her swing, and Boutier were also later on the end of a 5&3 demolition in an encounter that marked Megan Khang's sixth consecutive win in Solheim matches and her eighth in the past nine - this time alongside the metronomic Alison Lee.

Europe's fightback in the opening session was initiated by Swedish duo Maja Stark and Linn Grant who defeated Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho 3&2.

Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit followed that up by holding their nerve to defeat Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan in another match that went down the 18th.

The victory meant Maguire improved her career Solheim Cup record to nine wins, three defeats and one halved match, to give her the highest winning percentage o any European player that has played five matches.

On Saturday, eight more points will be available across the foursomes (alternate shot) and fourballs formats, before the singles on Sunday, which will involve all 12 players on each team.

Europe require 14½ points to regain the cup, while US need 14 points to retain it.

Surrogate who refused abortion over heart defect takes custody battle to US Supreme Court

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:55:06 GMT

A surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute over who should have custody of the baby.

McKenna West filed an emergency appeal asking the court to halt a previous ruling granting parental rights to California couple Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.

Ahmed and Gilkar had asked West to abort the pregnancy after a scan at 20 weeks showed the foetus had a severe heart defect.

Instead, West - who has been supported by several Republican officials - travelled to Texas where nearly all abortions are illegal and gave birth to the child.

The BBC has contacted lawyers for Ahmed and Gilkar for comment.

West has since been pushing for custody over the baby, born last month with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a defect where the left side of the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body.

The condition often requires multiple surgeries, which are not a cure. Infants with the condition can have lifelong complications, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

After West travelled to the state, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and won an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive medical care in the state. He had surgery soon after birth.

West said she denied the couple's requests to have the abortion after learning of treatment options and wanting to keep "this precious baby", according to the Supreme Court filing.

West has argued that the biological parents should not have custody because she worries they would not give the boy necessary medical care because they sought to abort the child after learning of the life-threatening condition.

In a previous court hearing, Gilkar said the baby - whom they named Rumi - was "our child" and "the love of our lives", according to the Associated Press. They said West travelled to Texas without telling them and blocked their access to medical information.

A California court previously granted parental rights to Ahmed and Gilkar, while a Texas court issued a restraining order blocking West from seeing the baby.

Last month, an attorney for the California couple said the child was in critical condition and seemed to be "suffering from potential complications".

West argued that without intervention from the Supreme Court, she would no longer have access to information about the child's medical condition. In the filing, lawyers for West suggested that the California couple could place the child in hospice care.

Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:45:14 GMT

The government scheme to support people injured by Covid vaccines and other jabs has cost £83m to run since April 2022, new figures have revealed.

The amount spent on administration costs and medical assessments is more than double the £32m paid out in financial support to victims so far.

The Taxpayers' Alliance think tank said the public would be "stunned" at the cost and called for the government to urgently review the scheme.

NHSBSA which runs the scheme for the government says rising numbers of claims are behind the increasing administrative and medical assessor supplier costs.

The latest data shows there have been 24,260 claims since November 2021, although just 264 have been successful.

The Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme (VDPS) was set up in 1979 to provide financial support to people who, in rare cases, had been harmed by vaccines of any type.

Since the pandemic the number applying for damage payments has increased sharply.

The vast majority of applications are now linked to the AstraZeneca vaccine and other Covid jabs.

The benefits of vaccination are well documented. The AstraZeneca Covid jab is credited with saving millions of lives worldwide. But for those who were harmed, the resulting injuries are devastating.

The full costs of the VDPS have now been revealed for the first time in the answer to a parliamentary question from the backbench Conservative MP Sir Christopher Chope.

In response, health minister Dame Diana Johnson said a total of £83m had been spent on staffing costs, administration and medical reviews between April 2022 and March 2026.

Under the scheme, claimants must have their application reviewed by an independent doctor, to check whether they have met the threshold of "severe disablement".

If approved, they can then receive a one-off, tax-free payment of £120,000. The process can take months or even years.

The costs of those medical assessments have increased from £4.3m in 2022/23 to £19.3m in 2025/26, according to new data published by the government.

Based on the latest available data up to June 2026, the total amount paid out in damages to those who died or were injured after being given a Covid vaccine has risen to £31.6m.

"The administrative costs and medical assessor supplier costs of the VDPS are driven by the number of claims received," said the NHSBSA, which runs the scheme on behalf of the government.

"We have seen a significant increase in the number of claims received since taking over administration of the VDPS in November 2021."

The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:22:39 GMT

MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270, majority 16, against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short-term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years if it had been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they did not vote on party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

There were emotional scenes outside Parliament from both sides after MPs voted against giving the bill a second reading.

Dame Esther Rantzen, who was unable to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC that it was "so sad that people in this country won't have the choice" that terminally ill adults have in other countries.

The Childline founder said: "I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won't come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it's a tragic day."

The broadcaster, 86, is terminally ill with cancer and has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

Edwards, the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood, said: "Parliament has dropped the ball today.

"It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand."

Those in favour of a change in the law have said they would try to bring forward legislation again, with Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original bill, telling the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.

Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Dame Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, who all opposed what they described the "unsafe and unworkable" bill, welcomed MPs' decision.

In a joint statement, they said: "This is not a moment for celebration, we understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.

"But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill."

They said there is a need to "fix our NHS and sort out social and palliative care before we even consider introducing assisted dying".

Sarah Wootton, chief executive of Dignity in Dying, said "thousands of terminally ill people will continue to suffer against their wishes in their last days and weeks".

She added she still believes "law change is inevitable".

Care Not Killing chief executive Gordon Macdonald described the vote as "decisive".

He said: "Our hope is that MPs now focus on repairing palliative care in the UK and securing the necessary funding to make sure that no matter what part of the country you live in, you can access the best possible care available and are treated with dignity and respect."

The bill in the last parliamentary session, brought forward by Leadbeater, cleared the House of Commons on 20 June 2025 with a majority of 23.

But it ran out of time to progress through all the necessary stages in Parliament after some peers in the House of Lords tabled more than 1,200 amendments.

Edwards brought forward the proposals again in a bid to ensure peers could "finish their job", although this will no longer take place.

During the debate, Labour MP Janet Daby was among those to confirm she would vote against the bill despite previously supporting it.

She told the Commons she had "nightmares about dying and death" after voting in favour of the last bill, adding: "I had to wrestle with myself, knowing that I was not entirely comfortable with the decision I had made, and my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."

In another of the personal testimonies during the debate, Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove spoke about her mother's decision to bring her late-stage terminal illness to an end "on her terms".

The MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke said the "harmful status quo" meant her mother died alone in October last year, after living with a rare blood cancer for half her life.

Hazelgrove argued "not all pain can be palliated" as she spoke in favour of the bill.

Conservative MP Martin Vickers said his "firm" view was that "if assisted dying is legalised we will be poorer as a society, we will have a crossed a line", adding it would also change the "relationship between doctor and patient".

Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon called for a change in the law and described the bill as "better than what we currently have, which offers no safeguards and no protections for people in those final moments".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not vote on the bill on Friday, previously describing it as "a matter for Parliament to decide".

He has previously said he personally believes that funding for end-of-life care in the UK should be improved before legalising assisted dying is considered.

Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:21:00 GMT

Most Americans remember exactly what they were doing and how they felt the day four airplanes were hijacked and crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania.

But now, 25 years on from the 11 September 2001 attacks, there is a new generation, too young to remember the day that permanently altered much of American life.

Members of Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were told - well after the fact - about the event that undoubtedly reshaped their futures.

They carry distinct memories not from the day itself, but from the moment years later that they learned about the attacks.

Avery Black, 20, a journalism student at the University of South Carolina, remembers hearing about 9/11 for the first time in elementary school, then going home and asking her mother about it, she told the BBC.

"She just started telling me where she was the day it happened, and just broke down in tears, explaining to me about all the firefighters that went in and never came out," Black recalled.

As a child, Black didn't quite grasp the day's gravity, but for her, certain details still stand out.

She remembers, most distinctly, the "falling man" – a famous image of a man plummeting, upside down, from the North Tower. A Dallas, Texas native, she also recalls teachers showing the video of then-President George W. Bush first learning about the attacks at an elementary school event.

For Annie Erickson, 26, who grew up in North Carolina, personal anecdotes, more than school or reports, created her first memories of 9/11.

"My mother grew up in New York City, so I remember my mom telling me about 9/11 and talking about how someone that lived in her building, who she was friends with, passed away in the towers," Erickson said.

She also was struck when learning about 9/11 at school that it was one of the few historical events teachers could personalise with their own memories.

Currently, there's no national requirement for US schools to teach students about the attacks, and the expectations vary widely by state. Twenty-five states require or expect public schools to teach the events of 9/11, while 13 make 9/11 instruction optional, according to a recent analysis by The Associated Press.

But not every state that requires it specifies a curriculum.

Allegra Tashjian, 28, who grew up in Wisconsin, said her teacher explained in first or second grade that it was a very important, sombre day and asked if anyone knew why. After a student responded that it was the day planes hit the towers in New York, Tashjian wondered why she had never heard of it before.

Later, at home, she recalls asking her mom if she remembered planes crashing in New York. "I remember she kind of paused folding her laundry and was like, 'um no, I don't think I've ever heard anything about that,'" the PhD student said.

"For whatever reason at that point, I guess she really didn't want to talk about it."

Tashjian, Erickson, Black and several other Gen Zs all told the BBC that they remember hearing a few details about the attacks in school and from their families, but only through their own research did they learn in depth what actually happened that day.

Black didn't realise as a child who was behind the attack. "That was the part that I wasn't really taught until I did my own research. It's really hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child."

"It really took me until I was like 13 or 14 to sit down and watch news coverage of 9/11, and really process this is a deeply harrowing, terrifying event," said Jack Coyne, 28, a Connecticut native who lives in Boston.

Now, as an adult, Coyne said he wishes people had a more nuanced perspective, recognizing 9/11 as a tragedy that also fuelled Islamophobia in the US and led to further deaths in ensuing wars.

Professor David Schanzer, who teaches "9/11 & Its Aftermath" at Duke University, wrote this week in a campus magazine commentary that there's still strong interest generations later. His course is full, with dozens on a waitlist.

"Ten years ago, I thought student interest was ebbing and I would need to find something else to teach about," he wrote.

But current world events, he said, only made young people more curious about what happened 25 years ago on 9/11.

"If you want to understand what has gone wrong over the past couple of decades it makes sense to learn about 9/11, the first global catastrophe of the 21st century (the others being the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic)," he wrote.

Several Gen Zs told the BBC that, despite gaining knowledge about the tragic day, it is still common among peers to actively lighten conversations about 9/11.

Thomas Schwartz, a professor of history and political science at Vanderbilt University, said in a recent class discussion, his seniors - born in 2004 or 2005 - remarked on their generation's tendency to "deflect and joke about 9/11".

He added that "students from the Northeast, who had parents with personal memories of 9/11, were more careful about this, remarking on the sensitivities in their family about the subject."

Erickson said many Gen Zs tend to downplay monumental events or tragedies because either they "can't fully understand their impact" or they're using humour as a coping mechanism "to not have to think too deeply about some of the larger anxieties in our world".

Even now as an adult, Tashjian said it's still difficult for her to fathom large numbers of people dying in any event, and she still gravitates toward individual anecdotes to help her understand 9/11's toll.

Schanzer contends that learning about 9/11 and understanding its impact remains crucial for younger generations without first-hand knowledge.

"But like most significant historical events, one can't fully understand our world today unless you understand why 9/11 occurred and how the United States responded to it," he said.

An extraordinary result - why did MPs reject assisted dying bill this time?

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:49:47 GMT

There were gasps and – to the intense irritation of supporters – cheers from opponents of assisted dying when the vote was read out in the Commons.

This was an extraordinary result.

After twice voting in favour of the bill, MPs have rejected proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing to an end the latest effort to change the law.

The debate itself was tetchier, more irritable than when Kim Leadbeater introduced a similar bill in 2024. Then it was the first time MPs had voted on assisted dying in nine years.

Since then the Commons has voted on this issue three times and had hours of debate. The sombre, respectful tone from 2024 has become more embittered.

Given the strength of feeling on both sides over such an emotive issue, perhaps that is unsurprising.

But on a deeply divided issue, both sides agree on why the result was different.

"We always said it would come to turnout and it did," one supporter of the bill text me. An opponent messaged to say the same.

The numbers tell a story.

Last time MPs voted on assisted dying in June, 315 were in favour and 291 against. Today, the numbers opposed were similar: 286.

But support for this bill has ebbed away. Just 270 voted for this bill, a fall of 45.

So why have fewer MPs backed it, compared to a year ago?

There are a number of reasons why support for assisted dying has dropped off.

Some MPs have changed their mind. Janet Daby, the Labour MP for Lewisham East, for example told the Commons that after she previously backed the bill "my conscience was not at peace, and I cannot again, in good conscience, vote for the bill."

But in reality those switching their position are a small minority.

For others, the influence of Andy Burnham may have been a factor. When MPs last gave their collective view on assisted dying, Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister and supportive of this bill.

Burnham, however, is not. For Labour MPs wanting to follow Downing Street's priorities, abstaining might have seemed a more appealing option.

There will be other reasons why supportive MPs did not turn up today. A wedding, I'm told, took some away from Westminster. A trip to Ukraine meant others missed the vote.

Already those in favour of a change in the law promise to try again. Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced the original legislation last year, has told the BBC another attempt could come as soon as next year.

Supporters have told me they see this parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, as a "unique moment" to pass this change.

"This result doesn't mean there isn't still a majority in parliament in favour of the principle of assisted dying," said one of those behind the bill.

But for now the momentum has fallen away from a change in the law.

That is a relief to those who worry such a change would risk harming vulnerable people. But it is a bitter disappointment to those who see it as a necessary and compassionate alternative to the status quo.

That bitterness from supporters is aimed in part at the House of Lords.

It was opponents' efforts there that ultimately led to this defeat. And it could hasten those calling for reform of Parliament's second chamber.

Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after attending brother King Harald's funeral

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:00:59 GMT

Princess Astrid of Norway, the sister of the late King Harald V, has died at the age of 94, two days after attending his funeral, the country's royal palace has announced.

The new king, Haakon VIII, said that "throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner".

Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years as king. His funeral was Astrid's last public engagement.

The princess will be buried at state expense and flags will be flown at half-mast across Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.

Astrid was the last surviving child of King Olav V, who reigned from 1957 to 1991.

She became Norway's first lady at the age of 22 in 1954, after the death of her mother Crown Princess Märtha. Olav did not remarry and Astrid retained the title until her brother's marriage in 1968.

"In her work, Princess Astrid was always particularly concerned with care and inclusion for the most vulnerable in society," her nephew King Haakon said in his statement.

Her health had deteriorated in recent months and in March she received hospital treatment for pneumonia.

Dozens of European royals and heads of state attended Harald's funeral on Wednesday, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings.

Thousands of people lined the route during a procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon.

The non-royal leaders paying their respects included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and five foreign prime ministers.

In the final months of Harald's life, Norway's royal family faced personal challenges and scandal.

Earlier this year, documents revealed that King Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, had had frequent contact with US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later said she wished she had never met the late disgraced financier.

Meanwhile, her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby - who is not a royal but grew up within the family - was given a four-year jail term for two counts of rape in June.

Høiby, who is under house arrest pending appeal, was granted permission to attend the funeral.

Sacked Grand Theft Auto worker claims Rockstar staff placed on 'watch list'

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:52:19 GMT

A worker dismissed by the makers of Grand Theft Auto claimed colleagues were placed on a "watch list" after signing a petition about remote working.

Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal Rockstar North "kept an eye" on a small group of employees who were union members after the petition was handed to the company in the spring of 2023.

Oram was among a number of employees claiming to have been sacked by the gaming giant for attempting to unionise in October last year.

Rockstar has denied those allegations at the employment tribunal in Glasgow and alleges workers were sacked for "gross misconduct" following the sharing of confidential information in an online forum.

Some 34 workers were believed to have been sacked last year, with 23 taking part in the employment tribunal.

Most of the sacked staff were based at the company's Edinburgh headquarters, with others based in Canada.

Oram, who is among workers being represented at the hearing by the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB), gave evidence on the first day of the tribunal.

About 150 Rockstar employees had signed the petition about working from home, but between 15 and 20 of them were union members.

Lawyers for Rockstar said there was nothing in the signatures that could identify them as union members, but Oram told the tribunal it could be "inferred" who was by those who handed in the petition.

Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, asked Oram how there could be a connection between the company having the list of names in February 2023 and the dismissals in October 2025 when there was a gap of two years and eight months between the events.

Oram said it was "not the sole reason" for their dismissal, but claimed the sacking was connected to other union organising activities.

Oram added the petition was used as "the basis of a watch list" for people carrying out "activities that were considered distasteful".

The tribunal also heard Oram was involved in setting up a Discord server that was used as a forum where around 300 Rockstar employees could discuss the company.

Cordrey read rules from the forum, which asked members to be "professional and constructive".

However, he put it to Oram that this was "routinely broken".

Oram said the rule was "more of a guiding principle" and that one comment referring to a specific manager had been removed because it concerned an individual.

Cordrey also asked whether Oram believed another post, where someone was described in a highly derogatory way, amounted to gross misconduct.

Oram said that was "misconduct" but denied it crossed the threshold into gross misconduct.

Oram added: "If I had to remake some of the moderation decisions, probably I would make them differently now."

Rockstar's upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 is expected to break sales records when it is released on 19 November.

It was previously delayed twice, in autumn 2025 and May 2026.

Pre-orders of the game - which features the series' first female playable character, Lucia and her partner Jason, as the main protagonists - are already thought to have been worth hundreds of millions.

The last installment of the franchise, Grand Theft Auto 5, was released in September 2013 and became one of the best-selling games of all time.

A spokesperson for the company said: "Rockstar Games' position has been clear and consistent throughout.

"Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity.

"We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal."

The tribunal, before judge Lucy Wiseman, continues.

Israel says it has destroyed major underground Hezbollah base

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:50:23 GMT

Israel's military says it has destroyed a large underground complex operated by Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.

It said it used more than 1,000 tonnes of explosives to destroy two tunnels spanning more than 2km (1.2 miles) beneath the Ali Taher Ridge.

The blast triggered seismic activity equivalent to a magnitude 4.1 earthquake, according to the US Geological Survey.

There was no immediate public response from Hezbollah or the Lebanese government.

Israeli forces took control of the ridge last week after months of fighting with the Iran-backed group there. The Israeli military occupies a large swathe of southern Lebanon captured after the conflict with Hezbollah resumed in March.

Images released by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) showed a fireball lighting up the sky.

"The sky lit up and about 15 seconds later we heard the terrifying sound," Ahamed, a resident in Nabatieh, about 6km west of the ridge, told the BBC.

"The house shook all together as if it was literally an earthquake."

He said people were screaming and children were crying, and that cars filled the roads as people left the area for Beirut.

Tremors were even felt in the coastal city of Saida 40km north.

The IDF said the underground infrastructure included a command centre used by Hezbollah's Badr unit and contained dozens of rockets, missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles, as well as anti-tank weapons, mines and explosives.

"This was strategic infrastructure that was constructed over two decades, funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime," the IDF said in a statement on Telegram.

"All of the terrorists who were inside the infrastructure were eliminated or fled."

The IDF said the destruction of the complex completed a mission to destroy eight tunnels and establish a "security zone" in the area.

The latest action comes amid renewed fighting in southern Lebanon, where Israeli forces have expanded operations against Hezbollah positions and continue to hold what Israel describes as a security zone near the border.

Lebanese media reported fresh Israeli strikes elsewhere in the south on Thursday, including Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Mansouri in the Tyre district.

The Lebanese army has increased deployments in areas outside Israeli control, including the southern city of Nabatieh, in efforts to strengthen stability and reassure residents, local television station MTV reported.

Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.

Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.

Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel.

The UN says about 330,000 people in Lebanon remain displaced by the conflict, with Israeli military activity, air strikes, destruction and restrictions on returning to Israeli-occupied areas preventing many from going home.

Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.

Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.

Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.

At least 4,383 people - including 395 women and 259 children - have been killed in Lebanon by Israeli attacks since 2 March, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians. At least 29 have been killed this week, the ministry says.

Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed in the same period.

Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".

Speaking to journalists, O'Leary said some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".

O'Leary doubled-down on his choice of words when asked about them at the time, and later refused to apologise when the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.

Ireland's deputy premier Simon Harris said it was "clearly an inappropriate use of language" and that O'Leary "should have moved to rectify it".

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told UK radio outlet LBC that victims of rape are "not going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest".

Asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate, he said: "Absolutely."

"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he added.

Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".

Following O'Leary's comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh wrote to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.

She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".

"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.

"Fusing legendary industry experience with a vibrant competitive spirit, our latest panel of icons is ready to discover and celebrate the most remarkable and exciting vocal talent emerging from every corner of the country," ITV said.

Dixon shot to fame as a member of girl group Mis-Teeq and has served as judge on Strictly Come Dancing and Britain's Got Talent.

She has previously hosted The Greatest Dancer and the Eurovision Song Contest when it was hosted by the UK in Liverpool in 2023.

Solomon came second on The X Factor in 2009, and is now known for hosting Sort Your Life Out and appearing on reality show Stacey & Joe with her husband Joe Swash.

Earlier this year, it was reported that McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones would also not be returning to The Voice, after they shared a chair as joint coaches for the last two series.

On Friday, ITV said: "We thank Emma Willis, Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones for their brilliant contributions, and who all brought so much dedication, expertise and energy to The Voice UK and wish them the very best of luck as they embark on their next chapters."

Willis will still be seen on screen for the rest of the current series of The Voice UK, as it was recorded last year.

That means viewers will see Willis hosting two different Saturday night prime-time shows this autumn, for BBC One and ITV.

She will front the new series of the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing from 19 September, alongside comedian Josh Widdicombe and dancer Johannes Radebe.

The trio replace Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left at the end of the previous series.

The Voice launched its UK version in 2012, hosted by Holly Willoughby and Reggie Yates, after the format was successful in the US.

Willis took over presenting duties in 2014, joined for several series by Marvin Humes of boyband JLS. The show jumped from the BBC to ITV in 2017.

The show differs from other singing competitions in that the coaches have their backs turned to contestants as they audition.

If the coaches like a contestant's voice, they can spin around in their chairs to see their identity and offer to mentor them during the series.

Other previous coaches on the UK series include Olly Murs, Jennifer Hudson, Kylie Minogue, Rita Ora, Anne Marie and LeAnn Rimes.

UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:07:07 GMT

The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

On Sunday OpenAI's chief scientist said the risk from increasingly capable AI models is "unfortunately growing" and humanity must proceed with "extreme caution".

Then on Wednesday an Anthropic employee resigned saying it and OpenAI were "gambling with lives".

This was followed by an admission from a senior Anthropic researcher, who said he believes there is a greater than 10% chance AI will "kill all humans" within the next decade.

Critics of the kill switch idea say it would be too slow - it took months for the rogue agent attacks to be discovered and that was only after the hacks had largely concluded.

For a kill switch to work, tech giants would have to be compelled to do it at scale - especially in the US where the largest data centres are based.

Kokotajlo said kill switches were "better than nothing", but urged politicians in the UK and beyond to instead focus on diplomacy with the US to encourage regulation that would meaningfully slow down development of AI.

A kill switch act is also being debated by US politicians but President Trump has said he does not believe the technology is a threat to humans - instead calling the industry a "golden goose".

The Cabinet Office said it was continuing to take "a long-term, science-led approach to understand and prepare for emerging risks from AI."

Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:19:21 GMT

Catherine, Princess of Wales has visited the hospital where she was treated for cancer after completing a charity climb earlier this year to help fund a new unit there.

"This was my small way of being able to give back and say thank you," Catherine told staff at the Royal Marsden in London on Friday .

The princess, who revealed two years ago that she was receiving cancer treatment, carried out the Three Peaks Challenge in aid of the hospital, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales within 24 hours.

The amount of money she raised has not been made public, but it will go towards a new unit offering complementary healing alongside clinical care.

The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

Another patient said she had gone from being aged 46 to feeling "like I was 86".

Catherine, who announced in January 2025 that she was in remission, agreed about the need to support the whole person - saying holistic treatment helped patients "adjust to the lifestyle change that cancer has brought".

She also heard from a patient who spoke of wanting to seek out new experiences after being diagnosed: "There are those moments where you fall down a bit, like, 'what's going on?' And you need to find inspiration."

The princess agreed, saying that it showed the importance of "making the most of life".

Speaking after Catherine's visit, one patient particularly welcomed her being there due to her personal experience of cancer: "I forgot that she was a princess. I was just talking to every other cancer patient who has been in this ward."

"You all become friends, part of a community, and I was talking to her on that level, rather than the Princess of Wales," he said.

Money raised by her mountain climbs in June will now be used for the The Centre for Holistic Wellbeing and Recovery.

It is intended to offer cancer patients a wider sense of recovery, beyond physical treatment, and addressing a sense of emotional, spiritual and social wellbeing.

She previously said the challenge was a "chance to explore life beyond diagnosis", as well as giving back.

Catherine's trip to the London hospital follows a visit on Thursday with her husband Prince William to support a suicide prevention project being launched in Liverpool.

As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next

BBC News Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:03:43 GMT

Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.

Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.

Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night.

"We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds.

"Then we'll worry about what comes next."

His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.

Over the two-day event, party activists were split on the wisdom of holding a midterm convention featuring a president who has record low approval ratings, and amid public frustration over the economy and war with Iran.

"I think it will make a difference. If anything it allows us to test the [campaign] message in front of a large audience," Jeff Ryer, the Virginia Republican Party chairman, told the BBC.

Others said the president's rambling, nearly two-hour convention speech on Wednesday wouldn't sway voters weighing whether to keep Republicans in power in Congress.

Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance to retake control of the House and the Senate is also in play, though viewed as more of a long shot for the party.

"Do I wish Trump gave a shorter speech? Sure, but that's not who he is," said one Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer a blunt view of Trump's convention appearance.

The source added that Trump's plea for voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot would fall flat.

"I don't think saying 'pretend I'm on the ballot' will work. He's not," the person said.

The convention offered a stark reminder that the Trump era is heading toward its final chapter.

Trump's presence loomed over the proceedings at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas.

Republican House and Senate candidates lavished the president with praise in speeches, and supporters showed up wearing the red Maga hats that have become synonymous with Trump's political movement.

The gathering was just two days, but still had the look and feel of the traditional four-day conventions staged by both parties in presidential election years. Organisers distributed signs and unleashed a balloon drop at the end as live music blared.

Republicans had never held a midterm convention before.

Vikki Consiglio, a party activist from Georgia, said it showcased Trump's ability to shake up political norms and capture the nation's attention.

Evidence of that came when Trump pledged in his speech to make a payment of $5,000 to all American adults if Republicans retained control of Congress.

"He's a visionary. This whole convention is nothing but a vision," Consiglio said.

But even as convention goers cheered Trump on, many seemed eager to discuss the 2028 presidential election.

"I'm very concerned about the next 10, 15, 20 years. I'm absolutely thinking about the future of the party," said Aiden Buzzetti, the president of The Bull Moose Project, a pro-Trump group.

Buzzetti, who is 26, credited Trump with reshaping Republican politics, but said at the same time he was looking forward to a "new generation of conservative leaders."

In interviews with the BBC, attendees at the convention most often mentioned Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the top contenders to replace Trump.

"Trump needs to pass the torch. We need to look forward," said Sandy Money, a Republican from Arizona who attended the convention. "I love Vance. But Rubio is my choice" if he runs in 2028, she said.

Trump has openly mused about Rubio and Vance's chances to succeed him.

But Vance and Rubio have deflected speculation about their political futures.

Rubio was on a diplomatic trip to Ecuador during the convention, so he wasn't among the small handful of cabinet officials who attended the festivities in Dallas.

The Trump administration has delivered "a great record of achievement," Vance argued, including improving the economy, strengthening border security and lowering the cost of prescription drugs.

Vance said the contrast was clear with a Democratic Party that he argued had shifted radically to the left and turned into the "party of crazy".

The vice-president also made a direct appeal to undecided voters, saying he wanted to win over "the people who are still making up their minds".

Never one to cede the spotlight, Trump returned to the stage on Thursday night after Vance to round off the convention.

For the president, the question of his successor was overshadowed by more immediate concerns.

"You know what happens if you don't vote?" he asked the gathered crowd. "You go to hell."
