Whanganui former stockcar racer Gerry Linklater shares recovery update nearly 18 months on from crash

New Zealand Herald September 11, 2026

Former stockcar driver Gerry Linklater in the "man cave" he made after a life-changing crash at Oceanview Speedway in April 2025. Photo / Fin Ocheduszko Brown

Whanganui’s Gerry Linklater says recovering from a stockcar crash that left him critically injured 18 months ago has been a journey.

“In some ways it’s gone quick but in other ways it’s taking its time,” he said.

Linklater had driven stockcars for 25 years, starting when he was 16.

The crash occurred at Oceanview Speedway in Whanganui during warm-up laps for his Wanganui Warriors Superstock Team on April 26, 2025.

Linklater said he had no recollection of the crash but, through footage, he was able to tell what might have happened.

After hitting a track wall, Linklater said he must have gone unconscious but the car kept going, scraping the side wall for several seconds before veering off track and driving front-on into the opposite wall.

“When I look back on it, I’ve done a million laps around that speedway and never, ever crashed like that before,” Linklater said.

“My wife said that after the first hit into the wall, she didn’t watch the bigger hit because she could see what was going to happen.”

Following the incident, he was taken to Whanganui Hospital, then flown to Wellington Hospital and put into an induced coma for two weeks.

He said it took a while to fully emerge from the coma and his memories started again in August – four months after the accident.

“One thing I learned was that it’s not at all like on TV, when they push a button and the person wakes up – it’s f***ing not like that at all,” he said.

Linklater suffered a broken spine in two places, a broken sternum, rib and arm, and multiple brain bleeds.

He said it took a while before he was told anything about the crash and remembered asking who crashed into him, to which his wife, Sarah Linklater, said “no one”.

“The only reason I wanted to know was so I could reach out to them and tell them ‘no hard feelings’,” he said.

Recovery had been a process and the brain injury had been the biggest challenge, he said.

“A lot of the times, when I wake up, I’m already tired and it doesn’t matter how long you sleep, sometimes you wake up and just feel tired,” he said.

“It’s not because I’m not interested in what’s happened or anything; your body just can’t fight the fatigue.”

He said fatigue, short-term memory loss and moving slower were the biggest effects of the injury.

Suffering a brain injury was like living in two worlds; one where you show up, smile and function, and the other where you recover in silence for hours, Linklater said.

He said other people only saw the first world and rarely the latter.

Linklater praised ACC, which modified his home to make it more usable and had approved further modifications.

Since the crash, Linklater has been busy; he got married, attended the NRL Magic Round in Brisbane, set up a “man cave” full of stockcar memorabilia and completed the 3 Bridges Marathon 5km walk.

He said completing the walk with friends and family, seven months after the accident, was awesome.

“It was funny because the night before I didn’t have very good sleep ... but to me, my thoughts were ‘you set your mind to something so do it’,” he said.

Linklater’s goal is to complete the event’s quarter marathon this year.

He thanked people for their support throughout his recovery.

“When I got out of the coma and went on Facebook, it was humbling,” he said.

Nearly $16,000 was donated to the Linklater family through a Givealittle page.

He said the Wanganui Warriors had been awesome to him, especially manager Rangi Dykstra.

He praised his wife, who resigned from her job to care for him.

“There’s nothing more that she could do – she’s amazing,” he said.

Linklater looked back on his career as a stockcar driver with pride.

“I still love it, I love the sport and I have no bad memories at all,” he said.

He was proud of the NZ Stockcar Championship title he won in 2007, his 2NZ in 2008 and the many regional events he performed well in over the years.

Linklater had to medically retire from his job as area engineer for Horizons Regional Council and is unsure what the future holds.

He wants to stay involved with speedway and stockcar racing and “just enjoy life”.

Fin Ocheduszko Brown is a multimedia journalist based in Whanganui.

Barbara Edmonds: Labour’s finance spokesperson set to take economic fight to Nicola Willis - Fran O’Sullivan

New Zealand Herald September 11, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

In an election campaign where everyone professes to care about the price of mince, Barbara Edmonds is one of the few politicians who can talk in the same breath about mums at Pak’nSave and section EE31 of the Income Tax Act – and sound credible on both.

Edmonds, who is Labour’s finance spokesperson – and the MP for Mana – is on track to become a household name. At the recent Politik election summit in Wellington, she showed why she should not be underestimated.

She currently represents an electorate that was once the third‑highest median income area in the country – despite encompassing Porirua and Porirua East – because of its heavy concentration of public servants and construction workers. In the 2026 election she is campaigning for the new Kenepuru seat.

At the Politik event she was brutally specific on cost of living issues: “When you have white bread that’s gone up over 70%, when you have beef mince go up over 33%, having mince on toast, the old usual kind of slap‑up meal that busy parents do at the end of the night, is no longer affordable for a lot of our families.

“The cost of living, to me, isn’t just about bringing inflation down. It’s actually around purchase power. If wages and incomes stay up to date with inflation, people have the purchase power to be able to buy the things they want.

“They’re working numerous jobs and they’re not getting ahead. So, they are removing themselves from the institutions that most people used to belong to: the sports club, the RSA, the Working Men’s Club. Because you can’t afford it.”

Her own backstory: child of a Samoan immigrant family; a law degree from the University of Auckland earned while a student mother to a growing family which numbers eight children; specialist tax lawyer at Inland Revenue, former tax adviser to National Revenue ministers Michael Woodhouse and Judith Collins – before she moved into politics.

She is also a former Cabinet Minister appointed by Labour leader Chris Hipkins to a range of portfolios in 2023 following his own accession to the prime ministership.

Labour is rolling Edmonds out across the country – particularly in Auckland. She has been hosted in many of that city’s boardrooms since first being appointed to the Shadow Finance portfolio after former Labour Finance Minister Grant Robertson retired from politics. The directorate circuit finds her straightforward.

Hipkins has rightly been criticised for being slow to roll out election policies. National’s “no new taxes” campaign has achieved cut-through in the meantime. Labour unexpectedly scored a recent poll slump.

Labour finally rolled out its fiscal strategy a fortnight ago, giving Edmonds a more solid basis to take the economic battle to Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

Among the aims: reach Budget surplus by 2029-30; aim to reduce net debt to 20% of GDP over time and invest in initiatives that support a growing economy; keep core Crown Expenditure and revenue around 33% of GDP; set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office to scrutinise government finances and election commitments; and give the Reserve Bank its dual mandate back so it considers price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

Both Edmonds and Willis are waiting for the release of the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2026 (PREFU) on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, before putting the finishing touches on policies.

All this is quite academic in a political system where post-election horse trading determines a new government’s agenda.

Edmonds indicates that if she becomes finance minister in a Hipkins-led government she will use transfers and targeted subsidies as a fast‑acting salve for stressed households. This plays out in the party’s plan to introduce fare caps for public transport and to get costs for doctor’s visits down.

At the election summit she stressed, “This is my 17th budget that I’ve had to analyse. I’ve been a tax practitioner for over a decade. I know how to do that stuff. I am fiscally responsible.”

For boardrooms and investors, that matters.

On productivity, Edmonds rattled off the familiar list: geography, small market, capital access, education, and weak uptake of tech and R&D.

Where she adds some cut‑through is on competition and small business. If you can’t conjure up a third big supermarket chain, she says, stop pretending it will appear and back the smaller independents who are still fighting.

She also wants a sharper focus on small‑business tax and compliance settings: “If 97% of our firms in New Zealand are small businesses, then we need to listen to them ...

“There was no debate between Chris Hipkins and I around small business policy and around repurposing investment boost. We spoke to small businesses, and this is one of the things they were telling us.

“The ability to immediately write off assets that you own under $10,000 straight away provides them with greater working capital in their profit tax period.”

That sly dig at National is deliberate. It signals that on small business, Edmonds regards herself as the architect.

Talk in political circles is that Edmonds has all the instincts to be a Labour finance minister in the mould of the late Sir Michael Cullen. Fiscally disciplined with an eye to the long term.

The problem Labour faces is one of trust.

Georgie Campbell’s death: Kiwi family launches charity to install safer cross-country horse jumps

New Zealand Herald September 11, 2026

Georgie Campbell, wife of Kiwi Olympian Jesse Campbell, died after suffering a rotational fall at the Bicton International Horse Trials in the UK in 2024. Photo / Instagram

After the tragic death of their daughter-in-law, Georgie Campbell, in a horse-riding accident, a Matamata couple is raising money to install safety equipment in cross-country jumps in the hope no other Kiwi family will have to endure the pain of losing a loved one.

It happened so quickly, the accident that ended Georgie Campbell’s life. Georgie’s husband, former Kiwi Olympic rider Jesse Campbell, was watching the love of his life charging around the cross-country course on her horse, Global Quest, at the Bicton International Horse Trials in Devon. Watching, too, was her mother, Debbie Strang, also an accomplished rider.

Without warning Global Quest collided with a jump, causing the horse to somersault in the air over the jump and crash down backwards on to Georgie underneath.

Jesse Campbell, watching in horror, ran across the course to his injured wife but there was nothing he could do to save her. She died at the scene from catastrophic head and internal injuries.

A Devon coroner would later rule that the 36-year-old’s death in May 2024 was the result of a “terrible, tragic accident involving a much-loved woman who died participating in the sport she loved”.

Now Jesse Campbell’s parents, Matamata couple Ezra and Craig, want to make sense of the family’s grief by ensuring no other New Zealand family has to endure the pain of loss from what they say could be a preventable accident.

They want to see safer frangible (collapsible) jumps fitted at equestrian centres throughout New Zealand to reduce the risk of rotational falls – when a horse somersaults or flips over after hitting a solid jump, often landing on the rider.

In July this year, two UK women died on the same day at separate events after suffering rotational falls. And earlier this year a young New Zealand rider suffered a concussion and a fractured pelvis from a rotational fall at the National Equestrian Centre at Taupō.

The Campbells have launched a charity, the All Together Safer NZ Eventing Charitable Trust (ATSE), to help fund Swedish-engineered MiMSafe clips to be fitted to jumps, starting with a $450,000 pilot scheme to install 80 frangible jumps at the National Equestrian Centre.

The MiMSafe clips fold the jump forward if it’s hit by the horse, helping to prevent deadly rotational falls. The horse might stumble but is likely to recover rather than somersaulting and landing on the rider.

ATSE’s pilot scheme at Taupō will also include tubbed plants, which help the horses (with monocular vision) to sight the jumps accurately; watering systems; the structure, or chassis, built beneath the jumps; security fencing; and equipment to install the jumps.

Rotational falls can occur at any level of cross-country eventing. Georgie was an experienced, top-level show rider before switching to eventing, representing the UK multiple times and competing in five-star events, the highest level, in the UK and Europe.

Jesse Campbell, 37, had not long returned from the Burghley Horse Trials in Lincolnshire when he spoke to the Herald from his home in Surrey this week. He remembers the moment of Georgie’s accident vividly. About to compete at Bicton himself, he was watching his wife on livestream when he saw Global Quest hit a solid jump, somersault into the air and land heavily on his back.

“I knew it was bad straight away.”

But he also remembers a happier moment, the day he met Georgie in 2017 at the Military Boekelo three-day event in Holland where they were both competing.

“We were at a barbecue ... and a very beautiful girl sat down next to me, and I thought, ‘I think I’ll marry this girl’ and that’s the way it came to pass.”

Campbell’s favourite photo of his wife was one taken on their wedding day in 2020, just four years before she died. Her smile, he says, would make him feel like he was the centre of the universe.

“She just had this incredible energy about her. People just gravitated towards her and she always had time for them. She was a very, very special person.”

Campbell wrote on Instagram after his wife’s death: “She would get as much joy from having a Greggs tea on the way home from the gallops as she would teaching a client in the pouring rain, or jumping and galloping around the biggest courses in the world.”

Being with horses helped him get through the tough weeks and months that lay ahead.

“They’re incredible animals,” he wrote, “kind, generous and very good at dealing with me being quite teary at times.”

He and Georgie were based at her family’s farm in Kent where they planned to build a top-class riding school, stables and arena. But there were too many memories; Georgie and her smile just around every corner.

“I didn’t really feel like doing that myself, you know, that was our dream.”

Seven months after his wife died, Campbell moved to a client’s property in Oxted, Surrey, and established an eventing yard.

He and Georgie’s sister, Jo Strang, founded the Georgie Campbell Foundation which aims to improve the safety of the sport and provide scholarships for up-and-coming riders. Campbell lists what the trustees will look for: riders with a strong work ethic, humble, a love of horses and talented. He’s effectively describing his late wife.

“What would a young Georgie need?” he says of the mentoring and support the scholarships will provide.

Campbell is proud of the efforts his parents are making to raise funds to improve cross-country safety in New Zealand in their daughter-in-law’s memory. He’d like to see more cross-country jumps designed so that frangible pins can be included on different styles.

“It’s important that when you have that moment of mistake or error from either party that it doesn’t result in a fatality.”

Ezra Campbell says safety equipment like frangible clips and inflatable air jackets are similar to airbags and seatbelts in a car. They won’t stop accidents occurring, but they will save lives.

At the time of Georgie’s death, the jump that caused her rotational fall could not be fitted with a frangible pin because of its design. Her accident was witnessed by a European course designer who has since worked closely with the Swedish manufacturers of MiMSafe to work out how to incorporate the frangible clips into solid jumps involving big logs and “table tops”.

As a result, a combination of science, design and technology will help mitigate the risk.

“I know that risk is part of sport but preventable risk never should be,” Ezra Campbell says. She still mourns the loss of her daughter-in-law, describing Georgie as “the most gorgeous person”.

The couple flew to the UK to watch their son compete in the Burghley Horse Trials in September 2024, where he blew a kiss to the sky after finishing the course.

A woman introduced herself to the Campbells, telling them she was at Bicton the day Georgie died. The woman told them she had watched Georgie walk hand-in-hand with Jesse to the show jumping arena shortly before she was to compete.

She told Ezra: “They were watching the show jumping and just standing there hand in hand and I remember thinking ‘if I could have a smidgen of what those two have I’d be a very happy person.’”

Less than an hour later, Georgie was gone.

Last year Jesse was awarded an Against the Odds award by Equestrian Sport New Zealand at its gala dinner in Parliament House to celebrate the organisation’s 75th anniversary. The Campbells flew to Wellington to accept the award on their son’s behalf.

“It was a very brave thing for Equestrian Sport New Zealand to do,” Ezra Campbell says, “because it was a night of celebration for them and here was this award which came about because of how Jesse had picked up and kept going, and kept the sport in a positive light.”

That night the couple talked to a course designer about safety on cross-country courses. They soon realised that the equestrian world wanted and needed more frangible pins but lack of funding was an issue.

The Campbells decided to launch a charity to fix that problem. To date they’ve raised $115,000 towards the $450,000 target, launching a Givealittle page to help boost funds.

After Taupō, they want to see more frangible clips incorporated into all cross-country courses throughout New Zealand to protect riders.

Ezra Campbell wants young Kiwi riders at all levels of eventing not to have to worry about whether or not a jump is safe.

“Their whole concentration should be their pony or their horse. It’s about us, the parents, the volunteers, the organisers. We’re the ones who have to be looking at what we can do better with safety.”

Horses, too, can be injured or killed from rotational falls although Global Quest, the Irish horse ridden by Georgie on the day of her fall, was uninjured. The horse competed this month at the Burghley Horse Trials, ridden by top New Zealander eventer Tim Price as a tribute to his late friend.

Equestrian Sports New Zealand CEO Julian Bowden described Georgie’s accident as an “absolute tragedy” that had led to significant changes in the way cross-country fences are designed and built.

“There is an absolute focus on safety.”

The Federation Equestre Internationale, the international governing body for equestrian sports, has led the way with ongoing developments around fence design and building techniques to improve safety for both horses and athletes, he says.

Dame Catriona Williams understands better than most the dangers of a horse hitting a non-frangible jump at speed. She’s spent the past 24 years in a wheelchair after suffering a rotational fall at the Kihikihi Horse Trails in Hamilton in 2002. Her horse cartwheeled over a fence, causing Williams, now a tetraplegic, to break her neck. She was 31 at the time.

Williams, 55, says she is “so proud” of the Campbells and the effort they have put into making cross-country events safer. She’s now patron of the Campbell’s charitable trust, and Auckland businesswoman Anna Mowbray is an ambassador.

“If these jumps had had the frangible pins, there’s a very high chance that I wouldn’t be sitting in a wheelchair.”

Williams is the first to support riders who want the challenge of cross-country riding, part of a three-day event that includes dressage in an arena and show jumping.

Speed and bravery is involved, something Kiwi riders are renowned for. She points to Olympic medal earners Mark Todd, Blyth Tait, Andrew Nicholson and Vaughn Jefferis.

But she also wants young riders coming up through the ranks to be safer with the installation of frangible jumps.

“It’s not taking away the challenge, but it’s making the sport safer.”

Young Auckland event rider Mackenzie Marlo, 21, agrees, saying that although some MiMSafe clips have already been installed at various cross-country courses she has ridden in New Zealand she’d like to see more.

Marlo has activated MiMSafe clips a few times which means her horse has hit the top of the jump. She hasn’t suffered a bad accident but she’s aware of others who have.

She’s well aware of the ongoing sadness around Georgie’s accident, having spent eight weeks on work experience at Jesse Campbell’s eventing yard in Surrey last year.

“I think there are always risks with the sport that we do, but it’s really exciting now that there is technology to potentially minimise these risks to some degree.”

In the past five years, equestrian-related claims have cost ACC nearly $109 million. Around 3300 claims are made each year and nearly 90% of those are women. One in three claims involves a rider between the age of 10 and 19 years.

In the first six months of 2026, ACC received 1809 new claims and handled 3171 active claims. Costs to July were more than $12m which did not include bulk-funded services, including ambulances and acute treatment in public hospitals. (ACC’s bulk-funding costs last year for all injury claims, not just horse riding, was more than $1 billion.)

Williams is an advocate of anything that will make the sport safer, including air vests, with a lanyard attached to the saddle so that if a rider falls, the vest will automatically inflate.

Both the frangible pins and the air vests are examples of how technology can help make the sport safer, she says.

“Why would you not have frangible pins? They’ve been developed, it’s been proven ... get behind it and back it. They weren’t around when I had my accident.”

Williams still has horses in her life because her husband Sam runs horse-breeding stud Little Avondale in Masterton. But she still needs a carer to get her out of bed, toileted, showered and dressed every day.

“What is the cost to the Government because I’m in a wheelchair or someone else is in a wheelchair?”

She and a group of friends launched the CatWalk Spinal Cord Injury Trust after her accident, partnering with the University of Auckland. To date the trust has raised more than $28m towards spinal cord injury research. And it’s raised a further $8.5m towards a target of $10.5m for the CatWalk Cure Program, a collaboration of international research involving five different areas of cure for spinal injury.

On December 30 this year, Williams will set off on a mammoth 4800km handcycle journey across the US from Carlsbad, California, to Jacksonville, Florida, to raise funds for spinal cord injury research.

Williams says she would give anything to be able to stand up and dance again with Sam. The research into cures might not benefit her in time, she says, but it will benefit others in wheelchairs and with neurological conditions.

Jane Phare is a senior journalist based in Auckland. Her roles at the Herald have included assistant editor of NZ Herald, editor of the Weekend Herald, founding editor of Viva, features editor and deputy print editor.

Officials warned intervention in Fonterra climate case could hurt investor confidence

New Zealand Herald September 11, 2026

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith who led the changes to the climate change law and Mike Smith (insert).

Officials warned the Government that prematurely intervening in a high-profile climate change court case to protect high-emitting corporates could damage confidence to invest in New Zealand.

That case – taken by activist Mike Smith against a slew of companies including Fonterra and Z Energy – has been at the centre of controversy after revelations the Prime Minister’s office incorrectly omitted lobbying documents issued on behalf of the two corporates in an Official Information Act request.

Smith’s 2019 case was initially thrown out – but when the Supreme Court in 2024 determined it could go ahead, official documents released by the Prime Minister’s department illustrate how officials and corporates went into overdrive brainstorming what to do next.

The primary concern, as revealed by the official documents, was whether Smith’s case would affect business confidence. But these documents also reveal warnings from officials that by intervening too early, they too risked spooking investors.

While the defendants wrote to the Government expressing concerns the case would affect confidence, officials struggled to find evidence there was a widespread impact.

Options of how to respond to Smith’s revived case included a world-first statutory block using rare retrospective legislation, resourcing officials to investigate if business confidence was really at stake and holding fire until the court case had played out.

The Government last month passed legislation to prevent replications of cases like Smith’s. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said such a claim “risks developing a new regime that contradicts the framework Parliament has already enacted”, meaning the primary tools for responding to climate change are those of Parliament, such as successive emissions budgets and reductions plans, and the country’s Emissions Trading Schemes.

The statutory bar was never implemented - instead this legislation stopped Smith’s case from proceeding via the Supreme Court.

“The courts are not the right place to resolve claims of harm from climate change, and tort law is not well-suited to respond to a problem like climate change, which involves a range of complex environmental, economic and social factors,” Goldsmith said.

Goldsmith’s comments followed lengthy deliberation on how to respond to Smith’s case once the Supreme Court had decided to honour it. Those fresh official documents show in 2024, then Attorney General Judith Collins, had investigated whether the Government could instigate a rare statutory block.

In October last year, Z Energy requested a five-minister meeting with its chief executive Lindis Jones, Fonterra boss Miles Hurrell and Genesis boss Malcolm Johns.

“The purpose of this meeting is to discuss the Smith v Fonterra litigation and to share our collective concerns regarding its potential impact on investor confidence and broader economic implications.”

From the documents supplied, there is no indication this meeting went ahead.

Smith wrote to Luxon in May this year - days after the first media reports revealed discrepancy over what documents Luxon’s office could find regarding the lobbying meeting. Smith said he did not receive a response. In that email, he sought an “urgent opportunity” to meet.

“The prospect of this case being barred has real consequences for my whenua and moana, including places of customary, cultural, historical, food-gathering and spiritual significance to my whānau,” Smith said in his email, seen by the Herald.

“The impacts of climate change are already affecting our lands and our livelihoods. Removing the pathway for me to seek accountability and protection would deepen the sense that those most affected are left without meaningful recourse.”

Officials said New Zealand would be the first jurisdiction to legislate a block of this nature and warned overriding court processes this way could affect the confidence of investors who “rely on strong and stable domestic processes to protect their investments”.

Although this particular instance of intervention “would likely be viewed by investors as favourable” because it would “remove a potential source of civil liability for businesses”, repeated interjections of this nature “could create a perception that the Government is willing to intervene in court decisions and effectively overturn them”.

The primary concern at this time appeared to be business confidence and the impact on overseas investors. Yet, officials said “we do not have evidence of wider industry uncertainty” beyond the defendants and they did not know whether the Supreme Court decision had affected wider business confidence.

Goldsmith responded to Collins via a letter, saying a statutory bar raised “important legal policy questions” about the rights of private citizens in the courts. Goldsmith’s officials warned “it could be premature to act” before the court had the chance to hear substantive arguments given “most negligence claims have been unsuccessful”.

“A statutory bar raises significant policy questions about the rights of private citizens, and officials anticipate that the lead agency will need to engage with a range of stakeholders during the policy process to help determine what is fair.

“The appearance of intervening so early to alter substantive legal rights in favour of one set of litigants over another could itself undermine certainty in the law.”

Goldsmith’s correspondence noted retrospective legislation would be needed to ensure the current case was not heard – but Parliament’s legislative design experts only advise using such legislation in “narrowly defined circumstances”.

“It would need to be clearly justified in the public interest and impair the rights of litigants no more than is reasonably necessary to serve that interest.”

Smith told the Herald the journey through the courts had been a “roller coaster” including disappointment over the case initially being struck out and excitement over the Supreme Court’s overturning.

“That has been up and down. What we expect a responsible Government to be doing is leaning into the issues of climate change, not trying to protect the corporates,” Smith said.

“They need to be finding ways to reduce our emissions. We would all save ourselves a lot of trouble if they just faced the future.”

Labour has committed to repealing Goldsmith’s legislation, which had halted Smith’s legal case.

“Then it would be on again. I am just waiting to see what happens after the election.”

Officials also urged the Government to engage with Māori on this issue – which was one where Māori groups had “expressed considerable interest”. Pushing on with a block could “raise relationship risks”.

“Usual practice is to engage with Māori in relation to climate change policy changes, especially on an issue such as this one, which may have significant implications.”

Julia Gabel is a Wellington-based political reporter. She joined the Herald in 2020 and has most recently focused on data journalism.

He’s one of pop’s great technological disruptors. But the AI era fills him with anxiety

Sydney Morning Herald September 12, 2026

A hero to the likes of Mac DeMarco and Harry Styles, 79-year-old Japanese pop pioneer Haruomi Hosono returns with a new album.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In the studio of the 79-year-old Japanese pop icon Haruomi Hosono is a bust of Ludwig van Beethoven, some flowers and a small bowl of water. He pulled the bust out of storage when it came time to record the track Figlio Perduto for his new album Yours Sincerely, his first collection of new music in seven years.

Hosono’s 23rd studio album features gently soothing electronics and acoustic guitar that feels whimsically reflective, like he’s reaching for his inner child late in life. “Maybe because of my age I might have gone back to being a child. I do have quite a lot of those memories from my childhood,” says Hosono, contemplating the idea.

“Rather than being stories of the past, they are still continuing even now. For example, Beethoven has been glaring at me since I was a child … Now it’s sitting here and I’m praying to it. Until then I had left it alone because I was a bit scared.”

Summing up Hosono’s career is almost impossible. His early work in the band Happy End (1969-1972), then as a solo artist on his debut Hosono House (1973), is frequently cited as a touchstone by indie artists, most notably the similarly prolific Mac DeMarco (the title of Harry Styles’ Grammy-winning album Harry’s House was a homage, too). His later outfit Yellow Magic Orchestra is one of the most influential synth-pop groups of all time.

But if there’s one consistent thread, it can be found on Figlio Perduto, a cover in Japanese of a track by Sarah Brightman that sets an Italian translation of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe’s poem Erlkonig to Beethoven’s Symphony No. 7.

This iterative, memetic layering of cultures, often with technology, has been a through line of Hosono’s entire career. Born in 1947, Hosono grew up in post-WWII Japan, after nuclear devastation in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, when US popular culture worked its way off military bases and into Japanese life.

“My mother is no longer with us; it’s been about five or six years now. She really loved Hollywood movies and music, and I was heavily influenced by that. From a young age she would play movie soundtracks for me. Her idol was Fred Astaire. I watched those movies a lot as I grew older. My father probably liked it, too; he even said he wanted to be a dancer because of my mother’s influence. That’s the kind of person my mother was. I’m very grateful,” says Hosono.

Happy End was a Japanese approximation of American roots rock. Next, as a solo artist, Hosono began a reflexive reappropriation of 1950s exotica records on his albums Tropical Dandy, Bon Voyage co. and Paraiso, the album on which he first worked with Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi. The three men became Yellow Magic Orchestra, Japan’s most influential band, whose first major hit in 1978 was a subversive synth-pop cover reclaiming the “oriental” melody of the 1959 exotica recording Firecracker by Martin Denny.

Hosono pioneered the use of electronic instruments with his YMO bandmates – each hugely influential solo musicians, producers, session musicians and composers in their own right – and Japanese popular music became increasingly dominated by electronic compositions in the wake of YMO’s peak 1970s and 1980s popularity. Some middle-aged Japanese businessmen still sport the group’s “techno cut” undercut hairstyle.

The first record Hosono bought as a boy was a version of Mon Oncle by the Japanese singer Jun Nakajima, taken from Jacques Tati’s film of the same name. The film is a comedic account of one man’s struggle at confronting modernity and technology – a prophetic first purchase for a pioneering technologist with his own questions about today’s technological advancements.

“For Jacques Tati I think there was some irony in how things would break down, but now we have entered an era where it is no longer a carefree matter. After all, with the Industrial Revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries, moving into the 20th century from the age of oil, machines began to work so that human workers didn’t have to use their muscles,” says Hosono.

“But now we’ve stopped using our heads, too. We don’t use our brain muscles because AI does it for us. What will happen to us before long? It is an era filled with anxiety that our heads might become completely empty.”

It’s no surprise, then, that Yours Sincerely finds Hosono turning to matters of the soul and the natural world. Rojiura (Walking Vibration) is a new version of a track originally recorded for the 2006 television drama Walkers, about a group of adults undertaking Ohenro – the 88-temple, esoteric Buddhist pilgrimage around Shikoku island. (This elicits his wide-eyed approval when I share that I completed Ohenro in 2023, with YMO records stuffed in my backpack, and he asks me to listen to Rojiura if I ever walk the trail again.)

Hosono attended an Anglican school but has been interested in Buddhism since reading the popular Chinese story Journey to the West as a boy. “I’ve always loved stories about various gods,” he says.

Yours Sincerely’s guiding principle is laid out on its opening track, Note of Mothership – a gently bubbling acknowledgment of the maternal force Hosono believes envelopes the planet. It’s a concept informed in part by an ongoing interest in the British chemist James Lovelock, who, along with the microbiologist Lynn Margulis, developed the Gaia theory in the 1970s. The theory posited that Earth is a self-regulating superorganism composed of both living organisms and their inorganic surroundings.

“Within [the Gaia hypothesis] there is an idea called ‘Daisyworld’. Daisies of various colours bloom on Earth. Why are there so many colours? If it were just a single colour, light would concentrate and the climate wouldn’t be right, which is why they are so diverse,” says Hosono. “Ever since then I’ve always loved that [maternal] world-view.”

Yours Sincerely is one of those late-career marvels in which all of an artist’s genre experiments and sonic excursions coalesce into a perfect jewel, no longer scattered across albums but contained here as a snapshot of their life and art. Still, even the most influential musicians get cold feet about their creations.

“When I made it I liked it myself but I was anxious about what other people would think,” says Hosono. “However, now, I feel it’s fine, and that everyone will probably like it, too.”

Haruomi Hosono’s Yours Sincerely is out now.

‘Is this something I want?’: Tove Lo, pop’s messy genius, ponders motherhood and domesticity

Sydney Morning Herald September 12, 2026

The Swedish star’s new album joins a canon of 30-something Millennial pop that contemplates maternal anxiety.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

It took a decade, but the world finally caught up with Tove Lo. For years, the Swedish musician has been pop’s professor of provocation, its scholar of squalor, its expert in excess, carving out a niche of gorgeously explicit filth with breakthrough albums like Lady Wood and Blue Lips (its title a feminine take on “blue balls”) that spun art from the personal chaos of drugs, drinking and wanton sex.

And then Charli XCX’s Brat Summer happened, sending messiness mainstream and making the internet’s prevailing “clean-girl aesthetic” a relic of a naive age. In a culture where electroclash is the defining influence (again), Slayyyter is pop’s new trashbag star, and hedonism is celebrated, it seems the world is finally vibing with ideas Lo has been playing with all along. Does it feel that way for her?

“Um … it kind of does,” she laughs coyly. “It’s nice to get to sing about these things without needing to defend myself any more.

“It’s in the ether right now. I don’t know if it has to do with female artists taking control of their own narrative, or if it’s just the state of the world. Whenever our feelings are in a pressure cooker for too long, they tend to explode, and I think that’s what’s happened.”

Few modern pop stars have turned sex into such a vital driver of their artistic process as Lo. Why is it so creatively inspiring?

“It’s something I’ve been trying to put my finger on – if it’s me just being a sexual person, or if it’s just the fact I do think music and sex have always gone hand in hand for me,” she says. “Maybe it’s because it comes from the body and it’s an instinctual form of expression; singing and dancing and working with emotions and everything that’s running through your body naturally makes it sexual.”

She grew up in the northern suburbs of Stockholm, among family and friends who were progressive and open-minded. “It never occurred to me that saying I’m a feminist and I’m bi and being sexual were political. To me, that was just the baseline of what everyone should be. But when I started touring the world and going to places where that wasn’t the baseline, I realised, oh, maybe it is political.

“But in terms of how I choose to express myself – the bluntness, directness, and it being provocative to some people – I just think it feels good to express desire without being judged. Or even if you do get judged, just having the freedom to play with that anyway.”

Lo is speaking from her home in Los Angeles, following a brief stint in Stockholm where she’s been rehearsing for an upcoming world tour around her new album, Estrus. The biological reference behind the title is to a female animal “in heat” and ready to procreate.

It’s funny, and perhaps typically defiant, that just when the world has caught on to her trashy wavelength, Lo is pivoting. On Estrus, the pop star – on the verge of turning 39 – is singing about settling down and contemplating the logistics of having a child.

“I’m thinking about these things, but I’m in no way ready for it,” Lo explains. “I feel I’m being told by the outside world that I’m a grown woman now and I’m supposed to set roots and settle down and act accordingly and be responsible and have answers for everything, and I’m just not there at all. I’m still quite messy, and it’s the only thing I’m good at.”

Inspired by her long-term relationship with husband Charlie Twaddle – a Kiwi producer and creative director she married in 2020 – the album finds Lo contemplating domestic malaise, and the expectations around 30-something women, with her usual brand of outrageous humour. On highlight I’m the Cake, her pent-up desire explodes to the point she’s yelling at (presumably) her husband for taking for granted what he’s got at home: “Babe, I’m a pop star, did you just forget?” she sings with carnal frustration.

She’s called Estrus her “Peter Pan record” – driven by a desire to never grow up, but feeling the burden that she might have to. “Being in a relationship for this long and having found someone I want to be with for the rest of my life is quite a new feeling for me in terms of my creativity. But I’m still messy and I party too much and I say the wrong thing a lot. So there’s some growth but this album is thinking about, ‘Is this even something I want? And what does growth look like when I still want to be me and I don’t really want to change?’ ” Lo ponders with a laugh.

The album closes with Source of Life (“the place between my thighs”), a moving song where Lo explores her anxiety about motherhood. As a man, I’m self-conscious about asking Lo to discuss her apprehension about something that obviously doesn’t affect us in the same social, physical or biological way – so, instead, I tell her that before I had two kids, I was so nervous about becoming a parent that I once Googled “I regret having children” just to see how many search results came up. It wasn’t many, which was very reassuring.

Lo bursts into laughter. “I mean, [parenting] does feel like the ‘final boss’ of adventures, right? So I am very curious about it. But, for me, I have a hard time picturing it. I’ve never dreamt about it, it’s never been something I’ve wanted, but now my body is telling me ‘It’s time!’ and my brain is like, ‘No!’ So I’m in that place … but also, I have said that if my husband could get pregnant, we probably would have a few kids by now. I think there’s a toll on the body that’s also clearly challenging for me. But everyone seems to be doing it, so I don’t know!”

Lo had already explored the idea on Suburbia, the conflicted centrepiece from her last album, 2022’s Dirt Femme. It’s a song that presaged the current wave of Millennial pop stars exploring their mixed feelings around impending motherhood, from Charli XCX and Taylor Swift to Carly Rae Jepsen and Robyn.

“It’s cool to see all my peers working through this, and no one’s shying away from talking about something that wasn’t that common to sing about in pop. Because I remember when I sang about it on Suburbia, I got a lot of different reactions – there was a lot of ‘oh my God, I relate to this so hard’, but also a lot of ‘how the f--- can you talk like this, you’re such a selfish bitch’,” Lo recalls drolly.

“Women speaking about struggling with this picture of motherhood as only a positive seems to really trigger something in people. So I love that the topic is just out there, and in pop as well. It’s really beautiful to see.”

Tove Lo’s new album Estrus is out on September 18. She will perform at Brisbane’s Fortitude Music Hall on March 1, Melbourne’s MCA on March 3, Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion on March 5, and Perth’s Ice Cream Factory on March 7.

‘It’s hard to tell anyone’: The debilitating, hidden injury affecting thousands of Australians

Sydney Morning Herald September 12, 2026

From devastated careers and struggles to recognise a friend to volcanic rage or abusive behaviour: the fallout from a traumatic brain injury is often invisible to outsiders.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Early one Saturday morning in July, 2021, Gold Coast triathlete Alexa Leary set off on a training ride with a group of elite cyclists in the hills behind Noosa, on Queensland’s Sunshine Coast. The route was demanding; an undulating 90-kilometre ride, including a 2.5-kilometre climb to the summit of a local landmark called Black Mountain. Her father, Russell, would tag along as a support rider. Her fellow cyclists had a reputation for riding fast and even for being a little reckless. But Leary, who was 19, had ridden the route before and was a fierce competitor: two years prior, she had won silver at the Women’s Under 18-19 World Triathlon finals in Switzerland in 2019 and she had her sights set on the Paris Olympics.

Leary kept pace with the group up Black Mountain and down the other side, then on to the top of the next hill, just above Cootharaba. Exhilarated, she texted Russell, who had fallen behind. “I made it with them,” she wrote. He replied: “Great effort. The universe is changing, keep trusting it.”

Leary then began her descent, pushing herself to stay with the group. She was charging downhill at 75 kilometres per hour when, in a split-second miscalculation, she clipped the wheel of the rider in front. She immediately catapulted over the handlebars before landing on the right side of her head, causing her helmet to fly off. She then flipped, slamming the left side of her head onto the bitumen with a cracking sound so loud that a fellow rider later likened it to a tree splitting.

When Russell arrived at the scene, some 30 minutes later, he saw a crowd of people, and two ambulances. He had no idea who was injured. As he approached, one of the paramedics remarked, “They don’t think she’s going to make it.” It wasn’t until he got closer that he saw it was his daughter. “She was unconscious, her eyes were rolled back,” he tells me. “There was blood everywhere, and her knee was ripped to pieces.”

Alexa was rushed to Sunshine Coast University Hospital, where she was put in the ICU. By the time her parents made it to the hospital, the pressure on her brain was already so great that, as Russell remembers it, “her eyes were bulging out of her head.” The doctors told Russell and his wife Belinda that their daughter had suffered what was called a TBI – a traumatic brain injury. It was so severe that if she survived, she would be a vegetable, unable to walk or talk.

Leary was placed in an induced coma and airlifted to Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital. In order to relieve the pressure on her brain, part of her skull was removed and placed in a freezer in the basement. (Unrestrained, Leary’s swollen brain bulged 20 millimetres outside her head.) Two weeks later, she emerged from the coma. Three months of rehab lay ahead, during which Leary, with the aid of doctors and therapists, would relearn the rudiments of human functioning, from how to chew, swallow and communicate, to the difference between a knife and fork and how to use them. After 111 days, she walked out of the hospital, against all the odds, alive and breathing.

Her family was traumatised, but Leary had survived. In November 2021, as a celebration, her parents took her to a cafe in Noosa for her favourite treat, an iced coffee. She took one sip, curled up her nose and told the cafe owner it was “shit”. Leary could be moody and intense, but she had never been rude or abusive. But other, more bizarre behaviours would follow. Soon after the cafe incident, Leary’s grandmother, Shirley, paid a visit. The minute Shirley walked through the door, Leary walked up and grabbed her breasts. She did the same thing with a waitress on a trip to Sydney. “I was grabbing random ladies’ boobs,” she tells me. “I just couldn’t control it.”

Leary’s parents would try to explain that their daughter had a brain injury, but strangers found it hard to reconcile. Leary looked fine. Her physical scars had healed. For all intents and purposes, she was back to her old self. But, as was becoming apparent, her brain was full of broken wiring. The fragile snow-dome of her mind had been shaken violently and beyond repair, with consequences that were both mysterious and terrifying.

Brains in museums often look rubbery and plasticised, but they are in fact, surprisingly squishy, with a consistency that has been likened to soft tofu or custard. The average specimen weighs 1.5 kilograms and is thought to contain about 88 billion neurons, including galaxies of axons and synapses, all variously connected by electrical signals and neurotransmitters. Different parts of it do different things, from the temporal lobes, which are located behind the ears, near the temple, and play a role in hearing and language, to the frontal lobes, which are involved in problem-solving, abstract thinking and how we act upon our emotions and impulses.

Roughly the size of two clenched fists, your brain floats in a sea of cerebrospinal fluid housed in a helmet of bone, up to 10 millimetres thick in places, otherwise known as your skull. If you get hit hard in the head, your brain can bounce around inside your skull, or twist and ricochet, causing the pathways between brain cells to tear and snap and your brain to start bleeding. This is followed by a secondary trauma, known as a neurotoxic cascade, when the injured neurons secrete free radicals and glutamate that further kill healthy cells.

“No traumatic brain injury is the same,” says Melinda Fitzgerald, deputy vice-chancellor (research) at Curtin University and CEO of Connectivity Traumatic Brain Injury Australia, a not-for-profit that advocates for people with TBIs and supports research. “The damage depends on where you’re hit and how hard, and everyone responds differently.”

TBIs are on the rise. A 2022 report from the Lancet Neurology Commission estimated that 55 million people worldwide live with a TBI and described it as a major global health problem. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 450,000 Australians have brain injury: TBIs account for 142,000 hospitalisations annually, placing significant strain on emergency departments. Most are caused by falls, car crashes, sports injuries and assaults. The accidents that occasion TBIs tend to be extraordinarily violent: one man I spoke to for this story was driving at night on a lonely stretch of highway when he hit a bull. The animal came straight through the windscreen, colliding with his face. “My doctor told me that I didn’t so much as break the bones in my face as totally shatter everything.”

Fortunately, victims rarely, if ever, remember what happened. Invariably, large chunks of their memory are erased. In Leary’s case, five years of her life prior to her accident were wiped clean. When she woke up, she didn’t recognise her mother – “I thought she was Dad’s best friend” – or her longtime boyfriend. “I had to look at photos on my phone to fill in the blanks, but I couldn’t date him any more because I felt I didn’t know who he was.” Leary has a love-heart tattoo on her wrist and a lightning bolt on her ankle, but she couldn’t remember how they got there. “My parents told me I got them with my best friend.”

TBIs commonly affect the brain’s processing speed. “When I woke up in the ICU, my husband, Eric, was talking to me, saying, ‘It’s Eric, your husband,’ over and over,” says Eloise Zoppos, a 39-year-old researcher in Melbourne, who was struck by a car during her morning walk in 2024. “But he seemed to be talking incredibly fast and I couldn’t understand why. In fact, as I found out later, he was talking very slowly, but my processing speed had been so damaged.”

Zoppos, who has soft brown eyes and dark, straight, shoulder-length hair, underwent several marathon surgeries and was in a coma for two weeks. “Eric was told that every minute I was alive was a win.” Today, her main challenge is cognitive fatigue. “It’s not the same as simply being tired,” she tells me. “Because of my injury, my brain has to work harder to compensate for deficits. This means I need an extremely high level of sleep and rest every day to even be able to do simple tasks and activities. Without adequate sleep, I can have trouble concentrating, mix up my words, forget words, slump, feel physically weak, forget to eat and drink, and drop things. I can have seizures. I’m even more sensitive to bright lights and loud sounds.”

She can no longer work or socialise as much as she used to. “And if I do, it takes meticulous planning so that the days immediately before and after are extremely quiet to allow for more sleep.” She doesn’t drive long distances or at night, watch much TV (it’s too stimulating), or read to or play with her two young children. “My cognitive fatigue is so debilitating that it feels like my family’s entire life revolves around managing it, and to me, it can feel like it casts a fog over almost every aspect of our lives.” And yet no one, save for her close friends and family, knows what she is going through because, as she puts it, “a TBI is invisible”.

Indeed, while TBIs cause a bizarre range of symptoms – from volcanic rage to giggling fits – the injury itself remains hidden. This can have its advantages, says Zoppos. “It means that I can decide how much of my injury I want to share with others.” Some people with TBIs carry cards in their wallet explaining their disability to strangers, and asking that they speak slowly and remain patient. Others prefer to disclose nothing: “It’s hard to tell anyone that you’ve had brain injury because you have to expect that you’ll never have a job again,” says Ian Lacy, who was working as a strategy consultant with Citibank when he was involved in a life-altering car crash in Queensland in 2005. “I was employed by Fortune 500 companies to tell them where to take their business. But would you like someone with a brain injury giving you advice about what to do with your business?”

On the other hand, not sharing your condition makes it hard for strangers to understand or empathise. This becomes especially problematic when the TBI has caused behavioural changes. According to studies from the UK, between 50 and 70 per cent of people with a TBI experience personality changes. Some of these can seem relatively benign. “Before my accident, I was a serious person,” says Rosey Morrow, a former journalist who was hit by a car in Sydney in 2016. “Now sometimes I’ll get the giggles and I can’t stop. I’ll laugh at stuff other people don’t find funny at all, but I just find it hilarious.”

But most people with TBIs, and their carers, report that the personality changes are negative. People can become more self-centred, narcissistic, colder to loved ones or less affectionate. Disinhibition is common, especially with people who damage their prefrontal cortex, the region sitting directly behind your forehead, which governs, among other things, impulse control. When Alexa Leary’s skull hit the tarmac at 75 kilometres per hour, one of the things it obliterated was her social filter. She would tell people in the street that they were ugly. If she didn’t like their outfits, she would tell them they “should go home and change”. If she didn’t like a meal, she would throw it back at the staff. If her parents were present, they would try to explain, to make excuses and smooth things over. If they weren’t, their daughter was on her own.

At the same time, her social world steadily shrunk. “If my friends said one word to me [that she found annoying], I’d say, ‘You’re a c---!’ ” says Leary. “I lost a lot of friends that way.” Those close to a person with a TBI – including family members – can find it hard to accept that the person they knew before the accident no longer exists. After a time, even Leary’s best friend – the girl with whom she’d got her wrist and ankle tattoos – stopped inviting her out. “I would see her on social media saying, ‘Hanging out with friends’, and it broke me,” says Leary. “I’d unfollow her, but then refollow her and get hurt all over again.”

Such social isolation is both a by-product and a cause of TBIs. “When people get isolated, they’re more prone to develop drug and alcohol problems,” says Adam Schickerling, acting CEO of the brain injury organisation, Synapse. “And when they develop drug and alcohol problems, they’re more prone to violence, which is one of the main causes of TBIs.”

It’s no accident that a large number of prisoners are thought to have a brain injury – research in the US suggests it’s somewhere between 40 to 60 per cent. But inmates are unlikely to get a formal diagnosis, let alone treatment. “Most people go, ‘These people need a psychiatrist,’ but actually, their brains are broken.” Women subject to domestic violence are especially vulnerable. If a woman has been abused for an extended period and never been to hospital, “her rehab prospects are long gone,” says Schickerling. “That window has closed, and often she doesn’t even know.”

It’s tempting to see your brain as a central command, a kind of flight deck for our executive functions. But the brain is also the seat of our identity. Somewhere in that ball of gluggy mush is a matrix of memories, beliefs, inclinations and values, all mediated, in ways we are barely aware of, by raw genetics and the passage of time. A study published in the journal Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience in 2021 suggests that much of our identity, that ineffable sense of self, may be located in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex, a small region at the very bottom of the frontal lobe, behind our eyes.

Some people with damage in and around this area report no longer fully recognising themselves. “Memories of my prior self feel complete but inaccessible,” writes Bruce Powell, a former doctor who sustained a TBI in 2018 and now blogs extensively about the condition. “I know who I was, but I do not feel like him any more.” This is not “a change in personality”, he adds, “but the traumatic termination of one life, reincarnated as another”.

Tall and beefy, with thick, snowy-grey hair, Powell, who is 59, lives in Perth with his wife, Anita. He was taking part in a bicycle race on the Great Ocean Road (bicycles feature prominently in TBIs) when he collided head-first, at 65 kilometres per hour, with a metal road sign. “I hit the pole so hard that it bent in half,” he tells me.

Before his accident, he was Western Australia’s director of organ and tissue donation, a highly experienced anaesthetist and head of department in the intensive-care unit in Rockingham hospital, south of Perth. All that was taken from him in a split second: his injury meant he could no longer practise medicine. It was like the loss of a loved one and has involved a similar mourning process. He cites “acceptance” – the last of the five stages of grief, according to Swiss-born psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross – as being particularly important. “We don’t get to choose when that acceptance comes,” he says, “nor any of the other stages.”

Unlike some of those with severe TBI, Powell is aware of how much he has lost. But this “insight”, as it’s often referred to, is a mixed blessing. “The person becomes a voyeur of their own decline,” as he puts it. “With insight, the comparison between past and present is relentless. At times, it makes life intolerable.” As part of rebuilding a new identity and direction, Powell has become an ambassador for Headway, a UK-based TBI association, and serves as an adviser on the brain injury unit at Fiona Stanley Hospital in Fremantle. The result is someone who looks much like his former self, but isn’t.

Nonetheless, insight has implications for recovery. “People’s chances of recovery depend on how much self-awareness they have,” says Connectivity’s Melinda Fitzgerald. “If they themselves can tell they aren’t like they used to be, they will be more open to therapies.”

Treatments for TBI have remained largely unchanged for years. (The main advances have been in diagnosis, where the use of CT scans and MRI has been replaced by testing for blood-based biomarkers, including a chemical called GFAP, which is released by damaged brain cells.) Standard rehabilitation includes speech-work, to increase clarity and word-finding abilities, and memory exercises, such as matching symbols in a collection of different shapes.

Group therapy is also popular. After her accident, Rosey Morrow – she of the giggling fits – took part in regular group therapy, where the participants would give an outline of newspaper articles they had read and answer questions about it. One of Morrow’s issues in the early stages was “cognitive communication disorder”, aka losing her train of thought. In response, she would shut her eyes to reduce visual stimuli and sometimes the thought would come back. Now she simply tells people, “I’ve lost my train of thought – what were we saying?”

Such coping mechanisms are common. Alexa Leary learnt to tap her chest, like a drum, whenever she felt the urge to squeeze someone’s breasts. She also underwent hyperbaric oxygen therapy, photobiomodulation (which uses light on damaged tissue to accelerate healing), and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), which delivers magnetic pulses to damaged brain cells via a device worn on the scalp. In her recent book, Sink or Swim, Leary describes it as feeling “like a little woodpecker tapping at my head”.

One of Leary’s biggest issues was anger. She regularly hit her parents, who became covered in bruises. At one point, Russell had to hide in his bedroom while his daughter attempted to kick the door down. The wider family became afraid Leary would actually kill them. “Rage was a huge problem,” says Lauren McNeil, Leary’s behaviour support practitioner. “But rage is just the end of the chain. So we did a lot of functional behaviour assessments to identify what happens right before she escalates, what happens during that, and afterwards. The idea is to see patterns, and understand what the rage is communicating. Is she overloaded, seeking connection, or in pain?” McNeil and Leary also mapped her fatigue, sleep and medications, which were changing every month. “After you do that, you can stop guessing at why her behaviours are like they are.”

Each Monday, the two would do “look-backs”. “We’d sit and go over the weekend, just like a sports replay,” says McNeil. ” ‘What happened? Who did she see?’ She might have had dinner with friends or had a row with her dad.” Simply recalling the events of the weekend helps Leary’s memory, but they also allow for a more detailed analysis via a schema that McNeil calls bugs, butterflies and webs. “The bugs were moments when things had gone sideways,” she explains. “The butterflies were the wins, where Lex had paused and thought before acting, and the webs are the strategies we weave for next time.” One of these strategies was called a “brain break”. “When Lex realises that things are moving too fast for her, instead of waiting until the emotion is expressed in rage, we got her to ask for a ‘brain break’. Sometimes, she’d be on the phone with her dad when she would yell, ‘BRAIN BREAK!’ and hang up, and he would understand what that meant.”

Such strategies are part of what is called “plasticity”, when the brain’s internal circuitry re-routes to develop alternative pathways and new ways of doing things. It’s important to recognise, however, that plasticity is not the same as healing. The brain has no capacity to heal itself: once a piece of it is smashed, it stays smashed. “I worked so hard for a couple of years after my accident,” says Morrow. “I thought I’d get my brain back to where it was before. But after a while, I had to accept that I would never be the same, that this was as good as it gets. That was a very hard moment.”

When Russell Leary walked into the Sunshine Coast hospital to see his daughter immediately after her accident, in 2021, there was a single black crow hovering, like a premonition, over the entrance. He felt a cold shiver: everything augured a catastrophe. But the following months would reframe what was plausible, both medically and spiritually. After the crash, Russell and Belinda employed a quantum healer, called Michela D’Addario, to communicate with Alexa while she was still in a coma. (Quantum healing is a fringe practice that purports to combine meditation and energy work with metaphysical concepts from quantum physics.)

Sitting by Alexa’s bedside for weeks, D’Addario would “meet” her on the quantum field, which often looked like a garden, and tap into her thoughts. One of the many messages that D’Addario relayed back to the family was that, after she recovered, Leary wanted to swim at the Paralympics. Not only that, but she would win three medals. Sure enough, Leary had barely begun to walk again before she started training in the pool. The International Paralympic Committee classified her S9, for swimmers who have severe weakness in one leg. She went on to compete in the 2024 Paris Paralympics, winning two gold medals and a silver. “It was weird,” says Russell, referring to the quantum healing. “But it happened.”

Needless to say, few TBI sufferers have such happy endings. “I don’t think that superhuman stories of recovery are especially useful,” says Bruce Powell, “because they are either incomplete portrayals of the issues or inconceivable for most of us.” The wins seem modest: remembering your bank PIN; tying your shoelaces; recognising your friend’s face in a crowd. Failed marriages are common in the TBI world, so just staying with your partner is a triumph.

In his writing, Powell makes an analogy between living with a TBI and playing a surreal game of golf. “Rehabilitation gives you therapists, carers, doctors and loved ones. But eventually, everyone steps back. It’s just you and the ball. Wherever the shot lands, it’s yours to play. You are in control, no matter how bad your golf might be. All you can do,” he writes, “is keep on swinging.”

Jakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000m

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 21:06:01 GMT

Norwegian leaves rival Hocker trailing to claim $150,000

Briton Jazmin Sawyers second in the women’s long jump

It is a scene that has become gloriously familiar down the years. Jakob Ingebrigtsen leaving the world’s best athletes gasping in his slipstream, holding one imperious finger in the air, revelling in his athletic genius. But this victory over 5,000m at the inaugural Ultimate Championships carried extra sweetness – and spice.

The sweetness? That came from winning a mammoth first prize of $150,000 after an achilles injury he feared might derail his career. And the spice? Well, that was provided by the way Ingebrigtsen utterly obliterated his great American rival Cole Hocker, a man he had branded a “coward” just a week ago.

Ingebrigtsen has never been shy of venturing an opinion, and he was aggrieved when Hocker insisted on having his own pacemaker for the 1500m Diamond League final – and then refused to follow him. That led to a high-profile war of words, and a rematch that was the talk of Budapest.

And, my, did it live up to the hype. The pace was quick, but the Norwegian was so confident he had time to look around twice on the final lap before launching a devastating final kick to win in 12min 59.24sec, with Hocker, the reigning 5,000m world champion, nearly a second back.

“I was predicted number 12 by World Athletics can you imagine?” said a bemused Ingebrigtsen, who is the Olympic champion at this distance after all.

Ingebrigtsen was then asked whether it was not only sweet to beat Hocker but … yet before the questioner had finished formulating his sentence, the Norwegian replied “but to crush him” before smiling.

His time over the final lap was a rapid 54.39sec, while over the last 100m it was 12.6 – which was particularly impressive given he was only able to step up his comeback from injury in July.

“Being injured I was fearing the worst outcome and did not know if I would be able to run at all, especially at this level,” he said. “This is amazing, I am extremely happy.

“I had a big hiccup in early May, with the flu, where I was not able to train properly. So I really started training in July but you can’t fake fitness. Fitness is very honest in terms of training. The guy that puts in the best amount of work for the longest period of time is usually the best runner.

“But I’ve gained quite a lot from the last couple of races that I’ve done. I felt stronger, stronger, smoother, smoother, and that gave me a lot of hope.”

Ingebrigtsen, though, was non-committal over whether he will race in Sunday’s 1500m against Josh Kerr. “I’ve been drinking a lot of coffee until now, so get a good night’s sleep and see how I feel tomorrow.”

There was British success too on the first night of the Ultimate Championships with Jazmin Sawyers coming second to the Italian Larissa Iapichino in the women’s jump with a final leap of 6.78m. That capped a fine season for Sawyers, who also won Commonwealth gold and European silver, and it also made her $75,000 (£55,000) richer.

“It’s an incredible amount of money,” admitted Sawyers. “Prize money like this just means a big sigh of relief … I will buy something – I’m going to upgrade my sewing machine.”

There was also a bronze for the British 4x100m mixed relay team behind the USA and Jamaica, much to the delight of Success Eduan, who anchored the British team.

At some point next week, Eduan will deliver the four babies she requires to complete her BSc in midwifery. But she said that her share of the $25,000 prize – around £4,730 – would help her start paying off her student debts.

“I’m finishing hopefully next week,” she said. “I still have one more placement. I’ve got four more left to deliver, I arrive in Manchester on Monday afternoon, and I have a Monday night shift that day. Three nights, so I finish on Thursday morning.”

There are still two days left at these Ultimate Championships, but this was an encouraging start. It was faster paced than the recent European championships. It also looked the part with a black infield and bright lights. There were plenty of impressive performances too, with Mondo Duplantis’s 6.25m leap to win the pole vault one of the standouts.

Keely Hodgkinson also made an impressive return in his first run back to win her semi-final in 1:57.57 before delivering her trademark clap. She will face her two main rivals Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol in Saturday’s final.

On the downside, it was cold. Cold enough, in fact, that the Ukrainian high jumper Yaroslava Mahuchikh wore sleeping bags between her jumps. Not that it unduly bothered her as she took victory in 1.99m.

Faith review – intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 20:30:14 GMT

Toronto film festival: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama

Erin Doherty and James McAvoy both bring their A-game in this startling, involving movie from British writer-director Paul Andrew Williams, whose productivity and creativity continue to be an industry tonic. It’s an eerie mystery drama that Doherty and McAvoy perform with ferocious commitment. There’s something of Atom Egoyan or even M Night Shyamalan here … and I even found myself wondering if Williams intended us to think of Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Laertes’ lines about his father, Polonius: “… to his good friends thus wide I’ll ope my arms / And like the kind life-rend’ring pelican, / Repast them with my blood.”

We are in a downbeat British town, perhaps somewhere in the London estuary, a place to which a candy factory provides employment. Mina (played by Doherty) is a smart, capable single mum to 9-year-old Jamie (Smylie Bradwell); she works on the production line in cap and hairnet like all the others: much liked by everyone there. She is not fussed by the absence of Jamie’s dad and is perfectly content with hanging out with her friends and her sister (Liv Hill).

One night at a raucous pub quiz, for which she has had to hire a local girl as a babysitter to look after Jamie back at home, Mina finds herself drawn to an enigmatic, self-possessed guy standing by the bar, smiling benignly and drinking something non-alcoholic: this is Michael, played by McAvoy. With easy confidence and a quiet kind of authority, he chats to Mina and she can’t quite read this handsome man or read his intentions. Is he flirting or what? McAvoy’s Scottish accent also blurs the class distinction that may or may not exist between them. After walking her home, charming her and even love-bombing her with devastating compliments, Michael is the perfect gentleman and says he won’t come in. Later, Mina is even more fascinated to learn that Michael volunteers at a local food bank. But how does he earn a living?

Mina’s suspicious sister notes how well-spoken he is; she has perhaps picked up on something that the audience might also have noticed, that Michael has something secretive and supercilious about him. She wonders if he is or was a teacher, or if this food bank is some sort of court-ordered community service. But Mina won’t hear of any disparagement of this obviously remarkable man who is paying her the kind of attention she hasn’t had in a very long time. Michael comes round to their house and is a huge hit with Jamie; he asks Jamie if he likes computer games and goes upstairs with him to Jamie’s bedroom to play Super Mario Kart, while Mina, glowing at Michael’s quasi-paternal instincts, stays downstairs to chat with her sister.

Williams shrewdly controls the film’s growing, complex mood: a cocktail of dread, fascination and something else, as if Mina has been made a party to some occult conspiracy that Michael isn’t in any hurry to reveal. He already seems to know something about Mina’s babysitter that Mina herself hasn’t suspected. The film’s central dramatic events then kick the mood up into a higher gear. Mina is passionate, bewildered and Michael assumes the priestly air of someone who has seen it all before and who is either here to help or is some kind of vampiric outsider. The problem seemed initially to be that he was too good to be true. Clearly that isn’t the issue.

Williams’s alpha-grade cast present this tale of mystery with intelligence and focus and Williams shoots his principals often in looming closeup, as if the drama’s strange secret could be read in the faces themselves.

Faith screened at the Toronto film festival.

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 20:00:10 GMT

Pakistan’s ninth-wicket pair put on 121 in 123 balls

‘You’ve got to give a bit more credit to them’

Marcus Trescothick described Pakistan’s late-innings onslaught as a “perfect storm”, after the 21-year-old debutant Razaullah and the 36-year-old Mohammad Abbas combined to score 121 off 123 balls and force a fraying England to come in on the fourth day to chase a target of 130.

The interim coach refused to characterise England’s frequently puzzling efforts in the field as embarrassing as Razaullah plundered nine sixes and four fours on his way to a score of 81, and Abbas two sixes – as many as he had scored in 46 career Test innings before the start of this series – in his 42, insisting: “You’ve got to give a bit more credit to them [rather] than trying to target everything that we’ve tried to do.”

Trescothick added: “You’d always like to think that you can do it better, and you analyse it afterwards and say, was there an error, or was there a tactic we missed?

“You just hope in those situations when you bowl in the right place, which we did on many occasions, that you get the nick, or you bowl them … We hoped to go through them pretty quickly, but they kept smacking it and the young fella came in and made it tricky because when he hit it, he hit it a long way.”

Trescothick praised the all-round performance of Razaullah, who has been a revelation with bat and ball in a much-changed Pakistan side.

“He’s been very impressive, not just with his batting,” he said. “I thought the pace that he bowled at was good to see. You want to see young players coming through into the game with a bit of something about them and he’s got pace, he’s on it in the field, and then he slogs it like that. Fair play, some of the sixes he hit were pretty impressive to watch.”

Razaullah has one previous century to his name, scored last year in his third first-class game – with precisely the same number of runs from boundaries there as here, 70, though with only five sixes – and considers himself an all-rounder.

“I was just attacking,” he said. “If the ball was there to be hit, I went for it.” He was one of the seven players added to the squad last week and travelled with just three bats, two of which he broke while flaying England’s bowling around Birmingham.
