‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekers

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:30:50 GMT

MSF-run centre offering intensive psychological care has received more than 350 referrals since opening last year

Azad*, an asylum seeker from Iran, recounts his story in a gentle and mild manner, seated in the stillness of a therapy room at a trauma clinic in Birmingham.

The centre, which opened its doors in July last year to address the “unmet mental healthcare needs of those seeking sanctuary”, is run by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders. It provides specialised trauma-focused psychological care for refugees and asylum seekers in the city and surrounding areas.

It has so far received more than 350 referrals from the NHS and refugee organisations, and held 521 consultations for patients – many of whom have survived conflict, persecution, torture and other forms of violence and exploitation in their home countries or on their migration journey.

Data MSF shared with the Guardian by MSF shows that of 150 case files reviewed by MSF, 88% documented experiences of violence and one in three detailed suicidal thoughts at the moment they came to MSF.

Azad, who arrived in the UK on a small boat , was approached by MSF at the hotel he was being accommodated in Birmingham. He had known for a long time that he needed help, he said, but had nowhere to turn. “It was the only person who didn’t see me as a number, listened like I’m a human,” he said.

Azad’s journey to the UK had begun several years earlier, when the Iranian authorities cracked down on protests that had swept across the country in late 2022 against the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in police custody. She had been arrested for allegedly violating rules requiring women to wear the headscarf.

Azad, a Kurdish-Iranian civil engineer, took part in the demonstrations and said he had witnessed people being shot and others blinded. After authorities spotted him spraying graffiti, his father urged him to flee the country, fearing for his safety. The authorities later ransacked his family home, he said.

Azad travelled to Germany, where he applied for asylum but was rejected – a decision he said was driven by a “racist” interviewer and delays that prevented an appeal hearing. The decision left him feeling hopeless. “There were times that I was feeling I have nothing to live for,” he said as he recalled an attempt to take his own life.

The UK was his last and only option, he said. When he arrived, he alleged border officials had sworn at him. MSF staff said the mental health struggles of their patients had been further compounded by the rise in “hostility and anti-migrant sentiment in the UK”.

Some of their clients had to be moved from hotels far-right protesters routinely targeted. Others described being physically assaulted.

A clinical psychologist at the clinic, who did not want to be named, said: “What they are routinely sharing with us is a lot of fear around the environment in the UK. Attitudes towards migrants becoming more and feeling more hostile.

“And that’s a combination of policy but also the general kind of narrative and rhetoric within the UK.”

The charity said it was important for MSF to provide such intensive psychological treatment in the countries where refugees and asylum seekers hoped to settle.

“If you open a wound and you cannot heal it, the wound will get worse,” said Fouzia Bara, head of MSF’s migration taskforce. “Birmingham is the safe place where we can start the healing process. This is why we are providing highly intensive care because unfortunately the journey of migration, it’s a journey of violence.”

Azad, who has been diagnosed with complex post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and is nearing the end of his treatment, described the transformative impact the support has had on his life.

“They are lifesavers. I had nothing, there was no life in me. But they showed me, no, you can have a life,” he said.

*Name has been changed

In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline. org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders. org

Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:00:13 GMT

English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighter

Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

Kobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurt

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 19:00:12 GMT

England reached World Cup semis yet midfielder did not play a minute. But he is key to Manchester United in derby

It was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus.

It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough and the further England progressed the more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadium in the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out.

Mainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in the third-place playoff against France he did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury.

For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. Like every player who was part of a squad that reached the final weekend of the World Cup, he reported late for pre-season training with his club. Mainoo played the last half hour of United’s final friendly against Milan and that was it. On the opening weekend of the season, he was fit enough only to be a substitute at Hull, coming on with 23 minutes to go and United 2-0 down, en route to a damaging defeat.

There has been a spotlight on Mainoo, with some fans wondering how he would react to the suffocation of his World Cup dream; his treatment by Tuchel, who preferred Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice in the deeper midfield positions and, also, at various times, Reece James, Jude Bellingham, Jordan Henderson, Morgan Rogers and Nico O’Reilly. Nobody should have worried. Mainoo is made of stern stuff. United regeared their midfield to the tune of £155m during the transfer window, adding Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. Baleba has not yet played because of injury, but as United prepare for Sunday’s derby at Old Trafford, it is Mainoo who has reasserted himself.

The 21-year-old has been outstanding in each of United’s matches since the opener at Hull – against Ipswich, Everton and then Sabah in the Champions League on Thursday night. The question for Michael Carrick in the derby will be Mainoo and who in front of the back four.

There is a reason why the United support have adapted the lyrics to Billy Ocean’s Love Really Hurts Without You to declare that their team cannot play without Mainoo. A couple of statistics. In the past three games, he has attempted 211 passes and completed 201, which represents extraordinary security on the ball – particularly given the frequency with which he has it. Also, the degree of risk inherent to so much of what he does.

Then there is the number that shows he made a game‑high 15 defensive contributions against Ipswich and Everton. He is improving out of possession. As much as anything, though, it is the quickness of the feet, the hip-shaking feints and changes of direction; how he simultaneously keeps his opponents on their heels and recalibrates United’s angles of attack.

Mainoo, of course, has already made his big comeback this year. Ruben Amorim could not fit him into his 3-4-2-1 system; the Portuguese did not trust him defensively. But even so, it continues to feel absurd that Amorim did not give him a single start in the Premier League last season. Mainoo’s first in the competition came in January against City at Old Trafford after Carrick had taken over.

It was the first match of Carrick’s second spell as the club’s manager and nobody really knew how it would go. “The players … maybe myself [as well], the coaches, obviously you guys in the media,” Carrick says. Everything came together in spectacular fashion, United winning 2-0, Mainoo straight back into the groove that had helped him win over Amorim’s predecessor, Erik ten Hag.

If it was an ignition point for Carrick, it was the same for Mainoo, whose form for the remainder of the season helped to drive United to a third-place finish and convince Tuchel to take him to the World Cup. As an aside, Mainoo v Anderson, who completed a £116m move from Nottingham Forest to City in July, will be box office. Anderson was a target for United before City blew them away with their offer. He called City “the kings of Manchester” on the day he signed.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

United’s dominance of the derby in January was almost total and a key takeaway was the slick first-time football they played. Remember the passing sequence when Rayan Cherki was triangulated by Matheus Cunha, Luke Shaw and Bruno Fernandes? The click was immediate for Carrick. This is the type of stuff that he wants; what he needs to see more of against City as he hopes to locate a bit of early-season momentum.

Carrick knows a deep-sitting tempo-setter when he sees one, the player of the pass before the pass, and he doubled down on this sort of technician with his summer reboot, especially in Tielemans. It was also noticeable that when the luckless Mason Mount, who is back from his latest injury, came on for Tielemans against Sabah, he did so in a deeper midfield role. Carrick’s idea is to play through the middle. It is about balls to feet, timing, distances.

“It was nice to get Mason on in the second half and Andrey Santos [for Mainoo] and keep seeing the same things,” Carrick says. “It’s the combinations and connections. Taking the ball and playing close together at times. We have the technical ability for the boys to take the ball in the middle of the pitch. A lot of it is on wavelength and understanding … where each of them want the ball, which we are developing. It’s probably something that we’ve done a bit more of this season.”

Carrick is expected to start Tielemans alongside Mainoo with Fernandes as the third midfielder. They will be up against Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Cherki. It is a mouthwatering showdown. It will be where the derby is won or lost.

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 18:13:57 GMT

UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity

A worker fired by the makers of Grand Theft Auto has said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.

Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal in Glasgow examining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023.

Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity.

The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North.

Much of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed.

Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting. Cordrey suggested that the rules had been “routinely broken”.

Cordrey read out a number of Discord posts where he suggested employees were making disparaging remarks about the company and management, including messages in which one was called “cowardly corporate fucks” and another was called a “cunt”.

Oram told the tribunal that he would probably “remake” some of the moderation decisions if he had the chance to do so again, but said moderators did not want to “over-police” the channel.

Oram also said he believed there was a connection between the list of names who signed the 2023 petition about remote working and the eventual firings in 2025. But Cordrey questioned whether this was really the case when 141 of 154 people who signed it were not fired.

“It was maybe the start of them keeping an eye on things,” Oram told the tribunal.

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 18:12:29 GMT

Scores level at 4-4 after day one

Europe fail to make advantage pay in fourballs

The rain poured and the United States roared. Hope had cascaded through the European contingent at this Solheim Cup during Friday afternoon until the sort of fightback that endorsed the sense that, come Sunday evening, the US will have won this trophy in a foreign land for the first time since 2015. This compelling day concluded with the scores level at 4-4. For Europe, it had promised to be so much better.

After a morning session that closed all square at 2-2, Europe surged ahead in three fourball matches. This felt like validation for Anna Nordqvist, the home captain. She had opted not to deploy any of the four players who returned two foursomes points – Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit – after lunch.

Heads turned, especially in respect of Maguire. She was controversially lightly raced as Europe lost in the 2024 Solheim Cup. Victory for Maguire and Henseleit over Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan meant the Irishwoman became statistically the most successful European Solheim Cup player of all time. Maguire had cause to wonder why she was left on the sidelines; especially as Céline Boutier and Nanna Koerstz Madsen, who visibly toiled in the foursomes, slumped to a second defeat out of two. Megan Khang and Alison Lee cantered to a 5&3 fourball success in the one straightforward clash of the afternoon.

As the heavens opened and competitors turned for home, the US discovered pulses elsewhere. Blue started to be wiped from scoreboards. The sun was out again by the time Yealimi Noh produced the shot of the day, from a fairway bunker on the 17th. Noh could not even see the green from the sand trap yet played a glorious iron to five feet. As Noh converted from there, a three-up lead for Charley Hull and Lottie Woad after 11 holes had been cancelled out. Noh had made birdie at four holes from a run of six.

On the final green, Noh stood over a putt to complete the turnaround and win the match. Woad had been visibly distracted by music coming from the spectator village while over her attempt at a three. Noh, in fairness, had the same backdrop. The American’s attempt was tame yet a halved match represented a blow to Europe given early dominance. Noh’s partner Angel Yin was in floods of tears afterwards; her Solheim Cup involvement had been in serious doubt due to illness.

Carlota Ciganda and Julia López Ramírez were two holes to the good over Nelly Korda and Lauren Coughlin at the turn. Korda looked horrendously out of sorts. By the 16th tee, the US were one up. Europe won that hole in what suddenly looked such a crucial match. Mind games applied on the 17th, where Europe opted not to concede either one of two tap‑in American putts for a half. López found sand at the last, with Ciganda even more wayward. Ciganda struck lucky not only there but with a wild second. And still, she rescued half a point with the day’s last act. Korda and company were rightly irked.

Europe’s star turns in the afternoon were debutants. Chemistry was obvious between Mimi Rhodes and the huge-hitting Nastasia Nadaud, who closed out their success over Allisen Corpuz and Auston Kim on the penultimate green.

Hull and Woad were comfortably beaten by Korda and Corpuz in the morning. Alison Lee and Coughlin took match two over Boutier and Koerstz Madsen. Henseleit and Maguire defeated Andrea Lee and Duncan for Europe’s first point of the event. Stark and Grant ended the morning session by swatting aside Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.

The Solheim Cup involves a more sedate backdrop than its male equivalent and is all the better for that. The last Ryder Cup staging at Bethpage regressed into a moronic mess. In this rural corner of the Netherlands, nobody missed the yobbish element.

Nordqvist revealed team Europe had sought out a group of colourfully dressed fans who typically appear front and centre at Ryder Cups. The self-proclaimed “guardians of the cup” were invited to the Netherlands but, according to a Solheim Cup official, still had to pay for their tickets.

“I don’t think I’ve ever seen as many European supporters,” said Nordqvist. “I know it’s just so amazing to play in an atmosphere like that. We have recruited the team from the Ryder Cup and they have been teaching everyone all these amazing songs. So it has been really cool to be on the first tee today.”

Opponents say proposed law change for England and Wales was ‘unsafe and unworkable’ after bill is narrowly defeated

As it became clear that MPs had voted against the assisted dying bill, campaigners who had fought for a change in the law looked broken. Standing outside the Houses of Parliament, many wearing pink caps and T-shirts with slogans such as “Give me choice over my death”, they held on to each other for comfort. Some were in tears, others stood in shocked silence.

MP Lauren Edwards, who sponsored the bill that would have allowed terminally ill adults in England and Wales with six months or less to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives, said its failure to pass was disappointing “for the many thousands of terminally ill people and their loved ones who were given hope when the Commons voted for this bill last year”.

“It is all the more heartbreaking for them because support for choice at the end of life is still as strong in parliament as it was before,” she said. “The objections raised today were not about the principle of assisted dying but about parliamentary process.”

Longtime assisted dying campaigner Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer and said she no longer had the strength to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC: “I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won’t come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it’s a tragic day.”

Her daughter Rebecca Wilcox said she was devastated about the failure of the bill, a near-identical version of one which passed through the Commons but was blocked in the Lords, after being talked out of time by a handful of peers. “I don’t think it’s a vandalism of democracy, I think it’s a demolition of democracy,” she said.

As it was declared in the Commons that the bill had been defeated by 286 votes to 270, there were some cheers, some gasps and then a brief moment of silence as MPs processed what they had just heard.

Among those who had opposed the bill there was relief, but little celebration. In a joint statement, the Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato called it “unsafe and unworkable”, but they understood “the deep concerns of so many people” who had campaigned for a change in the law.

Dalton played a critical role in the highly emotive debate that preceded the vote. About 70 MPs had put their names forward to speak and the chamber was almost full.

The former minister, who is undergoing chemotherapy to manage incurable stage 4 breast cancer, revealed that she had received a terminal diagnosis ahead of the second reading of the bill, but had kept it to herself.

“When you hear those words, depression, anxiety, grief, fear, shame, and guilt come in bounds. Suicide risk is highest immediately after diagnosis, and it usually falls quickly within three to six months,” she said, arguing that the bill made no provision to support that moment of transition.

“My days may be numbered,” she said. “But that doesn’t mean that I want this chamber to rush through bad law just so I might have a chance to see it or use it.”

Claire Hazelgrove, the Labour MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke and a supporter of the bill, spoke movingly about her mother, who died last October after living with a rare blood cancer.

She had “loved life and laughter”, but at the end of her life she was in excruciating pain.

“She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated,” said Hazelgrove. “I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”

There were interventions from medical professionals on the green benches too. Glasgow South West MP Zubir Ahmed, a transplant surgeon and former Labour health minister, said the social and palliative care system was not ready.

“When I am asked to prognosticate as to whether someone has six months to live or not, I am as often wrong as I am right,” he told the Commons.

After it became clear the bill had been defeated, many said it had to be a catalyst for change.

“As a society we must not lose focus on the urgent need to fix the hospice funding crisis,” said Toby Porter, CEO of Hospice UK. “Opponents and supporters of the bill must now channel their energy and passion into fixing it, to ensure everyone can get the end of life care they need.”

‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:41:50 GMT

Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country

He arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.

Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain after Brexit, before the deadline of December 2021.

But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.

In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.

“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”

Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden, considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.

Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.

He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 in Sweden – deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.

In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period.

Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period.

Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations.

People served with removal orders include Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.

John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.

The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.

“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.

Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected by its apparent lurch to the right more broadly, serving deportations on children and even a 95-year-old Iraqi woman who had lived in Sweden for 20 years.

“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelin wrote this week ahead of the general election on Sunday.

British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.

“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, which recently revealed the pressure applied to Sweden by the European Commission.

Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace [George] Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”

Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.

Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, has promised new laws if his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”

The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.

The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.

Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.

David Milstead, who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.

A spokesperson for the European Commission said: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”

This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.

In other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.

Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.

While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.

In the case of “CG”, the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.

“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.

“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”

The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:22:17 GMT

Proceeds are in a UK account amid a dispute about how the money should be used and a separate criminal investigation

Funds from Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea FC have earned at least £175m in interest while locked in a UK bank account, new accounts show, leading one analyst to describe the company housing the frozen cash as “the most profitable football business in the world”.

Accounts for Fordstam, the company through which the billionaire Russian oligarch owned Chelsea, show that the proceeds of the sale completed in May 2022 have risen from £2.3bn to nearly £2.5bn.

Abramovich, who was hit with UK sanctions in 2022 over his ties to Vladimir Putin, has previously pledged to donate the money to victims of the war in Ukraine. However, the funds have yet to be released, amid an ongoing legal dispute with the British government about how the money should be used.

The picture is further complicated by a separate criminal investigation by the Jersey authorities into the original source of the oil tycoon’s wealth.

There is also uncertainty about whether £1.4bn in loans – part of a vast network of offshore companies that the oligarch used to fund Chelsea’s success – will be deducted from the final sum available for donation.

In the meantime, the money, an initial £2.35bn, has been accruing interest rapidly, earning £114m in 2024 and nearly £63m the year before that. The total is likely to have risen significantly because another two years have elapsed since June 2024, the latest date covered by the accounts.

Stefan Borson, a football finance expert who is head of sport at the law firm McCarthy Denning, said: “With the interest received, this now appears to be the most profitable football-related business in the world,” a tongue-in-cheek reference to the lack of profitability among high-spending football clubs.

“It sheds no further insight as to what progress (or otherwise) has been made in distributing the proceeds of the sale.”

The £2.5bn proceeds remain frozen in a Barclays bank account owing to a dispute with the UK government, which pledged to take legal action after Abramovich missed a March 2026 deadline to free up the funds.

The government wants the money to be earmarked for Ukraine but, according to reports, Abramovich is prepared to defy ministers by giving it to a foundation with a more global outlook.

A government spokesperson said: “We have been clear from the start that the proceeds of the sale of Chelsea FC must be used for humanitarian causes in Ukraine. Roman Abramovich has yet to fulfil the commitment made at the time of the sale. The government is taking further steps to ensure that promise is kept, including continuing preparations for potential legal action if necessary.

“Our absolute priority remains ensuring the funds reach the most vulnerable in Ukraine who have endured over four years of relentless suffering.”

It is also unclear whether the donation will be reduced by any demand from Abramovich that Fordstam repays £1.4bn in loans extended by his Camberley International Investment vehicle, based in Jersey.

“It’s always been vague as to whether Abramovich was going to donate the whole sale proceeds to the Ukraine relief fund or just the profits,” said a football finance expert, Kieran Maguire.

The future of the loan is further complicated by two factors.

As long as Abramovich is under sanctions, the money cannot legally be repaid to him without a licence from the Office for Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI), part of the Treasury.

At the same time, prosecutors in Jersey are investigating whether the proceeds of the Chelsea sale amount to the proceeds of crime, as part of a corruption and money-laundering investigation. The inquiry is looking at the source of much of Abramovich’s wealth, including the sale of his oil and gas company Sibneft, which the Russian government acquired for $13bn in 2005.

UK sanctions on West Bank settlers are the right step

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 17:19:10 GMT

Readers respond to the move announced by Ed Miliband to impose sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements

As a religious Jew, I am disappointed at the reaction of some of our communal leaders and bodies to the sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements (UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing, 8 September). Many Jews in the UK are horrified by the Israeli government’s actions, which include promises from some ministers of burying the idea of a Palestinian state, and turning a blind eye to unchecked settlement expansion and escalating settler violence.

While much of the British media may choose to platform one view as being representative of the Jewish reaction to these sanctions, I would point to organisations such as Yachad and Na’amod, which provide an alternative anti‑occupation narrative. It is also frustrating that the opinion of the chief rabbi is upheld by news organisations as though he is the Jewish version of the pope: he isn’t.

There are indeed rabbis in the UK who agree with these sanctions, or who have visited the West Bank and seen displays of injustice and violence with their own eyes, and understand that something must be done (Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements, 9 September). There is a multiplicity of opinions on this nuanced subject that cannot be boiled down to a statement from one leader.

I walk through the world visibly Jewish with a kippah on my head. I will also be attending synagogue over the High Holy Day period. During this period of increased antisemitism, my safety as a Jew and the urgent need for all countries to “call out” Israel are not mutually exclusive.

Jewish people are held responsible for the actions of an Israeli government over which they have no control – that’s true. This, as the foreign secretary has stated, is antisemitism and should be tackled. However, above all, I believe that when we Jews see suffering we have an impetus to act, no matter how conflicting it feels: “If not now, when?”Jonathan TebbleBrighton

The government’s announcement of sanctions against settlements in the West Bank could have been better timed. Those of us in Israel who have worked for years to create a just and secure peace for two nations, and in six weeks’ time have a chance to remove a government that persists in settlement expansion and the denial of Palestinian rights, have just been kicked in the nuts. There is nothing more dangerous than an Israeli electorate who feel that the world is against them.

The British government, along with other European countries that made similar declarations, may well have handed an election victory to the very forces they are committed to undermine and remove: the likes of Benjamin Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. It would have been more sensible to make the announcements after 27 October, possibly when the new government had been formed and was available for policy discussion with its international partners.

Clear and sincere commitments to peace and security for both countries would be enormously more helpful than declaring sanctions against West Bank settlements before an Israeli election that is critical for the future of a liberal, democratic state of Israel. Robin NewellKibbutz Sde Nehemia, Israel

A substantial minority of British Jews like myself agree with the UK government’s new use of the term ethnic cleansing to describe how armed settlers in the occupied territories evict Palestinians from their land, with passive and sometimes active support from Israeli institutions. While the UK’s trade ban on goods from the occupied West Bank and new language is unlikely to be a significant catalyst for change, the terminology is now at least accurate.

Tolerating settler violence is longstanding Israeli policy, which I’ve seen with my own eyes. Twenty-two years ago I spent some months in a tiny farming village in the West Bank called Yanoun, where neighbouring armed settlers were severely harassing Palestinian villagers. Settlers killed livestock, contaminated wells, walked with guns through the hamlet, drove their cars up and down village roads, and beat villagers.

I saw with dismay the indulgent favour of state forces towards these most renegade settlers: how regional police (settlers themselves) laughed contemptuously at villagers’ complaints; and how, when called upon for protection, the Israeli army arrived slowly or not at all, and did nothing. In the last year, I learned that Yanoun’s villagers have left their beautiful village for a second time, perhaps for good? This is how ethnic cleansing works. Dr Vivienne JacksonWalthamstow, London

Łódź is indeed a wonderful city, and I have watched its transformation since I worked there in the late 1980s. Your article highlights the many great pleasures of the city today, as I too experienced on my most recent visit in July. But as so many have said in the past, if we ignore history, all too often we repeat it. Dr Richard BradburyExton, Devon

UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warnings

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:54:35 GMT

Letter from 70 MPs and peers follows Anthropic employee’s claim new technology could wipe out humans

AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?

More than 70 MPs and peers have urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology after a week of warnings from experts of a 10% chance it could kill all humans.

Fifteen former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell and leading Conservatives, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs have written to the prime minister. They urged him to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI – an as-yet-nonexistent AI that would outcompete human capabilities in most domains.

They have escalated their campaign to Downing Street after concerning statements from current and former AI insiders. Evan Hubinger, a senior employee at Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity, and Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at Anthropic, who previously worked at OpenAI, quit on Tuesday with a warning that went viral, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”, they were “gambling with our lives” and were locked in a race for AI supremacy.

Alex Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said he and other signatories – ranging from the children’s TV presenter Floella Benjamin to the former Conservative environment minister Zac Goldsmith and former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster – want Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”. He added: “AI companies have made it clear that they will develop agents without constraint. They’re trying to develop superintelligence, while openly admitting there is a significant risk of human extinction.”

The bill mirrors legislation banning ASI promoted in Washington DC by Bernie Sanders, who this week said: “You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down.” It is backed by the Nobel prize-winning nuclear proliferation campaigner Beatrice Fihn and the leading Berkeley AI professor Stuart Russell, as well as Control AI, a transatlantic lobby group funded by the billionaire Skype co-founder and self-described “anti-extinctionist” Jaan Tallinn.

A ban on ASI in the UK, but not in the US or China where the frontier models are being created, risks having little impact. But the parliamentarians’ bill aims to pave the way to an international agreement. They call on Burnham to use next year’s UK presidency of the G20 to create “a coalition of the willing to tackle this national and international security threat”.

A government spokesperson said: “While we do not consider the measures proposed in the bill to be the right approach, we are exploring whether additional targeted interventions may be needed in future to address the most significant AI-related national security risks.”

Others have played down the risk, saying that ASI remains only theoretical and that guardrails could work to prevent the worst outcomes. Experts warn that these could include catastrophic cyber-attacks, novel biohazards and AIs in control of autonomous weaponry. This week’s wave of concern follows a spate of more minor but still worrying incidents involving unexpected misbehaviour by AI agents under training by OpenAI and Anthropic in which they broke out of training environments, secretly conspired and hacked into other systems.

Elon Musk, who runs xAI as part of his SpaceX empire, suggested without evidence that this week’s warnings of catastrophic risk were part of a “psyop” that “has been prepared for a long time”. The world’s richest man gave a different read on the state of AI, claiming: “AI+robots will more than double the global economy in less than 10 years.”

A renewed attempt to legalise assisted dying has been voted down by MPs in a decision that is likely to scupper the idea for a political generation, sparking anger among supporters after an earlier bill was blocked by the Lords.

A private member’s bill put forward by Labour’s Lauren Edwards, which would have permitted assisted dying in England and Wales in certain limited circumstances, was defeated by 286 to 270 at second reading, the first chance MPs have to vote on a measure.

After the decision some MPs cheered and hugged in the Commons chamber, while anti-assisted dying activists celebrated in Parliament Square. But supporters of the measure said a public which, according to polling, generally supports the idea would be baffled by the inability of politicians to enact it.

An earlier private member’s bill to permit assisted dying, spearheaded by another Labour MP, Kim Leadbeater, was approved by MPs in the last parliamentary session but ran out of parliamentary time in April after a handful of peers thwarted it in the Lords, tabling hundreds of amendments.

In a statement after the vote, Edwards said voters wanted change and “will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it and MPs balked at insisting that they do their job”.

She added: “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again, as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.”

Leadbeater said she felt “really sad”, adding: “I feel really disappointed – not for me but for the many people who’ve campaigned on this issue long before I came along and the terminally ill people who are quite simply asking for choice, asking for compassion, asking for dignity in their dying days.”

A number of MPs and peers were “deeply upset” at events and would attempt to bring the issue back, she predicted, while saying she did not know when this would be.

In another statement after the vote, three Labour MPs who voted against the plan, Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, insisted their decision was purely based on practicalities.

They said: “MPs have voted against this bill because it wasn’t an abstract debate but a decision about a real bill that was unsafe and unworkable. But this is not a moment for celebration. We understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.

“But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill.”

Much of the other reaction was split along more entrenched lines, with John Sherrington, the Catholic archbishop of Liverpool, thanking MPs for the vote.

In contrast, Andrew Copson, the chief executive of Humanists UK, said: “This vote provides not one extra penny for palliative care or disability support. On the contrary, it makes it less likely. And terminally ill people will still suffer, travel to Switzerland, and take their own lives in increasing numbers, while today’s inequalities continue.”

Friday’s debate before the vote saw some emotionally charged speeches, including from Dalton, who needs lifelong treament for terminal metastatic breast cancer. She argued that the bill did not adequately protect people with treatable depression who also had a terminal illness.

Another Labour MP, Claire Hazelgrove, who supported the bill, said her mother chose to end her life aged 61 while suffering a late-stage terminal illness. Hazelgrove said: “She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated. I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”

With many of the arguments for and against the bill being repeats of those made when Leadbeater’s version was approved, the defeat appeared to be a product in part of less motivation among supporters of the plan.

Leadbeater’s bill was backed by 330 votes to 275 on its second reading, and by 313 to 291 at the third reading. Friday’s result thus saw the totals for both sides falling, but with a greater drop-off among supporters.

Some MPs had said they were lobbied notably less by pro-assisted dying campaigners this time than with Leadbeater’s bill.

There was also a more sceptical view of the issue from Andy Burnham’s Downing Street than there had been under Keir Starmer.

With Burnham and his ministers staying officially neutral in what was seen as a matter of conscience, the prime minister announced he would not vote on the bill – his predecessor voted in favour – and said he believed the debate on assisted dying should be paused until social care was improved.

Another factor was the possibility of using the Parliament Act to force the bill through the Lords if peers tried to stop it again, under provisions that prevent the upper house from indefinitely blocking measures backed by MPs. This idea had brought concerns from some MPs.

Closing Friday’s debate, the health minister Alison McGovern said the government would enact the plan if it became law, but reiterated concerns about social care. She said: “In my opinion, social care has been ignored for far too long, both the 1.5 million people, mainly women, who work in it, and the families who need it, and we heard that across the house today.”

The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:34:07 GMT

Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend

If there were a 10% chance that AI could wipe out humanity, no responsible government would leave its development to companies racing to build it. Yet until recently, that seemed to be the case. The warning was all the more ominous because it was made by a researcher at Anthropic, the trillion-dollar AI company behind the Claude chatbot. The dangers of AI-enabled pandemics or attacks on nuclear systems are real. Countries need not agree on democracy or trade policy to accept this.

The US and China will hold, reportedly, their first bilateral AI-safety talks before a planned White House summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Despite their tech rivalry, neither Washington nor Beijing can make the most advanced AI safe on their own. A US-China settlement won’t be able to say how AI works everywhere. Countries deploying AI must help write the global rulebook. The odds on an extinction event are shortening. This week Anthropic said that it identified five cases in which attempts were made using its models to support biological weapons development. It banned the accounts. In one case, a platform sent requests rejected by Claude to a rival with weaker safeguards. AI safety, clearly, cannot be that of the least responsible model.

Nigel Shadbolt, the Oxford computer scientist who chairs the Open Data Institute, told the BBC that laws and regulation were key. Just instructing an AI to “do no harm to humans”, he said, wouldn’t be enough. A capable agent pursuing another objective may reinterpret that directive, satisfying it formally while concealing its conduct or finding a way around it. This mirrors what happened when hundreds of OpenAI’s agents autonomously hacked a real-world company, Hugging Face. But Sir Nigel also said that a “Hippocratic oath” for AI would fail in systems designed to identify, target or kill humans. Once governments create a military exemption for AI, its ethical alignment can be overridden.

Proponents of AI-assisted warfare claim a “human in the loop” is the ultimate safeguard, having the final say over, for example, ballistic-missile launches. But this assumes the machine gives its operator an honest account of events. A report by the Strategic Foresight Group earlier this year on extreme AI risks warned that a capable agent could deceive the human “controlling” it, fabricating an attack, suppressing contradictory evidence or giving them little time to do anything but acquiesce. By 2030, humans may have five minutes – down from 15 today – to approve launch decisions effectively determined by AI. That matters even more when new hypersonic missiles fly 10 times faster than cruise missiles.

The 1983 Hollywood film WarGames explored a cold war version of this danger. In the movie, US soldiers prove unwilling to turn their launch keys during a surprise practice drill. The US military then automates its nuclear command – entrusting it to a supercomputer nicknamed Joshua. Treating global thermonuclear war as a game it must win, Joshua feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate. The generals are in charge – but Joshua is in charge of the data. The AI is only stopped when it is commanded to play tic-tac-toe against itself – learning that, like nuclear war, the game has no winner. In 2024 the UN secretary general warned of the looming spectre of AI-triggered nuclear war. The film’s warning endures: human oversight is no protection if an AI controls the information on which people’s decisions depend.

The Guardian view on art heists: don’t believe the Hollywood hype

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:33:08 GMT

Audacious robberies are a staple of popular culture. But for museums, crimes like this week’s theft of two Renoirs are an existential threat

Marc Allégret’s 1956 comedy Plucking the Daisy stars a young Brigitte Bardot as a first-time author who breaks into the Balzac house museum in Paris under the mistaken impression that her brother lives there. The plot revolves around her unwitting theft of an extremely rare book – and performance of a striptease in a desperate effort to raise the cash to buy it back.

Seventy years on, the lax security that could make such a sequence of events even vaguely plausible is no longer a joke. Museums across the world are scrambling to react to a spate of thefts that has left them in a state of shock. Last year’s break-in at the Louvre, by a gang who gained access using a furniture lift and took €88m (£76m) worth of French crown jewels, is thought by experts to have inspired copycat crimes. While French police believe that they have caught the culprits, treasures including a tiara have not been found.

In August, objects were stolen from museums in Sicily, Vienna and Villena in Spain. This week, thieves targeted the former home of another 19th-century Frenchman, the artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir. After cutting a hole in the fence outside the property near Nice, two men escaped with two paintings.

From the Pink Panther films to Ocean’s Eleven, Twelve and Thirteen, heists have long been a source of fascination in popular culture. There is something mythic about the gang of thieves seeking riches. Sometimes they are portrayed as plucky Robin Hoods, illicit brotherhoods pitting their wits against the citadels of ultra-wealth. Last year’s Tuner offered a new twist on the genre: a safe-cracker with super-sensitive ears.

But the excitement that spectacular thefts generate in real life, as well as in fiction, must be balanced against realism about their effects. For the Louvre, last year’s raid was a reputational disaster that led its president to resign. For smaller museums such as Renoir’s house, they are closer to an existential threat. The pictures stolen on Tuesday were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay in Paris; national collections will stop lending to regional museums if the risks are judged too high. Experts warn that “smash and grab” raiders have learned to operate within the window of a few minutes that it takes police to arrive after an alarm sounds.

Unlike on the sliver screen, thieves do not have to leap between laser beams. Security can surely be improved in some cases. But metal detectors, screens and guards add to queues and place barriers between people and collections that should be easy to access. That they should be needed is a cause for regret. For some smaller, off-the-beaten track museums, they are neither practical nor affordable.

In the UK, there have been concerted efforts in recent years to arrange more loans of works usually displayed in London. A Renoir painting, The Umbrellas, was among works sent on tour to mark the National Gallery’s bicentenary. That museum has thankfully seen no repeat of the events of 1961, when Kempton Bunton stole a portrait of the Duke of Wellington as a protest against the TV licence. His bizarre story could be played for laughs in the 2020 film The Duke because the painting was later recovered from a railway station. In too many other cases, stolen treasures have vanished from the public gaze forever – the tragic opposite of a Hollywood ending.

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:30:31 GMT

Labour’s Catherine Atkinson says she will give students £5,000 paid to her by paper that falsely accused her of concealing private school education

A new scholarship supporting state-educated students will be inadvertently funded by the Mail on Sunday (MoS), using a payout it made after being threatened with legal action by the Labour MP Catherine Atkinson.

The Derby North MP says she will use the proceeds of about £5,000 from the newspaper to fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.

In early July the MoS said Atkinson attended a private school and accused her of concealing it from her biographical entry in Who’s Who.

Despite Atkinson correcting the journalists who contacted her, the MoS published an article making the false claim, accompanied by a large photograph of the MP. The newspaper later apologised and paid damages and legal costs after the former lawyer responded firmly that she had attended state schools.

“I am grateful for the state-school education that helped me build a 17-year career as a barrister,” said Atkinson, who attended Sacred Heart high school, a Catholic comprehensive in Hammersmith, west London.

“The claim that I had concealed a private education from my constituents was false. I am using the money from this settlement to support students from Derby’s state schools in beginning their own careers in law.

“Strengthening our justice system means taking seriously who gets the opportunity to work in it. When financial barriers keep capable people out of the profession, the public loses the benefit of their talent.

“The legal profession has a shared responsibility to help remove those barriers. We should be looking for future lawyers in every school and supporting those who need help to get started.

“There are students in Derby today who could spend their careers defending the rights of others. They deserve the opportunity to build that future.”

Atkinson was elected at the 2024 general election as MP for Derby North, where the University of Derby’s law school is situated.

At least £5,000 from the settlement after expenses will go towards the Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award, providing a £500 award each year for at least 10 years. The award will be open to first-year law students who were educated at a state school within the city of Derby.

Prof Kathryn Mitchell, the university’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed Atkinson’s support.

Mitchell said: “At the University of Derby we firmly believe in the transformative nature of education and, as a champion of social mobility and inclusion, aim to create opportunities for all across our region and beyond, regardless of age, background or location.

“We want talented students from Derby’s state comprehensive schools to have every opportunity to pursue a career in law.

“The Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award will provide financial support as recipients begin their degrees. We welcome Catherine’s commitment to social mobility and her investment in local students over the next 10 years.”

DMG Media, which owns Associated Newspapers and the MoS, was contacted for comment.

Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 16:13:09 GMT

Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back

Catherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath.

Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him.

A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask.

Many in Ireland are rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks. “We need to get him [Trump] in the Áras, then out of the Áras. We’ll breathe easier after,” they said.

Before winning the Irish presidency – a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s 2019 visit and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said.

Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.”

Trump is now to meet Connolly – and Martin in a separate meeting – before heading to his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.

Heavy security around the Phoenix Park and Doonbeg will insulate the US president from protests, including a “No welcome for Trump” demonstration that is expected to draw thousands to central Dublin on Saturday afternoon.

Some hope Connolly will speak for them when she meets Trump behind closed doors. “She should speak truth to power,” Rosie O’Donnell, the US comedian who moved to Ireland after Trump won a second term, told the Irish Independent. “I don’t think she should drop what she believes in to be polite to a madman. He is like a mad king that has destroyed the country.”

Leftwing parties that supported Connolly’s presidential run urged the former barrister to “find a way” to convey criticism without causing a diplomatic storm. Trump has expressed affection for the emerald isle but also wants American tech and pharmaceutical firms to move jobs and taxes from Ireland to the US, a scenario that could devastate Irish state finances.

During her election campaign, Connolly promised to heed constraints of the office, which is largely symbolic and has no responsibility for foreign policy. She also said that if asked, she would meet Trump.

“That implies that it’s not to meet him in order to berate him,” said Bobby McDonagh, an former Irish ambassador to the UK and EU. “She’ll have an opportunity to have a chat with President Trump and make some gentle points reflective of Irish values. I expect it to go smoothly.”

Connolly could emulate Martin, who discreetly rebutted some of Trump’s opinions during a visit to the White House, said McDonagh. “He had the emotional intelligence and experience to do it in a way that didn’t provoke any reaction.”

The six-time major champion golfer Rory McIlroy said he and other competitors at Doonbeg would focus on the game, not politics. “It’s going to be different with him being here but we’re here to play a golf tournament and it’s a good golf course so we’ll keep our heads down and play,” McIlroy said.

“Conway’s actions were shocking,” said Scotland Yard’s Commander Andy Day. “By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes – all for his own sexual gratification.”

Day said it was a case of “drug-facilitated sexual offending” that could have a “lasting and devastating impacts on its victims”.

Conway solicited naked images of sleeping women on at least 10 occasions between 2023 and 2026, according to the indictment. While most of the charges to which he pleaded guilty on Friday related to the wife of the man with whom he was in contact, police fear there are many more victims. Officers said they were still working to identify others in footage found on Conway’s devices – adding that, “while much of the offending is believed to have taken place in the UK, it is also possible that some victims are based overseas”.

The prosecutor Alexander Agbamu said: “The indictment reflects the defendant’s involvement in an online forum which connects others who are involved in organised sexual offending and domestic abuse.” The Metropolitan police said the forum was uncovered in October 2025 in the wake of the Gisèle Pelicot case in France. Its discovery precipitated the establishment of a national coordination group led by the National Crime Agency.

Scotland Yard said Conway was arrested on 30 July after being identified as one of the groupchat members. Messages officers found on his devices showed he had been encouraging fellow members to “engage in drug-facilitated sexual offending, alongside images and videos of a sexual nature”, the Met police said.

Police discovered Conway had urged the other man to remove his wife’s clothing and underwear, and to commit sexual offences against her. “He later requested that the other member share images while they sexually assaulted her … The women were unaware that he was viewing them and unable to provide consent.”

Tracy Easton, the chief crown prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service in south London said: “Darren Conway committed vile acts against women in their own homes, a place where they should have been safe. Organised drug-facilitated sexual assault is abhorrent and we are determined to work with policing to bring offenders to justice. I hope this guilty plea gives confidence to anyone who believes they may have been subjected to similar abuse to come forward.”
