Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:55:32 GMT

Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports

Why the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stake

Yemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.

The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, including the loss of the port city of Mocha on Thursday.

Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.

The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude since Iran has been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.

Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments. Oil prices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.

Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and the Houthis have been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.

In a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.

British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

The Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.

The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.

The US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025 after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.

On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.

Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.

On her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.

Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.

He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.

“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.

The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.

A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.

“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”

Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.

Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.

There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.

Labour’s manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, but the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank are seeking environmental approval for existing licences.

Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, and Fahnbulleh has since been considering her response.

Campaigners say the fields would produce as much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced.

Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian firm Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.

AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:43:01 GMT

Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt

Why is the AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next?

The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.

German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.

Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.

The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.

An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.

His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.

Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.

Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.

Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.

Siegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms in Germany to the party’s planned deportation offensive.

after newsletter promotion

In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”

The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.

“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.

Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.

Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.

Gore, gimps and a potty-mouthed magpie: welcome to the Lisbon horror festival where nightmares are a dream

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:23:22 GMT

MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail

If horror happens in the dark, the midnight movie showing was once the perfect way of gauging the genre’s health. But those days may be over. “When we were a film club, our first ever cinema screening was Takashi Miike’s Ichi the Killer in 2003, and it was full,” says Pedro Souto, co-director of Lisbon’s horror-centric MotelX festival. “But you don’t have that many people at midnight any more. I don’t know why.” He’s right: the midnight slot I attend – of the gore-bathed Indonesian kung fu flick Ikatan Darah – is only half full. Only a few appreciative chuckles when meat-cleavers plunge into craniums suggest the old midnight spirit still lives.

No need to panic, though: horror has simply embraced the light. With the genre exploding in the 2010s and 2020s, and blockbusting grosses this year for the likes of Obsession and Backrooms, MotelX is able to gorge itself on this cultural jugular. Now in its 20th edition, the festival has expanded to 11 days, with more than 170 films from 40 countries. Flashy branding – a howling gimp and the signature X, both in inflatable PVC – is dotted on around city billboards. At the opening ceremony, a gigantic birthday cake – the self-same gimp emerging from a lake of gelatine “blood” – is massacred by the punters within 20 minutes. Crowds seem abundant at most screenings, dominated by a heatwave look (dark singlets, shorts and sweaty tattoos) best described as “goth Decathlon”.

MotelX, the only purely horror festival in Portugal, grew out of a private film club catering to the country’s emerging love affair with the dark stuff in the 1990s. “Living in the suburbs, there was nothing much to do other than go to the movies,” says the festival’s other co-director, João Monteiro, sitting with Souto in the São Jorge cinema, the coffee-toned modernist palace where most screenings take place. “As well as the cinema, there were video clubs, so we spent the whole time renting horror movies like the seventh Friday the 13th. It was our initiation, like when kids in tribes become adults.”

He puts it this way because Portugal had virtually no tradition of horror cinema; it was frowned on by the Estado Novo regime, so there was no domestic output. “You could only do comedies, or films with a nationalistic take, all about Lisbon basically,” says Monteiro. Their research efforts only turned up about 25 films between 1910 and MotelX’s inaugural year in 2007 that could qualify as horror – where in neighbouring Spain, there was a mini-boom in the late Franco years. Foreign imports – Hammer films and the odd giallo – were often heavily censored.

MotelX is hoping to help fill that void, through its award for the best unproduced screenplay and by showcasing Portuguese work (the majority of which is still in the shorts category). And then there is the job of irrigating the local scene with horror cuts from around the world. This year, there’s at least one gem in the rough: Mohammad Reza Ardalan’s Poultry Farm, an ultra-grim Iranian film that Souto and Monteiro knew nothing about when they were offered it by a sales agent they had previously worked with. It turned out to be a richly characterised slow-burner about a young Iraqi-Kurd recruit working the chicken sheds at a farm, where secrets are lodged as obdurately as the rocks they prise from the ground. With its roots in Iranian social realism, it patrols the frontiers of noir and horror with great effectiveness, as it scrutinises this quasi-feudal society and the immigrants at its mercy.

US horror-comedy Drag was a fun opening film: an antidote to the sprinting-zombie movie in which an inept burglar (Lizzy Caplan) puts her back out helping herself to “rich people’s shampoo” and must be painstakingly hauled from the crime scene. With its knowing placement of excruciatingly painful obstacles, the film plays like a Wile E Coyote cartoon – until the sinister owner, John Stamos’s abstract-expressionist artist, turns up prematurely to dose us with musings on the male gaze.

The artists are the guests in Corrin Evans’s 1990s-set Corpus, in which a grungy photographer/small town dealer is invited to a party at an upstate New York mansion by his it-boy model ex-boyfriend. With her interminable hangout scenes, Evans – who was previously an intimacy coordinator for MaXXXine – is clearly besotted with the decade’s club scene. But she only moves past self-conscious hipsterdom and finds a natural rhythm during the film’s carnal second half, when sexual onlookers and objects fuse to suggest something intriguing about the nature of desire.

There were no English-language subtitles at the Cinemateca Portuguesa for 1968 Estonian witch-panic classic Libahunt (Werewolf). But no matter: the cinematography’s incantatory flair spoke for itself, and I now know the Portuguese for werewolf (lobisomem), if I’m ever caught here on a full moon. Such pagan dalliances are becoming played-out in modern horror, but the Basque-language portmanteau Gaua (Night) is a lush example with rich production design. Indulging the occultist audience with a full-on flying pandemonium to finish, it exists somewhere adjacent to the Robert Eggers-Ari Aster coven.

The Virgin of the Quarry Lake, Laura Casabé’s impressive, febrile, supernatural coming-of-age tale, is almost as damning about Argentina as Poultry Farm is about rural Iran. Taking place in 2001, in a Buenos Aires of blackouts and standpipes, Dolores Oliverio is moping, petulant and ruthless, fending off a worldly rival for her childhood sweetheart. You could pretend The Fox, directed by Dario Russo, is trying to say something equally profound about small town Australia. But as it cheerfully admits, there is nothing whatsoever to be learned – or maybe just a little, about daft human desire – from this droll cautionary relationship fable. Jilted hunter Nick (Jai Courtney), eager to bring his cheating partner (Emily Browning) to heel, ignores the Antichrist rule: never trust the weird talking fox (voiced here by Olivia Colman). Not that Sam Neill’s potty-mouthed magpie is much better.

My only complaint is not encountering anything truly frightening (though I only catch a three-day sliver of the festival). Souto says finding such nerve-shredders is MotelX’s holy grail. But Monteiro counters that, now Portugal is growing into the macabre, such work has become tougher: “I think we become adults today. We don’t fear horror films. We have no nightmares. I’m trying to find films that can still make me feel as I did in the beginning, like when I first saw Alien. Because right now, it’s impossible.”

MotelX runs until 13 September

Welcome to the Madring, a new, brutal and unforgiving F1 challenge for Spanish Grand Prix

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:20:04 GMT

New hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunities

In Madrid’s Puerta del Sol this week, Formula One fans were not shy in calling on the gods to look kindly on their favoured drivers on a newly built circuit that appears punishingly unforgiving.

Legend has it that rubbing the paws or backside of the bear in the famous El Oso y el Madroño statue at the square’s heart confers good luck. The drivers may well need it. Day one of action at the Madring track began with F2’s Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak careening into the barriers and his car catching fire, leaving the onlooking George Russell shocked before the F1 drivers took to the wheel.

Despite fears the Madring would not be ready, it is done and dusted. What sort of racing it will present for the Spanish Grand Prix is now the question. Billed as a street circuit, it is in fact a hybrid of roads and purpose-built track; narrow, with fast corners and walls looming for much of the lap, there is going to be virtually no margin for error.

This was demonstrated in F2 practice on Friday. Russell, who had previously described the Madring as the “most risky” on the calendar was watching F2 practice with some members of the media in the Mercedes motorhome when the Art Grand Prix driver’s crash happened.

“Oh wow,” he said. “This circuit is mental.” Inthraphuvasak, who leapt out in short order after his car burst into flames, had crashed rearward at high speed into the barriers after spinning at turn 19, and Russell observed the Madring was set to be an even sterner test than Monaco.

“I would put this as a circuit that has less margin, purely because of the speed,” he said. “In Monaco the walls are closer but because you’re going slower – if you make a mistake you’re not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes. It’s more lock-up. Here, there’s less margin.”

The issue, explained Russell, was that the fast corners were combined with the angles of the barriers on exit. “You see at this barrier, it’s kind of like coming back on to the track,” he said, indicating where the smoking wreckage of Inthraphuvasak’s car was sitting. “So if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you’re not hitting it at the same angle as the car is going. The car is going towards the wall but the wall is sort of coming in.”

When F3 held a test here recently, there were 19 red flags and three cars suffered broken chassis. “They’re Formula 3 drivers, but it’s a track that kills cars,” was the assessment of Williams’ team principal, James Vowles. Russell said he was surprised it was only 19 red flags.

He was not alone in his concern, with Lewis Hamilton echoing his sentiments. “It’s a massively challenging circuit,” he said. “Of all the new tracks I’ve gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines.”

There was at least cause for optimism after first practice with the hour-long session proceeding without a stoppage and the walls receiving only some delicate glances at best. The drivers were up to speed with alacrity and no little composure, with Russell topping the timesheets for Mercedes, from his teammate, Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 66 points in the world championship. In the second session, however, Britain’s Arvid Lindblad came a cropper, losing the rear of his Racing Bulls car in turn 13 and slewing sideways into the barriers in another heavy impact, but from which he emerged unhurt. The session was halted by a red flag but resumed, and completed with Antonelli on top from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Hamilton.

Sign up to The Recap

The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action

after newsletter promotion

Certainly the sense of spectacle was delivered, as was surely the aim, with high speeds on a narrow track flanked by walls, and illustrated in its signature corner La Monumental, a 550m stretch of 13.5-degree banking, through which the cars are accelerating to great effect, compressing into the track amid an amphitheatre of grandstands before heading over a blind crest and barrelling downwards out of the corner. There is even a little history here too, with turn eight – “El Bunker” – named for La Mata Espesa, two bunkers built in 1936 by the Republican forces to protect Madrid from attack during the Spanish civil war. Their preservation was a condition of the track being built.

The circuit lacks the backdrop of Monaco of course, flanked only by the large, grey square boxes so beloved of convention centres situated in industrial estates. Some areas are still somewhat building site-esque too, but the bits that matter are in place and for the fans it is but a 20-minute subway ride from the city. Indeed, it is an achievement that might be considered no little feat given there were objections to it happening at all, relating to costs, the construction and complaints about sound levels exceeding legal levels.

The circuit, which sits around the Institución Ferial de Madrid convention centre area between the city centre and the airport, is perhaps exactly what F1 had in mind with its pursuit of “destination races” in cities. This means events that would be entertainment weekends, to rival the Superbowl and draw fans and finance to the host city. But it also faces a further acid test to come. There remains concern, though, as to quite what sort of racing will be possible come Sunday. The drivers were largely in agreement that it would be a thrilling technical challenge of inch-perfect execution, but equally sceptical about whether overtaking would be possible. As the four-time world champion Max Verstappen noted, the main braking zones such as turns five, eight and 17 are angled, making passing all but impossible with drivers simply putting their car in the middle of the track.

“You can’t really go for an overtake because you’re braking but you’re steering either right or left, which is the worst thing you can do for creating an overtaking opportunity,” he said. This will put huge emphasis on qualifying but also raises the spectre of a procession on Sunday, potentially only interrupted by what many still consider will be inevitable red-flag stoppages. A long, hot train of cars circling in unchanging order is certainly not the hoped-for debut at F1’s newest circuit and a threat for which the promoters might too be hoping for some ursine intervention.

‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:18:52 GMT

Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing

On a darkened rooftop in Tel Aviv, Israeli intelligence officers outline the details of their work. These men tell us how they helped develop an AI mapping tool that trawled for phone signals and recommended apartment buildings in Gaza to bomb. Indirectly, they admit, they are responsible for thousands of deaths, but they never spoke up because that wasn’t their place. “My role is technical,” says one. “I’m just a small cog,” says another.

NAZA – directed by the Israeli film-makers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham and produced by the Guardian – is a chilling documentary about a mass slaughter that was authorised at the highest levels of government. But it is also, primarily, about the process, the system, the little links in the killing chain. Szor and Abraham build their film around the accounts of 24 anonymised military and intelligence insiders. NAZA, we learn, is an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. The Israel Defense Forces prefer to target Hamas terrorists in their homes at night – and if they live with their family, or in heavily populated neighbourhoods, too bad. At one point, a source claims, approval was given to kill 500 NAZA for one Hamas member.

I meet Szor and Abraham at the Venice film festival, where NAZA is competing for the Golden Lion award. The pair won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’s No Other Land (co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank. “No Other Land documented horrible crimes,” Abraham says. “But at the same time it gave people … I don’t want to say hope, but some light to latch on to. It’s not a coincidence that this film is all in the dark. We are in a very dark place right now.”

The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties. NAZA briefly shows us the rubble, grieving parents, dead children on the ground. Its main backdrop, though, is placid, normal Tel Aviv, just 44 miles to the north, where rush-hour traffic drifts dreamily on the street and the cinematheque is showing a Claude Lanzmann retrospective. Tellingly, the film was executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the director of The Zone of Interest. Glazer, says Szor, supported the structure and creative approach she and Abraham had adopted, that fostered the sense of a home that sits next door to hell.

NAZA deliberately concerns itself with the system – the policy of mass surveillance, the industrial business of murder – more than the individual psychology of those involved. But presumably its sources must feel guilt and shame, otherwise they’d never have agreed to put their careers and liberty at risk.

Abraham is unconvinced. “Well, it depends which one,” he says. “There are many motivations for an individual to speak. Some people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertise. Remember that these people serve in sensitive units. They are not often asked what they do. So there is an attraction to [our] curiosity that drives them to speak up.”

The film uncovers a system that is fiendishly efficient. Its series of disconnects appears designed to distance the perpetrators from the crime. Many of these men work remotely from Tel Aviv. AI selects the target and a drone drops the bomb. Even the language feels purposely euphemistic and obfuscatory. NAZA translates as collateral damage, which in turn translates to human beings.

“Sure, it’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen,” Abraham says. “There is some truth in that, I guess. But equally it should be said that intelligence officers know the most. They listen to the cellphones. They know the house they are bombing is full of children. They can hear babies crying. They still order another strike.”

What is the status of these men now? Some discuss their work in the past tense. Others don’t, which suggests that they might still be at work, overseeing airstrikes each night. Abraham won’t say; he’s mindful of protecting his sources. “But you can imagine. We are dealing with 24 people, so there is a whole variety of statuses.”

NAZA prompts obvious questions about the creatures of darkness we see on screen. But it prompts intriguing ones, too, about Szor and Abraham, a pair of dissident investigative journalists from the country’s middle class. In the furious, febrile climate of post-7 October Israel, their work is liable to make them pariahs, if not enemies of the state.

Szor jokes that she just wields the camera and therefore keeps out of sight. “Nobody knows who I am, and I’m very happy about that. But some of my family – and some people I’m close to – don’t accept what I do. After the Oscars [last year] they were very ashamed, very angry. But this is a small price to pay.”

Abraham, by contrast, is more vocal and visible. After No Other Land’s premiere at the 2024 Berlin film festival, his family home was targeted by a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he says. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”

Even so, he adds quickly, let’s keep things in perspective. “We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic. So yeah, it was scary for my mum. But she went and slept at my sister’s and her house is still there. For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons. Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”

Rooftops at night are a good location, says Szor. They lend themselves to contemplation and help people speak more freely. One soldier recalls the “insane fun” of planning airstrikes. Another remembers visiting Holocaust sites as a boy and wondering how the German people could have acted as they did. “I still see the Nazis as evil,” he says. “But what does that mean I am?”

After its Venice premiere, NAZA is greeted with a 25-minute ovation. Variety calls it a “devastating exposé” of systematic mass slaughter. The Hollywood Reporter claims that its “bombshell” revelations are likely to provoke outrage and disgust “on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu”

(The Israeli military on Friday said it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary, and criticised the film’s use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified”. In its statement to the Guardian, the IDF said that it “makes unprecedented efforts to minimise harm to civilians” during its offensive in Gaza.)

At the official press conference, the film-makers are asked about parallels between the Holocaust and the killing in Gaza. Abraham points out that this connection was made by one of the soldiers in the film. But he takes the man’s point. “When we say ‘never again’ and that we have to learn from what happened in the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen and observed in the present. I’m not saying [the situation is Gaza] is the same or identical. I don’t think it is. But what we should be doing is recognising these similar patterns of dehumanisation and killing.”

Who are these men who we can barely see on the screen? The polite data analysts. The soft-spoken officers. Almost all, it turns out, are products of Tel Aviv’s middle class: intelligent, educated and liberal, at least up to a point. Or to put it more bluntly, these are Szor and Abraham’s people. They come from the same neighbourhoods, share similar interests and probably have friends in common. It’s the ultimate paranoid horror trope: the call that comes from inside the house. It shows the extent of the rot and the film-makers’ own proximity to it.

NAZA asks how these men helped kill tens of thousands of civilians. That’s somehow simpler and less frightening than asking why. Abraham shakes his head. “And I have to say I don’t have a clear answer as to why so many people took part in this. And why so few people – in fact, I don’t know of any – refused in real time to do it. It’s scary what that says about the state of Israel. When people talk about genocide, they often speak about it as something that spreads across society, this general atmosphere that normalises death. When everyone else is doing it, it’s easier not to ask questions.”

Additional reporting by Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem

‘Somewhere to be themselves, and be kind’: the Filipino folk-popper creating a hand-drawn world for gen Z to escape to

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:00:09 GMT

What started as a school project about plucky fictional kids in animal masks sparked an obsessive fanbase and a major label deal. Now the artist behind it all – known as Yaelokre – is ready to reveal themself

Harpy Hare by Yaelokre is the kind of song you might expect to have gone viral in the 1520s, not the 2020s. Backed by guitalele (that’s a guitar/ukulele hybrid), the lullaby begins with the line “Harpy Hare, where have you buried all your children?” performed by fictional kids from the equally fictional world of Meadowlark who are depicted in fey illustrations wearing animal masks. But two years ago it became an unlikely TikTok hit, reaching No 1 on Spotify’s Global Viral Songs chart.

That was in summer 2024, when the world of Meadowlark was a bit more DIY. Not only was its creator still making tracks and illustrations from their “diary turned storybook” in their bedroom, there was no Reddit community around them yet and only the faintest of whispers about Yaelokre online. These days, Keath Ósk, the Icelandic-Filipino artist behind the project, has almost three million monthly Spotify listeners; last year they played a sell-out UK and Ireland tour, and they have just released their first album under their own name, delighting a following of gen Z and queer listeners who write fan fiction about Ósk’s world and cosplay as their hand-drawn characters, prompting questions on Reddit such as: “My costume has bells [on it], should I remove them for the concert?”

Meadowlark’s kids transmit messages of bravery and courage and celebrate childlike wonder in a world determined to stamp it out. Ósk’s folkloric storytelling has created a deeply parasocial fandom, attracting followers who find solace in this outsider world, and some who find LGBTQ+ and neurodivergent readings in Ósk’s music. One mother wrote online that their 10-year-old child had “found her people” at one of Yaelokre’s live shows after being bullied.

The project started as a kind of escapism for Ósk, they say when we meet in a London cafe for their first proper interview. They don’t share their gender or age but appear to be in their early 20s, wide-eyed, playful, clad entirely in earthy shades of beige, with a messy bleach-blonde mop; they have a surprisingly plummy British accent for a recent transplant to London. “I wanted to be an illustrator for children but I was also enjoying the media my dad was sharing with me – video games like Skyrim and fantasy books. We are huge nerds!” Ósk used to sign their illustrations as Yaelokre, a portmanteau of yellow and ochre. They would also practise voice acting: “My mum would catch me talking to myself and be like, ‘Are you doing alright?!’” – which led them to fuse their love of fables with another passion, music.

Ósk grew up predominantly in the Philippines, on Luzon island, occasionally venturing to Iceland to visit their father’s family. They miss Filipino food, they explain, even if as a culture “we’ve absolutely botched spaghetti – we love making it sweet”. Singing is a big part of Filipino culture, and the nation’s love of enthusiastic home karaoke sessions is well documented. “It’s huge there,” says Ósk. “You’d know your neighbour was having a birthday party because you could hear their auntie screaming their lungs out.” Perhaps less known, at least in the west, are the regional singing contests that offer entertainment and a way out of grinding poverty for some. Ósk’s mother would enter such contests “when she needed extra money, to buy milk for me as a baby. I’m not ashamed of saying that I grew up really, really poor.” The culture of people singing competitively for money is, says Ósk, “such a wonderful and also a sad thing”.

Their own foray into music happened organically, they explain, as the Meadowlark concept expanded dramatically from a school project about a friendship between a hare, a goat, a tree and a baby moose. They contemplated writing a book about them, but deterred by the need to “build a whole plot” around the characters, they turned to music instead, creating a theatrical sound world that spun its own myths. It didn’t take long from Ósk putting music online to blowing up on TikTok and signing – as Yaelokre – with Atlantic Records in early 2025.

They moved to London earlier this year, where they rerecorded 11 original tracks for their debut album, Foreword, giving their sound a bolder update: sometimes belting karaoke-style, or channelling the Filipino rapper Gloc-9 on the scatter-gun delivery of And the Hound. There’s also a cover of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero: in their hands, it sounds more like an epic poem than an 80s power ballad. Ósk also sings in Tagalog. “I want to be able to represent where I came from,” they say. “I’m so patriotic. When people ask about my gender, I just go, I’m Filipino …” Ósk doesn’t see the shift in sound as a contradiction: “I have so many layers and [Yaelokre] is not my only world. I have my own history and truth outside it. A lot of my young audience are going to grow up with Yaelokre. I grew up with Pinoy hip-hop!”

They’re clear that this isn’t the end of Yaelokre and its animal mask-wearing child mascots; they’re working on new music involving the characters soon. But there have been challenges along the way, and perhaps Ósk is happy putting some distance between themself and their creations. Earlier this year, they removed two characters from Meadowlark lore after they were sexualised by some members of the fanbase. Some fans have seen it as a sign that Ósk is angry with them, but they say there’s no rage. “I want to be able to filter as much as possible so that the community is safe, but I’m not angry. I think people are still learning. My one rule is please don’t sexualise any of my characters, because they represent me.”

Ósk wants to keep the fandom as wholesome as possible, even staging sustainable clothing swaps at live shows, to help cherish a sense of wonder. “There’s a space for people to learn and to be themselves and to be kind,” they say, “and to have a community where they don’t feel like they’re alone in this world.” Is this a world they would have benefited from growing up? “Most definitely. Making this story is what I could call my moral compass. It’s less about getting into playlists or winning awards and more about reaching the kids who didn’t grow up with these principles – I want to be able to share my wisdom and what I’ve learned.”

Foreword is out now on Atlantic Records. Keath Ósk tours Europe and the UK from 7 October and North America from 9 November

In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for elsewhere?

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:29:23 GMT

For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all

Last week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put out an AI-generated video that showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building an execution site for Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel and taunted female prisoners who complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning to introduce crocodiles to patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while the law that he championed mandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks is built on public support.

Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand its illegal settlements in the West Bank.

It had been a widely held tenet that if enough people in the democratic western world knew the reality of what Israel was doing to the Palestinians, they would pressure their governments, and Israel would be made to observe the norms of international law. Eventually, a reality would be born in which Jews, Muslims and Christians would live as equals within some political system that would be as good – and as flawed – as others. South Africa was always cited as the example, where rising international pressure over the decades was decisive.

But what looked like the winning of the moral, rational argument was offset by an acceleration of the processes of occupation, an increase in the frequency and blatancy of settler attacks in the West Bank, and of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attacks on Gaza. The past three years have been the logical development of this. In the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks, Israel escalated its killing, maiming and displacement of the Palestinians to the level of certifiable genocide. The defence minister, Israel Katz, says he is committed to the ethnic cleansing of Gaza, while a West Bank settler proudly tells the BBC that one Jewish life is worth 10 million Palestinian lives. Social media is awash with Israelis – from pundits on TV news debates to IDF soldiers – stating and performing the outrages necessary to achieve the objective of a Palestinian-free Palestine.

And while people across the world now know the truth of what is happening in Palestine and repeatedly and full-heartedly reject it, many democracies across the west continue to send arms and provide intelligence to Israel – even in a time of genocide. The US president’s Board of Peace makes a mockery of Palestinians, while hundreds of Israeli trucks clear the rubble from Gaza – and, with it, evidence of war crimes. The US attacks international institutions, such as the international criminal court, that seek to offer some semblance of justice for Palestinians. And to repress the constant protests of hundreds of thousands of their citizens, western democracies compromise their justice systems, attack their educational institutions and undermine their own democratic freedoms. Some have belatedly announced sanctions limited to Israeli settlements – illegal settlements that have should have been sanctioned years ago.

In 2014, I served on the jury of the Russell Tribunal on Palestine. In the preface to the report, which came after Israel’s third war on Gaza in six years, I wrote: “If not genocide, then genocide is not far behind.” Today I wonder if the genocide is not also a trailer for something more to come.

If the genocide was not a surprise, neither is the fact that the old colonial masters have no particular aversion to it. In a line of continuity with their own history, western countries have for decades partnered with Israel on weapons production and intelligence and surveillance technology. The west has sought Israeli advice and training in counter-terrorism, interrogation and civilian population-control techniques. A selling point for Israeli weapons has always been that they have been tried and tested.

And now, as Israel’s genocide is livestreamed, the establishment watches, enables, protects and helps tidy up. We may be watching a research and development exercise, a blueprint, a template, an example being created. We are already in a world where – it has been argued – some populations are surplus to requirements. Some of them live in areas that are a property developer’s dream.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This war is not only about Palestinians and Israelis, but about ideologies of supremacy and domination that threaten the people of the world, its civil societies and what is left of its international organisations. For the moment, it is the Palestinians who are on the frontline, the Palestinians who are being killed and maimed and tortured and displaced. But the Palestinians are also standing between all of us and a world remade in Israel’s image.

Ahdaf Soueif is the author of Mezzaterra: Fragments from the Common Ground

Mossy catwalks, mycelial designs and Monty Don: the growth of gardener style

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:07:19 GMT

Aspirational clobber, hot horticulturists and a TikTok content rise suggest gardening has never been cooler

You could argue that photosynthesis, soil bacteria, chlorophyll and germination, by their nature, never go out of style. But somehow, as the news broke this week that Monty Don would step down from Gardeners’ World after 23 years behind the shovel, gardening is having a moment in the sun.

On Saturday, New Balance will launch a pair of trainers alongside the jewellery designer Bleue Wickham-Burnham in a campaign fronted by Don himself, photographed shrinking into a bush with a pair of the trainers around his neck. In high fashion of late, the gardener Charlie McCormick became the face of JW Anderson’s spring 2027 campaign, and Alfie Nickerson, who grows flowers biodynamically in Norfolk for his brand Burnt Fen Flowers, has recently been plucked by Jimmy Choo for its autumn campaign, Wild Rose. Catwalks have been mossy, designs have been mycelial.

In more everyday settings, a pair of beige hemp gardening clogs have become the kind of thing twenty-somethings Lime bike across London to bag. Gardener style – cords, gilets, Blundstones and barn jackets – is now as familiar on concrete as compost. Don might have been wearing a chore jacket – arguably not a gardener’s staple, despite its factory origins – on the telly for more than a decade, but they are now omnipresent in cafes, ad agencies and other places far from an allotment.

Online, gardeners are finding new audiences, in some cases for reasons besides their knowledge of gerberas: i-D magazine has hailed a new gen of “hot gardeners” as part of the catalyst for a 50% increase in gardening content on TikTok this year, alongside actual interest in it.

Fancy gardening tools and clobber are aspirational: a site called Gardenheir has made a name for itself selling hand-forged tools, £275 two-gallon watering cans and various items in collaboration with the French workwear brand Le Laboureur that seem more likely destined for a small-plates restaurant than a vegetable patch.

Niwaki is another site for very fancy gardening gear. According to Jake Hobson, its founder, the popularity of gardening togs is as much about the mindset it offers as practicality. “They communicate a particular attitude. They’re comfortable and loose-fitting, but they also suggest that you’re ready for action,” he says.

Niwaki has intentionally pushed its products to new, non-gardening markets. “We sell a lot from Chiltern Street to customers who may or may not have a garden, and who may or may not even wear it in the garden,” he says, drawing a parallel with the broader rise in the appeal of workwear.

He delights in seeing Niwaki’s gardening gear worn outside the garden, such as one of their hard-wearing canvas tool bags, designed “especially for the travelling pruner”, being worn to the airport. Or the brand’s Tobizubon, which he describes as “the very, very balloon-shaped Japanese gardening trousers” and which are “incredibly popular in France. I’ve seen some amazing people wearing them in Paris, often with boots or funky shoes, and sometimes with a smart jacket on top.”

As with all things gardening, it hasn’t happened in a rush. Matt Collins, the head gardener at the Garden Museum, in central London, thinks it has grown in tandem with an exaltation of the position of professional gardeners more generally, and an overdue understanding that it’s creative, worthy work. “For a long time, it was seen as quite a kind of lower-status [job] … gardeners are cool, gardeners do important work.”

According to Selina Ozanne, the head gardener at The Exchange, in Erith, south-east London, “gardening is often romanticised. It has charm, as well as aesthetic appeal.” Plus she thinks it “holds a lot of nostalgia for people. It’s often a hobby associated with parents or grandparents.”

Gardeners, both professional and amateur, are more visible now, says Collins. And not just on social media. “Galleries and museum spaces and communal spaces are investing more and more in gardens.” Plus, non-gardeners are doing more gardening in public. “People who don’t have the privilege of a garden of their own … are finding other places to garden,” in parks and local community gardens, says Collins.

Sign up to Fashion Statement

Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved

after newsletter promotion

The timing is key. With climate a central topic, people who are caring for our planet seem like logical recipients of adoration. Plus, as AI experts this week warned of the high likelihood of extinction by AI, the calming, eternal nature of gardening feels even more appealing. “There’s definitely a feeling that gardening is one of those crafts that can’t fully be automated,” says Collins. “Watering schedules can be automated, seed-sowing even, maybe, but the act of observing and engaging in gardens remains quite human.”

For younger people, there is arguably a more specific appeal. Ozanne, of the “Nokia 3310 generation”, spent her childhood “heavily outdoors, building dens and climbing trees”. For the current generation, she thinks gardening “holds a sense of intrigue and presents escapism from a chronically online society”.

Collins points out a few thorns. Where fashion might sell a glamorous ideal of gardening, all forms of it involve muck, and not just some photogenic mud. Public gardening in particular, he says, “can be really difficult”. There can, he says, be “dog shit, human shit, sometimes, and grimy waste bags”. For Ozanne, who wears brands like Gramicci and Toast – repaired over and over again – the work makes her want to dress up. “I knew early on that if I was going to be out in public, picking up litter and dodging all manner of nasty things, that I wanted to look good doing it.”

But, says Collins, the glorification of the gardener isn’t necessarily translating to “their pay grade and how their actual value has been translated into [the] real world”. Gardening isn’t, according to Ozanne, “a career that’s accessible to everybody – both physically and financially”.

Benn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title payday

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:02:34 GMT

Fight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championship

Four years ago Conor Benn’s career was thrown into limbo after two positive drug tests scuppered his blockbuster fight with Chris Eubank Jr. Two years ago Ryan Garcia was serving a one-year suspension after testing positive for ostarine at the time of his greatest victory.

On Saturday night they will each be rewarded with an eight-figure payday when they meet at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas for Garcia’s WBC welterweight championship. The purses have not been disclosed, although reports have put the combined pot at around $30m (£22m) with each fighter expected to haul in roughly $15m.

Their routes to one of boxing’s biggest stages on Mexican Independence Day weekend have been different, as were the cases against them and their eventual outcomes. Both men insist they are not drug cheats, with Benn having ultimately been cleared by the National Anti-Doping Panel. But their collision course offers a striking reminder of a sport in which scandal can derail a career without necessarily compromising the value of the fighter involved in it.

Garcia (25-2, 20 KOs), the 28-year-old from Victorville, California, one of boxing’s first Gen-Z superstars, tested positive for the performance-enhancing anabolic agent ostarine on the day before and the day after his surprise win over Devin Haney in April 2024. His majority-decision victory was overturned to a no-contest, he was suspended for a year and his team blamed contaminated supplements.

Benn (25-1, 14 KOs) went through a longer and considerably more complicated ordeal. Two positive tests for the female fertility drug clomifene, a banned substance that can boost testosterone by 50%, emerged before the Londoner’s proposed fight with Eubank in October 2022, launching a regulatory battle that prevented him from fighting in Britain for two years. Benn maintained his innocence throughout.

Three years later, here they are. Garcia will make the first defense of the WBC title he won by dropping and outpointing Mario Barrios in February. For the 29-year-old Benn, it is a first world title shot and a chance to follow in the footsteps of his father, Nigel, who captured the WBC super-middleweight title more than three decades ago.

That Saturday’s fight was made at all speaks volumes about professional boxing’s peculiar moral ecosystem, where there is no single governing authority, universal anti-doping system or commissioner capable of imposing consistent sanctions across jurisdictions. Much of the power instead rests with promoters, broadcasters and sanctioning bodies whose financial interests are rarely served by keeping valuable fighters out of the ring.

Dismissed by critics for his good looks, luxury-brand endorsements and huge social-media reach – upwards of 13.1m Instagram followers with 9m more on TikTok – Garcia has amassed a massive following while oscillating between elite performances and episodes of extraordinary self-sabotage. His return from suspension brought an immediate world title shot – and a flat unanimous-decision loss to Rolando Romero in May 2025 – only for him to rebound against Barrios nine months later and win his first recognized world championship.

Benn’s journey has been different but hardly quieter. After eventually returning to fight in Britain, he lost to Eubank in April 2025 before avenging the defeat seven months later. Those fights restored his commercial momentum but did considerably less to establish him as a leading welterweight challenger.

Benn has not fought at the division’s 147lb limit for four‑and‑a‑half years, having recently campaigned at middleweight before coming down to 150lb to face Regis Prograis in April. Getting back down to welterweight may be the biggest gamble of all. “People say: ‘Oh, you can’t go up to this weight and then go back down.’ All right, cool. Well, just watch me do it,” Benn said at Thursday’s final press conference. “Discipline prevails, and I will make the weight.”

Garcia remains skeptical, suggesting the effects of the cut could leave Benn vulnerable once the punches start landing. “Even if he makes the weight, your brain can’t rehydrate fast enough,” Garcia said. “Them punches going to do some real damage.”

There is, beneath all the uncomfortable baggage, an intriguing fight between two men who certainly talk a good game. Garcia expects Benn to come forward and “try to resort to some dirty tactics”. Benn’s description of his approach sounded remarkably similar: “Tenacity, ferocity, spite, experience. I’m here to come and really set the tone from the first round.”

Sign up to Sport in Focus

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

after newsletter promotion

Therein lies the danger for the challenger. Garcia is the more naturally gifted boxer, with exceptional hand speed and a vicious left hook that is most dangerous against opponents coming forward. Benn’s best route to victory may require him to walk directly toward Garcia’s best weapon.

Garcia has shown he can be vulnerable when forced backwards, but Benn does not possess the timing or precision of Gervonta Davis, who handed Garcia his first professional setback with a withering seventh-round body shot in 2023. Benn, meanwhile, insists that virtually every apparent disadvantage works in his favor because it leaves Garcia carrying the expectations.

“The pressure’s on Ryan completely,” Benn said. “No one’s given me a chance in this fight. Twenty amateur fights, just not made 147 for four-and-a-half years, the weight problem, the this, the that. No one’s given me a chance.”

There is also something more personal at stake for Benn, who has spent years carrying the advantages and burdens of his surname, including Garcia’s repeated contention this week that he would never have reached this position without it. There is a certain irony in Garcia attacking Benn as a nepo baby: Garcia has been a child of boxing privilege in his own right, enjoying nearly every advantage the industry can confer, never more than during his microwaved redemption. “It’s just a blessing to be in this position, to be headlining in Vegas, to be fighting on a mega show and put the Benn name back up in bright lights,” Benn said.

For all the talk of legacy, Saturday also offers a revealing snapshot of boxing in 2026. Two men once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests will instead fight for a world championship and another handsome payday. Few sports are better at turning yesterday’s scandal into tomorrow’s main event.

From ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabs

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:00:07 GMT

Do you gain weight once you stop using them? Do they make your face saggy? Can they improve your mental health? Experts explain whether 13 common beliefs about GLP-1s are true or false

FALSE “GLP-1 medications mimic Glucagon-like peptide-1 – one of the hormones involved in appetite regulation. It doesn’t completely suppress hunger, but it is powerful,” says Dr Federica Amati, nutrition lead at Imperial College School of Medicine and author of The Appetite Reset. “The medicine is about 1,000 times stronger than what we naturally produce from our gut,” she explains. As food passes through the gut, cells called L-cells sense the nutrients, which sparks the production of the GLP-1 hormone. Without the drugs, these bursts of GLP-1 production last a few minutes. “It’s a bit like a sparkler. In comparison, the drugs are like a bonfire that roars for a week,” says Amati. Because the GLP-1 hormone stays in your body for longer if you are on the drugs, you feel fuller faster and your appetite gets suppressed, but you will eventually get hungry.

TRUE “Nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and vomiting are well-recognised side-effects,” says Dr Adrian Brown, associate professor and specialist dietitian at University College London. “They tend to occur during dose escalation, and most symptoms improve over time.” Eating smaller meals, staying hydrated and limiting fatty foods can help.

“One of the best ways to prevent these side-effects is to prepare your gut, liver and pancreas before you start taking the medications,” says Amati. “If you go into treatment with existing reflux or constipation, it’s only going to get worse.” She advises eating more plants and gradually upping your fibre intake. Once taking the drugs, never push past the point of fullness. “The gastric emptying is so slow that you need to stop straight away.”

PARTLY TRUE The drugs themselves don’t make you want to drink less, but people can experience this as a side-effect. This is partly because we get a lot of water from food, especially fruits and vegetables. “These drugs massively reduce the amount that you eat – up to 40% reduction in calories,” says Amati. You may also drink less if you’re experiencing nausea, constipation or reflux. “It’s important that you do drink, because dehydration is one of the key reasons why reflux and constipation may be worse,” she says. As well as drinking water, she recommends having hydrating foods and smoothies, especially on the day you take the drugs (typically, the injections are used once a week, while the pills are taken daily), when you can have the most appetite suppression.

TRUE Taking GLP-1 medication can “substantially reduce food intake, and that creates the potential for nutrient deficiencies if the quality of a person’s diet is poor,” says Brown, who has researched this area. He found that some people on these drugs may not get enough vitamin D, vitamin B12, iron, calcium and protein.

“If your diet was relatively healthy to begin with, that’s fine because you’re just eating less. But this is not true for many people,” says Giles Yeo, professor of molecular neuroendocrinology at the University of Cambridge and an obesity expert. “For those whose diets were not great to begin with, there’s a danger of going into malnutrition. You can’t just inject yourself and hope for the best. You have to think about your diet and exercise.”

PARTLY TRUE “Obesity is a chronic, relapsing, progressive condition. When medications for obesity are stopped, a person’s body will attempt to regain the weight,” says Brown. “Studies have shown that people can regain about 60% of the weight lost following stopping the medication.”

In fact, one study from the University of Oxford found that people who stop taking GLP-1 medication will return to their original weight within two years. “For a lot of people, these are likely to be long-term or for ever drugs,” says Yeo. “Your appetite is only suppressed when you’re on them. If you stop, your hormonal levels will go back to what they were. You’ll feel as hungry as before, which means the weight will come back.”

While the idea of taking medication for ever might sound scary, Yeo points out that many people take medication for high blood pressure and statins, used for lowering cholesterol, for life. “I think the same is going to be true for these drugs,” he says.

TRUE “Whenever people lose weight, they don’t just lose fat, they also lose muscle. The key point is whether we can minimise it,” says Brown. “Current evidence suggests that up to 40% of the weight lost with GLP-1 medicine may come from lean mass [bone, muscle and connective tissue] rather than fat alone.”

This is why it’s important to prioritise protein-rich foods and resistance training when taking GLP-1s. “It’s not negotiable – you have to do it if you want to preserve lean mass,” says Amati. “If you have excess fat mass and you engage in resistance training, you will lose fat first because that’s the stored energy source.” She recommends resistance training three times a week, including high-quality protein in every meal, and eating that first.

TRUE “These drugs don’t work for everybody – they’re not a magic bullet,” says Amati. “The data shows that 5-20% of people lose less than 5% of their body weight, so they’re classed as non-responders. If you’re someone who doesn’t have a very sensitive GLP-1 receptor, GLP-1 medications won’t have the desired effect.” While we don’t yet know why this is, Yeo says that it’s only a matter of time before we do.

FALSE GLP-1 drugs were originally developed for people with type 2 diabetes. Now, they’re also licensed for people with obesity, or people who are overweight and have weight-related health problems. Despite this, many people are using GLP-1s for aesthetic reasons because they’ve become so easily accessible.

“I see a lot of people accessing them to lose weight before a wedding or a holiday,” says Amati. “These drugs are not designed for that.” People taking GLP-1s in this way could end up with a worse body composition, she explains. “It’s much easier to regain fat than muscle, so you could find yourself with increased fat mass compared to before you started. Losing lean mass is not helpful for longevity.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

PARTLY TRUE When it comes to how GLP-1s impact anxiety and depression, Michael Browning, professor of psychiatry at the University of Oxford, says, “The evidence that they’re beneficial is pretty thin, and some studies are ongoing.”

Things are more promising for addiction, particularly with alcohol, where there have been some randomised controlled trials. One of these showed that taking semaglutide (the GLP-1 agonist in Wegovy and Ozempic) reduced the number of heavy drinking days for participants. For other addictions, such as nicotine and other drugs, more research is needed. “There’s work in animals that suggests they might reduce nicotine dependence, but the evidence is not there in humans,” says Browning.

MORE RESEARCH NEEDED Is “Ozempic breath” a thing? “There is a lot of anecdotal evidence, but not any epidemiological studies,” says Dr Praveen Sharma, an associate professor at the University of Birmingham’s School of Dentistry.

While there’s no hard evidence yet, it could be side-effects like vomiting and dehydration that lead to a dry mouth, he says. Saliva “keeps the mouth hydrated and the bacteria level low”, so having a dry mouth can mean “you get a proliferation of bacteria, which can result in bad breath”.

As for burps? Dr Lindsey Ann Edwards, senior lecturer in microbiology at King’s College London, says that by slowing gastric emptying, GLP-1 medication can “cause food to remain in the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract for longer, creating more opportunity for the gut microbiome to ferment partially digested food. This microbial fermentation can generate gases which may contribute to unpleasant-smelling or “sulphur” burps.

TRUE Your body goes through a stress response when you take GLP-1 drugs, says consultant dermatologist Dr Angela Tewari. “That puts stress on the hair, and you can experience telogen effluvium, which is stress response hair loss. It puts your hair into a shedding phase,” she says.

The good news is that this kind of hair loss is reversible. As your body gets used to the medication, this side-effect will ease off, although the pace at which your hair grows back will vary. “It can be an inch a month for some people. Generally, how fast your hair grows is a genetic thing,” says Tewari, who recommends taking the lowest possible dose of GLP-1s and eating food rich in protein, zinc, iron and vitamin C to encourage a healthy scalp.

TRUE You may take GLP-1s to change your body, but what do the drugs do to your face? Under your skin, you have a “support system”, explains Tewari. “There’s your collagen, and under that you have a fat layer and a muscle layer. That all makes the skin look plumper.” When you lose the fat layer quickly, the top layer of your skin is still expanded, as it has stretched over time to support the other layers. This means your skin will sag as there is less support underneath, so it can look wrinkled and dull. To counter this, many people end up spending money on injectables, says Tewari. “I wouldn’t jump into any procedures straight away. Allow your body to settle into its new look before you do anything,” she says.

MORE RESEARCH NEEDED As more people take GLP-1s, researchers are looking at the benefits beyond weight loss. One study found that people on GLP-1s were 30% less likely to develop breast cancer. Another found that patients with breast, lung, bowel or liver cancer who took them were up to 50% less likely to have their cancer spread.

“What’s challenging is disentangling the direct impact of these drugs and the secondary impact of losing weight,” says Dr Simon Cork, associate professor of physiology at Anglia Ruskin University’s School of Medicine. “Obesity increases your risk of at least 13 types of cancer. By reducing your weight, the likelihood of you developing cancer will also be reduced.”

Cork has researched GLP-1s and cardiovascular disease, and found that “the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with obesity taking GLP-1 was reduced by about 14%”. More research is needed, but if there are “weight-independent effects of these drugs”, Cork says the difficulty will be in trying to separate those benefits from weight loss, as some patients won’t need to lose weight.
