I tested 40 lunch boxes – here are the best in the UK for leaks, looks and sustainability

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 14:00:06 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Tired of squashed sarnies and spilt dressing? From stainless steel to insulated to plastic-free, here are the lunch boxes for kids and adults we rate the most

The best water bottles

If packed lunches are a high-stakes game in your household (as they are in mine), the right lunch box is crucial. There’s nothing worse than opening the lunch you’ve been looking forward to since 8am to find yoghurt has leaked on to your sandwich and your cucumbers have dried out.

A lunch box may look like a simple bit of kit, but keeping food contained from kitchen to school dinner hall or workplace desk is a surprisingly demanding job. And the humble lunch box has come a long way from the simple plastic tubs that used to contain our clingfilm-wrapped, squashed sandwiches at school. Today, you can find bento boxes with multiple compartments, stainless steel containers, silicone pouches and leakproof designs promising to keep everything from yoghurt to salad dressing safely contained.

But more choice doesn’t necessarily make it easier to choose one. If you’re trying to cut down on single-use packaging, a good lunch box should be durable enough to last, practical enough to use every day and, crucially, capable of keeping its contents where they belong. I tested 40 to find the best lunch boxes for packed lunches at all ages.

Best lunch box for adults overallBlack+Blum Lunch box Original

Best lunch box for kids overallMunchkin Kids’ bento lunch box

Best budget lunch boxBrabantia Make & Take lunch box bento

Best lunch box for sandwich loversStanley Legendary Classic Useful box

Best stainless steel lunch boxBlack+Blum Stainless steel lunch box

Best insulated lunch boxThermos Icon Series food flask

I’ve spent the past six years testing products for articles like this one. That’s meant sorting the wheat from the chaff in various situations, whether setting up seven side-by-side trampolines in the garden (my kids loved that commission) or filling my house with flowers to the point my delivery drivers worried there was something gravely wrong with me. So I’m well versed in assessing products.

As luck would have it, my lifestyle also requires the frequent use of lunch boxes. I have three primary-school-age children, so I am often found in the kitchen at 7.30am, cramming lunch boxes full of healthy delights that will doubtless be discarded in the school dining hall. I’ve suffered the thrills (few) and spills (many) of several different lunch box formats, so I was eager to find ones that actually keep things in place and still appealing by 1pm.

I started testing the lunch boxes (40 in total) with my kids at the end of the school year. By this point, I was at a low ebb of patience with packed lunches, so if I was wowed by a lunch box, I knew I was on to a good thing. But lunch boxes aren’t just for kids, so I also packed my own lunches for days out to the beach, the park or just a nearby bench to get away from my desk.

My kids dutifully and unwittingly tested the lunch boxes to their absolute limits. They were crammed into school bags, chucked across playgrounds (and I mean chucked), and left on school playing fields over the weekend. If you haven’t had to fish three lunch boxes out of the mouldy lost property on a Monday morning, are you even living?

I took a slightly more scientific and mildly less chaotic approach at home. I filled the lunch boxes with water and shook them hard, checking for drips. I then left them on their sides for 30 minutes to see if any water found its way out.

Of course, yoghurt, salad dressings and hummus don’t act in exactly the same way as water. I also made a range of lunches to see how they stood up to the pressure. Could I squeeze in a bag of Walkers? Did my salad end up tasting faintly of metal? Did dressing survive the walk to my favourite bench down the road?

No one wants to lug around a lunch box that weighs the same as a small baby, so I also weighed all the lunch boxes when they were empty. I looked at how practical the compartment sizes were – it may be delightful to see lots of little boxes, but do they work in the real world? And I spent a lot of time at the kitchen sink, washing up lunch boxes to assess how easy they were to clean.

Lastly, as this is the Guardian, sustainability was an important factor. I investigated the materials the lunch boxes were made from, how durable they seemed (this is where the chucking became key), how easily I could find replacement parts, and how recyclable they were at the end of their life. A manufacturer’s warranty or stated lifespan was welcome, too.

After testing I donated all the lunchboxes to the Salvation Army, which sells secondhand items to raise funds for its work.

Black+Blum is best known for its stainless steel lunch boxes (more on that later), but this plastic lunch box will turn heads. It comprises a 1l clip-top main box, an inner dish with a lid fitting a stainless steel fork, a sauce pot and a “garnish area”. It also has a vacuum seal and a lifetime guarantee (with limitations). Black+Blum sells the lid separately if you ever lose it or the seal goes.

Why we love itHowever fancy you go with your packed lunch, this lunch box is probably up to the job. Did I mention the “garnish area”? I whacked in a trusty chicken caesar salad for my walk to the park bench, and found I was able to keep most vital components separate until I wanted to mix them. Chicken, parmesan and croutons in the inner dish, salad leaves in the main compartment and dressing in the sauce pot. I liked that I could clip the fork on the outside of the box if I didn’t take the inner dish with me – although storing cutlery on the outside of the box does slightly give me the ick.

This lunch box definitely feels more grownup – I wouldn’t trust my kids to bring all the components back from school, and they’d probably find it boring. But as an adult, I loved it. The clips are robust and won’t prise open when they shouldn’t, and the vacuum seal keeps everything fresh. I also found it easy enough to open. The sauce-pot lid screws firmly shut and is fairly leakproof, except during vigorous shaking. The inner-dish lid just fits on with no seal, so this won’t lock in anything too saucy. Washing it didn’t fill me with deep joy, due to the many components, but it lacks any nooks and crannies.

It’s a shame that … while it says it’s dishwasher and microwave safe, the lid isn’t. Also, it’s pretty bulky.

Material: BPA- and BPS-free polypropylene, Tritan and siliconeCapacity: 1lWeight empty: 510gDimensions: 20 x 20 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe? Yes (but not lid)Microwave safe? Yes (but not lid)Freezer safe? YesNumber of compartments: 4

A versatile little box with everything kids should need for lunch: plenty of compartments, cutlery and an easy-to-open clip. This colourful lunch box also feels seemingly indestructible, surviving a school day and a night in lost property.

Why we love itMy mini testers were drawn to these boxes in tropical colourways. Inside, there’s a moulded plastic inner tray with five compartments. The lid has a removable silicone inner, which also has nodules you can snap the stainless steel fork and spoon into. That’s right – there’s a spoon and fork included, which is great for primary-age children. All the compartments are a decent size for smaller appetites. I could just about fit a sandwich in the main compartment and empty a packet of pretzels into one of the long, thin compartments.

As the silicone seal encloses each compartment separately, you can chuck a pasta salad in one compartment, and it won’t filter into the yoghurt in the neighbouring area – not the case on many kids’ lunch boxes I tested. My kids seemed to find the bento format exciting, and anything that focuses them on actually eating in the school lunch hall is a big tick for me – the box came home empty.

It’s a shame that … it’s a hefty bit of plastic, and there’s no way to buy spare parts – my kids lost the spoon. While it’s dishwasher safe, it takes up a huge amount of space in there, and as the bottom compartment doesn’t lift out, hand washing is a bit more annoying.

Material: plastic and siliconeCapacity: 500mlWeight empty: 740gDimensions: 23 x 20 x 7cm (WDH) Dishwasher safe? YesMicrowave safe? NoFreezer safe? NoNumber of compartments: 5

This is a practical – if large – lunch box. Inside the main compartment are two smaller boxes, one of which has a lid. There’s also a lift-out divider, which means you can lift everything out in one go if you want. Two clip fastenings and a seal around the lid of the main box keep things secure. All in all, it’s functional if not super sexy (and how sexy do you expect a lunch box to be?).

Why we love itI was impressed with the number of useful compartments in this lunch box. They’re all large enough to be genuinely useful – you’ll easily fit a side salad or a decent portion of fruit in one of the smaller boxes. Some compartments in other lunch boxes seemed only suitable for a mouse’s lunch. With the divider in place and the boxes in situ, there is still enough space in there to fit a sandwich. It’s a shame that the divider isn’t adjustable, though, which would make it more flexible. But its rigidity does make it easy to take out everything in one go.

This lunch box is easy to clean, and you can stick the whole thing in the dishwasher. It feels robust and rigid, and the opaque colour means it didn’t pick up any unsightly discoloration in testing. Brabantia offers a five-year guarantee as well as spare parts – the seal on the main lid and the container with lid can be bought separately on Brabantia’s website.

It’s a shame that … it’s so big. You might need to carry a separate tote to take it to and from work. It’s great for picnics, though.

Material: BPA-free plastic, silicone seal Capacity: 2lWeight empty: 400gDimensions: 26 x 17 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe? YesMicrowave safe? YesFreezer safe? YesNumber of compartments: 3

Stanley is a big force in the water bottle market, and its lunch box kept following me around the internet when I was researching this article. It’s a satisfying functional stainless-steel design with two flip latches to hold the lid on. The inside is pretty capacious, with no frills.

Why we love itIt’s surprisingly hard to find a lunch box that will properly fit a sandwich without a hint of squashing: I really hate finding my sandwich crushed and sad at lunchtime. The Stanley Legendary was up to the job – with extra room for a packet of crisps and a piece of fruit. You could even fit a baguette sandwich in here with room to spare. Satisfyingly old-school. With a capacity of 1.18l, this box is slightly larger than the Black+Blum lunch box above. There’s only one compartment, though, so if you’re taking a range of dishes, everything will need to be premixed. And there’s no seal on this lunch box, so things are prone to leaking.

It looks great and feels well made – it’s rigid and would survive being dropped. In fact, at 480g, it feels incredibly robust. The mechanisms are simple, and with no seal to give way, this lunch box feels as if it would last and last. It’s easy to wash, too: dishwasher safe and with no bits and bobs to scrub (or lose).

It’s a shame that … it’s quite pricey for a single-compartment lunch box, and it’s definitely not leakproof – but it is a great pick for sandwich lovers.

Material: stainless steelCapacity: 1.18l Weight empty: 480gDimensions: 25 x 16 x 6cm (WDH) Dishwasher safe? YesMicrowave safe? NoFreezer safe? NoNumber of compartments: 1

This large stainless steel lunch box has a capacity of 1l, just slightly smaller than the Stanley lunch box above. Unlike the Stanley, there’s a strong vacuum seal here, meaning it’s leakproof and will keep your lunch fresh. Inside is an adjustable divider, and on the outside, a coloured silicone band holds the metal fork and keeps the lid shut tight.

Why we love itThis lunch box was the perfect size for me, whether I was packing a salad or a sandwich. It’s a bit of a squeeze, but it can fit a sandwich as well as something on the other side of the divider. It can also fit a decent-size salad and keep it satisfyingly fresh thanks to that super-strong vacuum seal. It’s so tight, in fact, that you need to lift the valve before opening the box. In return, it’s totally leakproof. There’s no salad dressing pot provided, but you can be confident that a predressed salad won’t leak.

It’s safe to put the box in the freezer, oven or dishwasher (after removing the lid and silicone band). I liked being able to batch-cook a lasagne or macaroni cheese directly in the box before chucking it in the freezer for later. It comes with a lifetime guarantee, and you can buy spare parts on the website if you lose something.

It’s a shame that … the lid goes on so tightly that those with dexterity problems – and kids – might find it difficult to open.

Material: stainless steelCapacity: 1lWeight empty: 460gDimensions: 20 x 14 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe? Yes (except the lid)Microwave safe? NoFreezer safe? YesNumber of compartments: 2

If you want to take a hot lunch on the go without access to a microwave, an insulated lunch box is a practical answer. This Thermos one has a decent 710ml capacity, which is enough for soup, pasta or noodles – even for bigger appetites. There’s also a lid that can double as a very small bowl if you’re in a bind, and a folding spoon that can be stowed in the lid.

Why we love itThis food flask is vacuum insulated, meaning there’s no air between the two metal walls of the container and very little material for the heat from your food to escape through. The result is that your food stays warm until lunchtime. Thermos advises filling the flask with hot water to warm it before putting food into it, which worked well for me – my testers said their pasta was still hot at lunchtime.

I also liked that there’s a spoon inside the lid. Often schools won’t allow you to use their cutlery if you have a packed lunch, and I’ve also had to scramble around to find cutlery during my own lunch break at work. This also meant I could take the flask to a park bench without worrying about forgetting cutlery (it has happened). Thermos offers a five-year guarantee and will, at its discretion, replace it with the same or an equivalent model if it’s defective. The brand also sells spare parts, including the seal and stopper.

It’s a shame that … it’s quite heavy, and the inner lid may be tricky for kids to open.

Material: stainless steel plus BPA-free plastic stopper and silicone sealCapacity: 710mlWeight empty: 510gDimensions: 10 x 10 x 19cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe? Yes Microwave safe? NoFreezer safe? NoNumber of compartments: 1

Best for: a plastic-free lunch box

This Elephant Box lunch box is extremely robust – great for kids, adventurous types, or just surviving the office’s fridge Tetris. It’s made from food-grade stainless steel and has a silicone seal in the lid. There are also sturdy clips on each long side and a movable, removable divider inside. It’s genuinely leakproof – it withstood all my leak tests, including filling it with water and dropping it on a hard surface. If that’s not enough, the bright green elasticated strap is great for sliding in cutlery (not included). It’s a little on the small side, though, and the inner divider isn’t leakproof, so it won’t keep wet and dry stuff separate.

Elephant Box offers a 15-year guarantee on this lunch box, as well as a repair service and spare parts separately. There are some exceptions to this guarantee, however: it doesn’t cover normal wear and tear, or the seal or strap. There’s also a take-back scheme if you struggle to recycle your container at the end of its life. Elephant Box is also a Certified B Corporation and a 1% for the Planet member. The latter means Elephant Box has committed 1%of sales revenue to environmental causes. If you want to round out your set, you can also buy some excellent dressing pots to match.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s quite small and the clips and strap are a bit faffy.

Best for: a bento lunch box

The ubiquitous Sistema bento can be found in school lost property up and down the country. My kids have been using this box for years, and I’ve found it pretty indestructible, with a robust but easy-to-open click opening. There are plenty of compartments – the larger section has two layers, as does one of the corner sections – and the pot is leakproof, great for transporting yoghurt or hummus. The main compartment is big enough to hold a sandwich in the top. However, the bottom layer isn’t big enough to fit a packet of crisps or juice carton.

If your food container cupboard is a hellscape like mine, it’s also a mercy that these boxes are designed to be stackable. It’s dishwasher safe, but it does take up a lot of space in the dishwasher – and it’s a faff to hand wash.

It didn’t make the final cut because … there’s a lot of plastic, and only the pot is properly leakproof.

Material: phthalate- and BPA-free plastic; capacity: 1.65l; weight empty: 314g; dimensions: 22 x 19 x 8cm (WDH); dishwasher safe? Yes (top rack); microwave safe? Yes (except lid, which is attached); freezer safe? Yes; number of compartments: 5 (plus a yoghurt pot)

Best for: breakfast on the move

This two-compartment breakfast bowl is great for fans of overnight oats, bircher, granola and yoghurt. A screw-top compartment with a transparent lid is designed for dry goods such as nuts, seeds, fruit and granola, and underneath, a screw-lid sealed bowl has enough capacity for even the biggest morning feasts.

If you want to avoid those expensive Pret breakfast runs, this is a decent solution. I liked that I could keep my dry and wet foods separate until I wanted to combine them. Initially, I was concerned that the upper compartment wouldn’t be secure, but despite there being no seal, the lid stayed put during testing. The capacious bowl beneath fits a generous serving of overnight oats. And the real selling point of this bowl is that you can keep the dry food crunchy and unsquashed. This meant I could keep fresh raspberries intact or clusters of granola crunchy until I was ready for them. It comes with a five-year guarantee, and spare parts, including the silicone seal, are available separately.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it doesn’t offer the same versatility as other lunch boxes here.

Material: BPA-free plastic; capacity: 500ml; weight empty: 510g; dimensions: 11 x 11 x 11cm (WDH); dishwasher safe? Yes; microwave safe? Yes; freezer safe? Yes; number of compartments: 2

Best for: kids’ (and adults’) snacks

This cute box of tricks is the solution I wish I had when my kids were younger. It’s for slinging at them on the back seat of the car or in the pram when you’re out and about. There are four small compartments inside, which are the perfect portion size for smaller appetites.

The whole thing is made from silicone, including the valve. Remove this valve (the star on the lid) and compress the box slightly to squeeze out excess air, then reinsert it to seal it and keep everything a bit fresher. You can also remove the valve if you want to microwave the contents with the lid on. The whole thing feels pretty childproof – it’s soft and literally bounces if you drop it. Most importantly, it doesn’t leak, even when dropped from a height.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the compartments are small, so they lack versatility for bigger appetites.

Material: silicone; capacity: 500ml; weight empty: 298g; dimensions: 14 x 14 x 6cm (WDH); dishwasher safe? Yes; microwave safe? Yes; freezer safe? Yes; number of compartments: 4

A continuous, tight seal around the container gives you the best chance of a leakproof lunch box. This is usually a silicone strip that fits snugly around the inside of the lid. The lid should also compress evenly around the whole box to seal it shut. A clip closure can also help keep the seal locked down when the lunch box is being jostled around in a school bag or during a work commute. Just keep the seal free of grease or crumbs – any residue will affect how well it works.

There’s no definitive answer – sorry.

Stainless steel is durable and doesn’t retain smells or stains. On the downside, however, it can dent, is heavy and usually can’t go in the microwave.

Plastic is better if you want something lightweight that’s more likely to be freezer and microwave safe. However, it often holds on to smells and stains and can become brittle over time. You may also be keen to avoid it for environmental reasons.

Silicone is more unusual as a material for the whole lunch box, but not unheard of. Silicone lunch boxes are flexible and durable, but noticeably heavier than plastic and can retain grease – so cleaning them can be a real pain.

Glass lunch boxes are great for food storage, as glass doesn’t retain stains or odours and is relatively easy to clean. It can also often go in the oven, microwave and dishwasher. But again, they’re heavier and less robust, and you may not want your kid to be slinging around glass at school.

To keep your lunch box in tip-top shape for as long as possible, it’s imperative to wash it as soon as you can after eating. Salty or acidic food can be particularly damaging to a food container if it’s left to sit. Use a non-abrasive detergent and try to avoid scourers, as these can damage the finish. For hand washing, use washing-up liquid and warm water. If your lunch box has a removable silicone seal, take it off and wash it thoroughly from time to time. After you’ve washed everything, leave it to air-dry fully. Don’t reassemble a lunch box that’s not completely dry: trapped moisture creates conditions for mould, mildew and unpleasant smells.

Check whether your lunch box is dishwasher, freezer, oven and microwave safe, and always follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Don’t put metal containers in the microwave – no good will come of that.

A pricey lunch box isn’t automatically better than a cheap one. Look at the construction and durability. If you want to invest in a genuinely good lunch box, look for a good seal, tougher materials, replacement parts and a decent warranty. A £30-£40 stainless steel lunch box that remains leakproof for years and has replacement seals available may be better value than a £10 box that needs replacing every year.

It’s probably not worth forking out for a super fancy lunch box with loads of compartments or clever features if they don’t actually solve a problem you have.

Zoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s put many things to the test, from mattresses to makeup. She has become the go-to person friends and family consult with before making any purchase, earning her the nickname “Zoogle”. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and reading. He was at his desk at the Pentagon on 9/11. As the chaos unfolded, he refused to leave

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 13:16:52 GMT

Matthew Klimow recalls the day a hijacked airliner crashed into the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, Virginia

“All day I had been a good soldier: stolid, resolute, unemotional, rational, and dispassionate,” writes Matthew Klimow, recalling the wave of emotion that overwhelmed him as he arrived home from the Pentagon on 11 September 2001. There was sadness for the lives lost. But there was another emotion, too: humiliation.

“We, as a nation, had been humbled,” writes the retired army colonel, who remained at the Pentagon even after it was struck by a hijacked airliner, killing all 64 people onboard and 125 inside the building. “The fighting force of which I was part had been impotent, unable to protect our fellow citizens. The darkness I felt matched the darkness inside my house as I opened the door.”

Klimow recalls the longest day of his career in As the Pentagon Burned, a study in leadership and a first-person account of the chaos that unfolded at the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, Virginia, on the day that planes also hit New York and Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Donald Trump will mark the 25th anniversary of the United States’ worst terrorist attack in a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday.

Klimow’s book recalls how leaders at all levels suppressed their emotional shock to respond with calm determination and grace under pressure. But it also tells how the attacks revealed a tension between military protocol and the need for improvisation, and how coordination was plagued by erroneous intelligence, overlapping chains of command and communication gaps – including a critical half-hour when Donald Rumsfeld, the US secretary of defense, was unreachable.

Born and raised in Johnson City, New York, Klimow’s career spans more than half a century of military and diplomatic service. He entered the military academy at West Point in 1970 and graduated in 1974, commencing a 29-year army career that took him from commanding paratroopers in the 18th Airborne Corps to earning the Silver Star for gallantry during the Gulf war.

On the morning of September 11, Klimow was executive assistant to Gen Richard Myers, vice-chair of the joint chiefs of staff. The chair, Gen Hugh Shelton, took off early for Hungary. The acting role fell to Myers, who would assume the position full-time on 1 October.

Klimow was in his office by 5.15am. Since Myers’ confirmation hearings before the US Senate were imminent, he left for Capitol Hill around 8.45am, taking along his young aide-de-camp, Capt Chris Donahue. Klimow remained at his desk, his eyes drifting to a television monitor kept on mute.

Suddenly, the screen filled with the horrific image of the World Trade Center’s north tower on fire. Speaking by phone from Monterey, Tennessee, Klimow, 74, says: “When I looked up, there was the newscast of the World Trade Center burning and I turned the volume up and I was just dumbfounded because it’s such a clear blue sky. I was in denial. I kept thinking it’s some freak accident, a small airplane maybe, and they were speculating the same thing on the newscast.”

The secure “red switch” telephone began to bleep. On the other end was Gen Ralph Eberhart, commander of North American Aerospace Defense Command (Norad). “That set off alarm bells with me as soon as I heard his voice, which I knew. He asked for General Myers. I said he’s on Capitol Hill. And he said, ‘Colonel, it’s urgent. Get hold of him. Get him to a phone. I need to talk to him now.’”

Klimow immediately called Donahue, and told him to barge into a senator’s office and retrieve Myers. The red switch rang again. This time Eberhart’s words were chilling: “We have several airplanes in the air on radar. An unknown number of them have been hijacked.”

As Klimow frantically took notes, his secretary waved wildly: Shelton was calling on an unsecure line. Klimow found himself with the secure red switch handset pressed to his left ear, and the unsecure telephone to Shelton in his right. He began a frantic double-relay, feeding the developments to the towering, impatient four-star general across the ocean.

Then, the ground shook. “All of a sudden, Mary Turner, our secretary, jumped up and said, ‘I think the building moved!’ Then there was absolute pandemonium outside our door. People were shouting, running down the corridor and I yelled, ‘Shut the door, Mary, I can’t hear!’”

In his deep focus, Klimow had not heard the thunderous impact of Flight 77 slamming into the western facade of the Pentagon. Finally, a National Military Command Center (NMCC) watch officer broke into the red switch conference: the Pentagon had been hit.

By chance the plane had smashed into a newly renovated wedge of the Pentagon, outfitted with state-of-the-art ballistic glass. This helped reduce the casualty count, but prevented the kinetic energy from escaping, channelling fireballs through the long corridors and hallways.

Klimow went to the river entrance to meet Myers, and the two men fought their way back up the stairs into the burning building. Two police officers tried to bar their entry. Myers and Klimow pushed past them and descended into the NMCC, a windowless cold war labyrinth.

Early reports via the red switch incorrectly stated that American Airlines Flight 11 – which had already struck the World Trade Center – was confirmed hijacked, and heading toward Washington.

A critical friction point existed between Norad and the air national guard. Norad scrambled jets from Langley air force base, but initially lacked the rules of engagement (ROE) to shoot down civilian aircraft. Meanwhile, the Secret Service prompted the launch of fighters from Andrews air force base, outside the normal military chain of command. Those aircraft were operating under a more permissive “weapons free” rule of engagement.

The Langley pilots initially flew east because an erroneous generic flight plan sent them that way, and they believed they were responding to the threat of a cruise missile attack from the sea. This lack of “situational awareness” delayed their arrival in Washington.

Klimow, meanwhile, experienced a sudden dread when he turned around and realised Myers was gone. As the executive assistant, Klimow’s sole purpose was to remain at the acting chair’s side.

“I panicked,” he confesses. “I tore out of there. I ran as fast as I could into the corridors of the Pentagon and I can’t tell you how eerie it was because there are 22,000 people who work in the Pentagon and the place was deserted, there was a film of smoke in the air and they didn’t turn off the fire alarm. There’s this blaring alarm with a recorded message to evacuate the building just echoing.

“I ran to our office. It was absolutely deserted and I stood in the centre of our office thinking, where did he go? It struck me, he’s with Secretary Rumsfeld, which is the office above us, so I ran up the staircase and darted into the outer office. Gen Myers was coming out of Rumsfeld’s inner office and he shook his head and said, he’s not here.”

When Flight 77 struck, Rumsfeld’s immediate instinct was to run toward the fire, helping carry stretchers and rescue survivors. Klimow regards it as an act of personal bravery that nevertheless created a serious operational problem.

“For 30 minutes, no one could get hold of the secretary of defense when our country is under attack,” Klimow says. “He eventually made his way into the NMCC and described the destruction outside and he was calm and cool, like everybody. But when he talked to Vice-President [Dick] Cheney, I knew something was amiss, and it took me weeks later to figure out what had happened.

“He was briefed by General Myers on Norad’s response and the rules of engagement, and the vice-president was talking to him about fighters coming out of Andrews air force base with different rules of engagement, but they were talking past each other. They didn’t realise they were talking about two different responses by the air force.”

Klimow’s wife, Edie, a retired army nurse and major whom he met in Germany, had spent the day racked with anxiety. Their son, Daniel, in middle school, had been told by teachers that the Pentagon was under attack. “He had this vision of terrorists running through the hallways with machine guns,” Klimow says.

It was after midnight when Klimow finally walked out of the smoking ruins of the Pentagon. Covered in grey soot and smelling of burning jet fuel, he drove home to Arlington, Virginia. The silence was broken by a sound he had never imagined hearing over the capital.

“It was the eeriest thing. It was the sound of American jet fighters overhead. When I realised that my own neighbourhood, my own capital city and my own country had to be protected by a combat air patrol, it was humiliating to think that we had been so surprised by such a devastating attack.

“The lights were off in the house and I thought Edie must be asleep, but I opened the door and she was there waiting for me. That’s when we had this big emotional embrace and knew that we would get up the next day and start working on a solution.”

The solution that Klimow and his colleagues began drafting on 12 September would eventually morph into the “war on terror”, a sprawling military campaign that would redefine the global order, not necessarily to the US’s advantage. Looking back from the vantage point of 2026, Klimow views those choices with sober realism.

“Everything looks different with hindsight but, that cliche aside, we had little choice but to enter Afghanistan militarily and to make sure that the launching pad for what al-Qaida used to do to us was eliminated from Afghanistan.

“Did we make wise decisions tactically or operationally? Sometimes yes, sometimes no, but strategically I don’t think in the days and weeks following 9/11 there was any doubt in most people’s mind that this required military action, not just diplomacy.”

Diplomacy became Klimow’s own second act during a five-year spell as the US ambassador to Turkmenistan. It gave him a close perspective on the end of the US’s longest war: the 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan after 20 years and the return to power of the Taliban.

Amid the mayhem was a familiar face: Donahue, the captain whom he ordered to barge into a senator’s office on 9/11. Donahue rose to become a major general commanding the 82nd airborne division. On 30 August 2021, a night-vision photograph was beamed across the world, showing a solitary US soldier boarding the final C-17 transport plane out of Taliban-controlled Kabul airport. It was Donahue – the very last US soldier to leave Afghanistan.

“Talk about the irony of being there at the beginning and being there at the end,” Klimow muses.

The days and weeks after 9/11 were arguably the last time the United States was truly united. The Iraq war, financial crisis, social media, rise of Donald Trump and Covid-19 pandemic have divided and redivided the nation. But 25 years later, Klimow refuses to despair.

“There were seams that were ripping in our society in the 1960s, and I was witness to that. But we pulled things together,” he says. “It’s not the same situation, of course, but I have a firm belief that we go through cycles like this, and America’s principles, and our resilience, and our devotion to liberty and freedom are unshakable.

“I’m still a big believer in the American dream and what we can do together, and the belief that we will continue to pull together, in ways that may be different from some of our historic past, but our resilience and the brilliance of our nation’s founding still make that possible.”

George W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessness

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 13:00:05 GMT

The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence

If George W Bush’s abusive response to the September 11 attacks had been prosecuted rather than swept under the rug, Donald Trump would be less able to pursue his lawless policies. We can’t rewind history, but we can learn from our historic failure.

Twenty-five years ago, on a clear and crisp morning, I was sitting in the Human Rights Watch office in the Empire State Building with an unobstructed view of the World Trade Center towers as al-Qaida operatives flew two commercial jets into them. The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo.

At first, Americans were so fearful of another al-Qaida attack that many accepted the Bush administration’s argument that extraordinary measures were required. But as the utter brutality of the response became apparent, dissenting voices grew more pronounced. Yet the reluctance of later administrations to repudiate these measures laid the foundation for Trump’s misconduct.

A May 2009 meeting I had with Barack Obama epitomized the problem. He had recently assumed office and invited me and several colleagues to the White House to discuss his counter-terrorism program. The meeting was disappointing.

Our top priority was securing prosecution of the senior Bush administration officials who had ordered the systematic torture of terrorist suspects. Obama declined, wanting to look forward, not back. His priority was working with Congress to secure healthcare reform (ultimately the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare) as well as on issues such as education and climate change. He felt that prosecuting senior Bush officials would be too contentious.

Other steps had already been taken to end the torture. Public outrage, hastened by the leaked Abu Ghraib photographs of US servicemembers mistreating detainees in Iraq, led even the Bush administration to stop. The Detainee Treatment Act of 2005, sponsored by the senator John McCain, himself a torture victim, closed some of the legal loopholes used by the Bush administration to justify the unjustifiable. But no senior official was ever prosecuted for the torture.

That left a legacy of impunity that haunts us. Later presidents have not revived the torture, although the administrations of Joe Biden as well as Trump have continued the flow of military aid to Israel despite its systematic torture of Palestinian detainees.

Yet the deliberate use of excessive force by Trump’s deportation agents suggests confidence in a similar impunity for today’s declared crisis du jour: immigration. The Trump justice department has closed its eyes even when immigration officials gratuitously shoot, and sometimes kill, people.

Bush’s lengthy detention of suspects without trial at Guantánamo has had even greater lethal consequences. Ordinarily, a criminal suspect must be charged and tried within a reasonable time or released. But the Bush administration often had no evidence to justify charges beyond confessions secured by torture. The military commissions designed to allow prosecution despite the torture proved to be travesties that to this day have not even begun the trial of the principal 9/11 suspects.

The legal device that the Bush administration used to justify endless detention without trial was to call the suspects “enemy combatants”. In war, it is possible to hold opposing combatants without trial until the end of the armed conflict, but there was no armed conflict with al-Qaida, only a series of horrible terrorist attacks.

Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side to justify invoking the rules of war. Rather, the rhetoric was a contrivance to sidestep the requirements of criminal prosecution.

At the time, I argued that allowing this legal subterfuge could have dangerous consequences. If a declared but fake enemy combatant could be held indefinitely without charge, why could he not also be shot? After all, in war, there is no duty to capture combatants from the other side. So long as they are not in custody, they can be killed.

I made the argument in the meeting with Obama as a reason to close Guantánamo – to charge or release all its detainees. I couldn’t imagine that the US government would really start to shoot suspects whom it could detain. But that is what Trump is now doing, not with alleged al-Qaida terrorists but with drug suspects, using a similar theory.

Like Bush, Trump has concocted a war, this time with drug traffickers, even though there is no organized military force on the other side fighting the United States. He then declared suspected traffickers in boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific to be “narcoterrorists”. His aim is to justify summarily killing them by drone rather than capturing and prosecuting them. Trump has taken the Bush theory, modified it for the new enemy, and intensified the consequences.

Precursors to these murders can be found in the actions of the Obama and Biden administrations. They summarily killed people in Yemen and north-western Pakistan but at least maintained the pretense, though untenable, that these terrorist suspects posed an imminent threat to the United States because arrest was impossible in the relatively lawless terrain of these distant lands. That is, they invoked an exception in policing rules that allows lethal force rather than the fiction that these people were enemy combatants.

But that misuse of policing rules isn’t available for the drug suspects whom Trump is targeting because the US Coast Guard has a long tradition of successfully interdicting them at sea. Trump thus relies on his fake war to order them murdered instead.

The lesson I take is that when past abuses are glossed over rather than prosecuted, they set precedents that can come back to haunt us. It is never easy to establish the rule of law when the perpetrators are powerful officials. An administration rarely prosecutes itself, and later administrations have their own priorities. Addressing the past is often believed to require too much political capital.

But the rule of law is important. It is a value worth upholding even at a price. It is too late to address the Bush-era atrocities, but it is not too late to address Trump’s. He won’t do it, but we should insist that the next administration does. Meanwhile, state and international prosecutors should start now.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

Digested week: Prince George’s hair has such brio as he starts at Eton

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 12:35:21 GMT

Plus, AI doom-mongering, a drag Ann Droid and how your toilet flush can give you norovirus

In a news cycle to make everyone older than gen Z feel ancient, we start the week anticipating the 25th anniversary of 9/11 at the end. Social media floods with poignant interviews and images from lower Manhattan that day, triggering memories for the rest of us of where, who and how young we were. Ridiculously, I was having my eyebrows done in Hendon, north London, and came out to find a white van pulled over at a crazy angle to the curb, doors flung open, radio cranked up, and people stopped in the street to listen. I remember looking over the city and wondering if I’d seen jets, or explosions.

And just as we’re wrestling with that marker of time, photos of Prince George starting at Eton college come out, juxtaposed with photos of his father doing the same at that age. This triggers an even worse sense of whiplash, as we bob back and forth to 1995. How nice Prince George looks, I think; happier, or at least more confident, than his father had been at that age. After which – and I apologise for this – the main focus of my interest is his hair.

I wonder if the young prince has been bothered by thoughts of the male pattern baldness in his family. The royal men age awkwardly, as we know; sooner or later they all wind up looking like the Spitting Image puppet of Prince Philip (there’s a reference to age me). But here comes the cavalry, in the form of Kate Middleton’s fun, less tightly bred genes, which might send the royal bloodline in a different direction!

“Look, his hair’s standing up on its own,” says a friend, as we scrutinise pictures of the young George. She’s right; while William at that age had the floppy posh fringe, George’s hair has such brio! “I reckon he might keep it,” we conclude, a sure example of generational progress.

How will you spend the remaining decade or so we have left of human life on this planet? As forecasts of an extinction-level event via AI tussle with headlines about the climate feedback loop, I find myself considering, for example, taking out a giant mortgage I won’t have to pay off owing to my own and everyone else’s extinction; pulling out pension money, given retirement isn’t going to happen; or, within easier reach and requiring less decision-making, taking (another) nap, since, times being what they are, we may as well do what we want and to hell with the rest.

The AI thing is scary, not least because of my total ignorance and the sense of powerlessness to do anything – not even throw a bottle, pyrrhically, in the recycling. This latest round of AI doom-mongering kicked off when Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, posted on social media on Tuesday that Open AI and Anthropic were both wantonly ushering humankind towards destruction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Coxon is 27 and recently unemployed. I mean, he’s probably just trying to audience-build before launching a podcast, right? On the other hand, a few years ago I met a consultant whose job it was to go into companies and teach people how to formulate better prompts for AI. He told me, half-jokingly but not, that he had taken the precaution of embedding a bunch of code in [insert wherever bunches of code go], in which he identified himself and prompted future AI armies: “If you’re going to go on a murdering spree, leave this guy alone, OK?”

More quotidian ways of being brought down, this week: your toilet flush can give you norovirus and watching TV with your laptop on your stomach can give you something called “toasted skin syndrome”, which I would recommend you don’t Google for images.

First, the toilet. Particles released during a “turbulent” flush cycle can leave microbes floating in the air for up to 20 seconds, according to new findings from Flinders University in Australia. Researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, which sounds like a niche area even by the standards of niche areas. There was, said researchers, a lack of clarity as to whether or not closing the toilet seat might help with this, but, at the risk of sounding anti-intellectual, I think we can deploy our common sense here, right? That, or campaign for the reintroduction of outside toilets.

And then, toasted skin syndrome. In the British Medical Journal, doctors from University hospitals of Leicester NHS trust warned against prolonged contact between your abs and your laptop, citing a fishnet pattern on the skin caused by heat from the device. Customarily, they said, this injury would be seen in older people using hot water bottles or heating pads, but is increasingly showing up in school-age children addicted to their screens. For the avoidance of a scabby and painful mess, you’re advised not to use your midsection as a desk!

Two forthcoming documentaries causing excitement this week: Alex Gibney’s four-hour opus about Elon Musk, about which its subject has been whining all week on X; and You Can See Everything, the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, which sounds even wilder. In it, the Theranos founder, currently serving an 11-year prison sentence for fraud, gives startlingly intimate access to Nathan Fielder, better known for his comedy, and the documentary-maker Lance Oppenheim. The trailer alone suggests that despite all the hoopla, it isn’t over-hyped.

After the film’s opening at Telluride, the review site RogerEbert. com said it was “like no other film I’ve ever experienced”. CBS News called it “the wildest documentary ever seen”. Variety called it “a shameless, fascinating, reality-TV-eats-its-tail look at entitled duplicity”. In the trailer, Holmes stares at Fielder while rocking a baby in a bouncer with her foot, the little-girl hair and big Kewpie-doll eyes a reminder of what an uncanny figure she is. Fielder, meanwhile, doesn’t seem fully to have recovered from meeting her. “I’m really struggling to this day to understand what I experienced,” he said in a Q&A after the film, making the whole thing sound like a horror movie I can’t wait to see.

A beat late, but worth drawing attention to: the presence at Manchester Pride, recently, of a drag rendition of Linda, AKA Ann Droid, from the brilliant BBC show of that name written by Diane Morgan and starring her and Sue Johnston. The figure in lilac fatigues raised a huge cheer, and it’s interesting to note how quickly it has been taken up by camp culture.

This is something you can’t engineer. For example, I have a feeling the creators of Riot Women, a show most lesbians I know disliked and a lot of straight women loved, thought it had queer energy, but I would be surprised if anyone dressed up as those characters at Pride. Diane Morgan, on the other hand, has a sensibility that puts her in a very gay-adjacent zip code and, with antique robotic moves and a shout-out to “Sue! Sue! Sue!”, we love and appreciate her accordingly.

Memo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the script

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 12:31:49 GMT

If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works

Once again, it has been a lively week for the Real Housewives of Windsor franchise, with Harry and Meghan back in the UK for precisely 12 days before the king fired out a letter via the lord chamberlain on Monday, reminding viewers that the Sussexes are “private citizens” and not to treat them as working royals. You have to say the producers on this unscripted reality show are truly at the top of their game with these targeted provocations. Harry and Meghan duly took the bait and issued an intemperately hurt rejoinder – but we’ll get to that in a bit.

First, let’s deal with King Charles’s missive to “relevant senior stakeholders across government, the military and Lord Lieutenancies”. Ugh. Not to be too aesthetically sensitive, but I think we can all live without the sovereign being reduced to the ghastly language of “relevant senior stakeholders”. What next? Seeking “buy-in” for ribbon-cutting events and referring to posies as “high levels of audience engagement”? It does all rather reinforce the idea that the Windsors’ cringe-makingly self-styled “the firm” really is some dreary mid-range company with a wan Meet Our Team page on its website, in which Prince William – carefully photographed without a tie – explains that he “enjoys long walks with the dog and is a passionate Aston Villa supporter”.

Either way, the letter sent on Charles’s behalf was guaranteed to send the plot into overdrive, much as it does in any Real Housewives franchise when one of the cast sends a cease-and-desist letter to one of the others. (An event that basically feels like it can occur weekly.) Typically these letters then become dramatic drivers. Far from suppressing stories as supposedly intended, they always end up sparking whole new public debates and plotlines in themselves. This is what happened with the Windsors this week – and, indeed, was always going to happen, given the appearance of a pre-emptive slapdown.

The royal household must be able to see that the key thing about the Sussexes is that they are forever desperate to be taken seriously, like a music act that was put together on a TV talent show but now wants you to think they’re up there with Patti Smith and Nick Cave.

And so it was that Meghan and Harry’s spokesperson immediately hit back in public, announcing that the couple “were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance”. Ouch. Never show weakness, guys! A briefing given to the Telegraph added that: “The Sussexes prefer the term ‘public figures’, and would have liked an acknowledgment that, on a personal level, they remained members of the royal family, despite no longer receiving public funding.”

As indicated, this all hints at a season of endlessly messy dramas to come, given it took less than a fortnight of the pair being back in the country before a public blow-up occurred. In terms of the kind of bizarro unintended consequences you might see on a Housewives episode when someone’s kicked off at a girls’ spa day, the military chief of Uganda promptly announced his country was pulling out of Prince Harry’s Invictus Games because they didn’t want to participate in something “that does not have His Majesty’s approval”. What can you say? Other than: deploy the reaction gifs.

You don’t have to be a reality TV obsessive to spot the faultlines here that should guarantee that the Sussexes’ unexpected return to the UK will result in endless drink tosses. It’s all there in their immediate reaction. Harry and Meghan are really wholly formed reality TV stars now. Not only do they do the tit-for-tat media release to move the plot along, but they also let you know what they were feeling when they read the original press-released letter from the king. In reality TV, moments like these are gleaned from “master interviews” (MIVs), filmed at the end of a season to provide useful retrospective commentary that the producers can cut the main action with. So you’ll see Hell’s Kitchen contestants helpfully reflecting on the scene you’ve just watched, and going: “And I’m standing there thinking – Chef Ramsay is going to go crazy when he sees this.” Or, in this case, “I was a little surprised not to have been told by Chef Ramsay about this in advance.”

This is precisely how the Sussexes now conduct public life, and it remains incompatible with the way the royal household does it. For all their supposed desire for a quiet life, Harry and Meghan have done that thing that the Beckhams – and indeed the secessionist Beckham-Peltzes – seemingly cannot help but do, where they claim to enjoy privacy but in fact live life out loud in a way that has come to feel normal to them but is really anything but.

Which brings us back to the burning question of why on earth you’d move back somewhere you are on the record – multiple times – as absolutely loathing in all its aspects. Increasingly, and faster than predicted, it feels like the answer to that is “for content” – scripted or otherwise. It’s fairly difficult to see the Sussexes’ relocation as anything other than laying the groundwork for a sequel to the only story of theirs that has ever rated with audiences: their own struggle with the forces of the British establishment/media/enemies within the royal household. Or as Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star Lisa Rinna once put it – and her head would be right up there on the franchise’s Mount Rushmore – “you better believe I’m gonna talk about it”.

‘The place lost its way. Now that’s changed’: can a Manchester art museum move beyond its troubled past?

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 12:00:04 GMT

The Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new mission

In March 2020, the visual artist JJ Chan was assembling video footage for a group exhibition scheduled at the Centre for Chinese Contemporary Art in Manchester. Centred on family VHS tapes, and titled A New Constellation: Chinese Diaspora Now, the artwork was an exploration of Chan’s emotionally complex relationship to Hong Kong, their parents’ birthplace. When Chan asked for guidance after the sudden departure of the initial curator, the artist discovered that the gallery did not employ anyone who was Chinese: 12 out of the 13 staff members were white, while most of the front-facing (unpaid) volunteers were of Chinese descent.

Fearing their art would be shaped through a white lens, Chan withdrew and published an open letter to the centre, writing: “My experience, and my trauma, are being used as a leg-up into an industry for an already overrepresented demographic.” Later that year, the organisation recruited seven artists of Chinese heritage to address the lack of diversity before that initiative was cancelled when the artists raised issues surrounding institutional racism with the gallery. The artist-led working group subsequently petitioned for an international boycott of the institution resulting in the resignation of six board members and several employees. After closing due to Covid in 2020, the arts space never reopened.

Two years on, Shanghai-born artist Xiaowen Zhu reattained public funding and relaunched the venue in 2023 under a new name, esea contemporary – incorporating the wider east and south-east Asian diaspora – alongside a new team primarily made up of first- and second-generation migrants. The director’s ethos, defined following a series of artist surveys and community focus groups, seeks connectedness in an increasingly polarised world.

As part of a year-long programme celebrating its 40th anniversary, the charity is hosting Two Improvisations, the first UK institutional solo exhibition by London-based, Wuhan-born Chris Zhongtian Yuan. There’s also an online interview series tracing the gallery’s shift from a community-oriented Chinese visual arts festival to its role today as the UK’s only non-profit gallery dedicated to local and global art informed by east and south-east Asian cultural backgrounds. In addition, Japanese film-maker Umi Ishihara’s experimental film Nocturnal Melody will preview on 9 October.

Zhu believes the four-decade milestone presents an opportunity for reflection, as well as for clarity: who is esea contemporary accountable to, and why does it exist?

“We want to demonstrate that an organisation rooted in Manchester can contribute meaningfully to global artistic conversations while remaining deeply accountable to its communities,” says Zhu, who is based between Manchester and Berlin. Explaining that east and south-east Asian perspectives are underrepresented in UK institutions, particularly within major galleries and permanent collections, she adds: “Our role is not simply to provide visibility but to create the conditions for artists to develop ambitious work on their own terms.”

Yuan’s Two Improvisations – an original experimental film – bleeds punk. A pair of obscured musicians sing loudly. The band’s frontman, projected as a dark shadow, represents the “Yeren”, a lingering mythical Chinese misfit creature rumoured to roam the mountainous regions of Hubei. Adjoining the film, which shows musicians singing lyrics about deception and marginalisation, is an installation of Yuan’s architectural models of urban houses and skyscrapers (some built in China, and others handmade in the UK) which sit on an illuminated stage in the gallery foyer, mirroring Manchester’s Northern Quarter outside the window.

For Zhu, the showcase – like much of the work exhibited at esea contemporary – illustrates the dual reality of living between cultures, and across borders, while challenging certain narratives. Typically punk is not associated with Chinese people in the west, who are often stereotyped as reserved, “or worse, powerful”, Yuan tells me. “And Wuhan is always the city people talk shit about,” he adds. By drawing cultural comparisons with Manchester, both past and present, Yuan encourages the viewer to question traditional narratives about rebellion in China, as well as in his home town. Yuan relates to the Yeren, he tells me: living in the diaspora, the artist is deemed an outsider.

Alongside the gallery’s physical exhibitions, 40 Years, 40 Voices continues the celebrations online, inviting artists, stakeholders and longstanding collaborators to reflect on the organisation’s legacy and future. Art worker Kwong Lee, now director of London’s Deptford X festival, recalls participating in Beyond the Chinese Takeaway in 1992, marketed as “the first exhibition of its kind researching the innovative works of contemporary artists of Chinese origin living in Britain”. Meanwhile, trustee Xu Wenkai, a digital artist known as aaajiao, hopes “esea contemporary remains a space where Asian artists don’t have to justify themselves – where the work speaks first”.

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

It’s a marked change for a venue that – long before 2020 – had been embroiled in controversy. During the late 90s and 00s, the gallery changed dramatically due to China’s growing cultural and economic influence. In 2013, the Riba award-winning space launched Conservative MP George Osborne’s Manchester China Forum, playing host to global trade deals and geopolitics.

According to Chan, the British government’s pro-China policy determined and ultimately restricted the artworks that were exhibited: “The gallery couldn’t be directly critical of the people the government were trying to do business with,” they say. “Galleries are shaped a lot by the political landscape, that’s where their money comes from. There’s often a manipulation of information.”

Today, Zhu has re-rooted the institution within the community. Her popular Esea art outreach programme encourages east and south-east Asian residents over 50 to create art, combating loneliness and providing an opportunity for migrants to speak their native language. She also invests in local talent: the organisation’s events and visitor experience manager was initially hired as front of house while working as a cashier at Wing Yip, a nearby Chinese store. At the same time, Zhu intends for the gallery to appeal to a broader audience, and uses more “accessible” artforms – including video, music, food and games – to do so.

It’s a marked change for an institution that had been embroiled in controversy. “The place lost its way for a while” says the artist Gayle Chong Kwan, who presented her first solo exhibition at the gallery in 2002 – and who facilitated the boycott in 2020. “Thankfully, that change happened.”

Chris Zhongtian Yuan: Two Improvisations is at esea contemporary, Manchester, to 13 September.

Wake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the world

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 11:00:04 GMT

The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait

If Americans vote for a Republican majority in both houses of Congress in November, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” But they must not spend it in Canada or China or anywhere else outside the US. So said Donald Trump in Texas on Wednesday in advance of the forthcoming midterm elections. He further told voters to “Pretend that I’m on the ballot”. It was a climactic moment in an almost two-hour rant.

Trump does not have the required trillion dollars in his pocket, and it would be illegal to disperse such a sum without congressional approval. In any case, JD Vance now appears to have rowed back on the promise.

Observers from abroad must beware: it is unwise to subject Trump’s populism to the discipline of truth. Trump also said Americans should thank him for attacking Iran since that country was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”, which it intended to use against them. It was the old Saddam Hussein gambit.

The problem is that almost every one of Trump’s speeches refers back to himself, as if he and the United States were synonymous. He claimed to have won the presidency three times. He says: “If we hadn’t won the last election, I’m not sure that our country right now would even exist.” He added that the arena where he was speaking was packed, with crowds outside clamouring to get in. Pictures show it half empty.

Anyone watching can see why there has been much medical debate over whether Trump is exhibiting signs of narcissism disorder. Key symptoms are mendacity and inconsistency. In 2021 members of the House of Representatives called for the constitution’s 25th amendment, by which a president can be declared unfit for office, to be invoked over the Capitol Hill riot. But that has a high constitutional threshold, requiring a majority of his sycophantic cabinet to declare him unfit.

As for more conventional checks on a wayward president, they have proved extraordinarily weak. A Congress over which Trump exerts a populist terrorism has been reluctant to use its powers to call him to account. He has flagrantly declared wars without congressional authority, abused executive orders as “emergencies” and frozen federal spending to halt the “advance [of] Marxist equity”. He has even tried to redefine US citizenship, which is unconstitutional.

Very gradually some institutions supposed to hold the White House in check are finding muscle. Judges have blocked attempts to limit birthright citizenship. Trump’s blanket firing of public officials is being legally challenged, although the supreme court has often sided with him. Even the Senate Republican leader, John Thune, has balked at Trump’s proposed Save America Act – which would require anyone voting to show documentary proof of US citizenship. Its outrageous gerrymandering would shrink Democrat votes and aid Republicans. It is an echo of the Jim Crow laws of the post-civil war south.

Where this president leaves the US’s longstanding allies overseas is less clear. Visitors to the British embassy in Washington are traditionally warned that “we disagree with America about almost everything, but remain the closest of friends”. Britain distanced itself from war in Vietnam but joined the US, inexplicably, in Iraq. But nothing has come near Trump’s sustained abuse of Britain in the past year on everything from defence spending to wind turbines. He sees the UK as “weak” and “on the edge of disaster”. It was “once” the US’s greatest ally. But by implication, is no more.

This opens the central weakness in Anglo-American relations that Trump has made explicit. This is the assumption that the US would honour the principle of collective defence and go to war with Russia, in the event that Russia declared war on Europe. This held during the cold war, with the US’s guarantee of Europe’s security taken as axiomatic.

Since the end of the cold war, that guarantee has become ever more flimsy. Despite events in Ukraine, it has long seemed implausible that Russia would declare nuclear war on the west, let alone on America itself. It is therefore equally implausible that the US could threaten Russia with nuclear retaliation.

At which point a central essence of the Nato alliance starts to crumble. European governments have seen a president ready to annex foreign countries, invade others, disrupt world trade with aggressive tariffs and defy international law. Can such a wayward and egocentric man, devoid of domestic constraints, really be relied on to exercise extreme caution and dependability in circumstances where nuclear weapons are at issue – whether or not the end of the cold war has diminished the threat of east-west confrontation?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In other words, nations should start looking realistically at the defence of their own continent and their own borders. There is no new world order any longer. That balloon has been punctured.

Friends of the US have always relied on its constitution to hold autocratic presidents to the straight and narrow. But not since Andrew Jackson in the 1830s has there been one who flouts law and convention as brazenly as Trump. Over the next two years his nation’s political institutions are to be sorely tested. But then he will be gone. Perhaps only then will Britain learn his legacy.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 10:00:01 GMT

AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late

Another day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work is probably going to kill us – that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard.

But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s very public resignation from the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “crunch time”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself.

The frisson of alarm over AI running through Westminster this week was real, sharpened by news of Anthropic – which pitches itself as being more safety-conscious than its rivals OpenAI – declining for the first time to submit a new model for scrutiny by Britain’s AI safety watchdog. We are now entering a far more disruptive era of AI, dominated not by relatively basic chatbots but by agents designed to undertake tasks on humans’ behalf, making their own decisions about how to complete them. Unfortunately, it turns out even basic life admin requires the kind of fine judgments that come instinctively to humans but seem remarkably hard to codify for machines.

Take the over-zealous agent tasked recently by its Australian client with booking him into a pilates class, which responded to finding the class full by hacking the gym’s website and booting other people off the waiting list. Now imagine it blundering into something more life-threatening than a gym class. When Coxon says his industry hasn’t fixed problems with alignment, and when OpenAI’s chief scientist warned last week that no lab had solved them well enough to carry on scaling this fast much longer, what they’re talking about is this failure to replicate in machines the values and assumptions humans apply to decisions without even really knowing they’re doing it – including the sense of how far it’s justifiable to go in getting what you want.

A series of reported escapes by agents supposedly confined to OpenAI’s lab for testing, some of which contrived to access the internet behind their human supervisors’ backs and conduct real-world cyber-attacks, has meanwhile raised serious questions over the industry’s ability even to experiment safely. (Unnervingly, Coxon says newer models seem to know when they’re being tested, making it easier for them to deceive researchers.)

And agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life: think how easily a cyber-attack on air traffic control, or NHS data systems, or even water purification systems could cause mass fatalities.

What’s happening in some frontier AI labs now is arguably the equivalent of the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb, but this time led by private companies in a mad dash for wealth and market dominance, not scientists under an elected government’s command. Britons meanwhile got more say in sugar taxes on junk food than we’re getting over regulating something theoretically capable of rendering us extinct.

Given time, of course, it might prove possible to replicate in machines the vast ecosystem of social ties, moral codes, intensive parenting and state policing that humans have developed to stop us behaving like sociopaths. (Only this week, Google’s DeepMind reported an experiment where 100 agents were given a maths problem and told not to cheat: though a minority promptly did cheat, a larger group either snitched on them to the humans or helped devise technical fixes.) But time is the one thing nobody dares to give themselves in the middle of an arms race, which is why it’s high time for governments to act. We need an international agreement to press pause, not on AI research as a whole, but on the riskiest projects, until we better understand whether it will ever be possible to mitigate the dangers or control the results. Since it’s hard to imagine Donald Trump voluntarily sacrificing US geopolitical or commercial advantage over China for the good of humanity, leadership may have to come for now not from above but below, where industry insiders spooked by their own work are making common cause with the rest of us.

More Americans are now concerned than excited about AI, according to polling this summer from the Pew Research Center – and unusually it’s the young who are most hostile, afraid it will not only take their jobs but make it harder to form relationships or think creatively. (That’s what growing up on social media seemingly does for trust in tech.) Even big business seems increasingly sceptical, with almost two-thirds of international executives surveyed by the consultants McKinsey this summer reporting no measurable impact on earnings from using the admittedly basic AI tools now available to them.

Warnings about an AI bubble triggering another 2008-style global financial crash haven’t helped, while plans to build giant, energy-guzzling datacentres are meeting angry local resistance on both sides of the Atlantic from people who can’t see what’s in it for them. Pressing pause on potential Armageddon looks in the circumstances less like the luddite option, and more like a smart way for tech companies to avoid a full-on backlash that will sweep away the good with the bad.

But if the AI doomers are right, then the window to do so may not always be open. It’s time for humans to stop and think about what we’re doing to ourselves – while we alone still have the power to do so.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

It’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaos

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 07:00:04 GMT

I’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-up

It’s finally happened. National treasure Monty Don is hanging up his TV garden shears and saying goodbye to Gardeners’ World after more than 20 years as the BBC show’s lead presenter. I’ve been a grower for more than a decade myself, and Monty has been a steady and wise omnipresence throughout my journey – especially as he’s been on the right side of contemporary gardening debates over the environment and wildlife, and the use of chemicals and peat in horticulture.

That is where the overlap between our worlds of growing end, though. My modest patch of a few veg beds at the end of a small, chaotic and mostly gravelled garden is a universe away from the two-acre dreamscape that is Longmeadow, Don’s garden at his home in Herefordshire. I suspect I’m one of millions who’ve looked longingly at Monty’s remarkable space and the impressive infrastructure (not to mention hired hands!) that make it so special, and cursed the fact that such an ideal garden will never be within reach of us ordinary folk. That’s not to say that it hasn’t been a glorious setting for Monty to share his abundance of plant wisdom from, but now that the search for his replacement is presumably on, perhaps this is an opportunity for a little reimagining.

A handful of times over the years, television production companies have asked whether I’d present a new show they were trying to get commissioned, which they hoped would capture the attention of the next generation of gardeners. Unfortunately, not one of them had an idea that wasn’t just a rehash of a makeover show, and that approach is the antithesis of my growing ethos. I’d want to persuade more gardeners to nurture their plots intentionally – so you wouldn’t catch me encouraging anyone to bring that unhinged (and mostly unsustainable) Changing Rooms-style energy to their outside spaces. As a format that honours the true nature of gardening – embracing the steady process of cultivation and not looking for quick results – Gardeners’ World has got the market cornered, and I hope it keeps going for many years to come.

And while I’m not not saying the next Gardeners’ World presenter should be me (wink-wink), I do have some thoughts on who it could be. There are clearly potential successors waiting in the wings, all of whom have proved themselves worthy. The favourite appears to be Frances Tophill, who would be my first choice from the shortlist too. But what I’d really like to see are dispatches and insights from different gardeners in different regions.

The UK might not be the largest country, but its weather and climate vary massively. A gardener in Cornwall is going to encounter a very different set of conditions to a gardener in Cumbria. And as we face a future in which the seasons become less predictable, tried-and-tested gardening advice may well become moot. Wouldn’t it be wonderful and highly informative to instead see what is possible – and impossible – in different parts of the country, following a consortium of gardeners and their outdoor spaces throughout the growing season?

While I’m dreaming up my perfect show, let’s say that some – perhaps all – of those spaces should be ordinary gardens tended by ordinary gardeners. People who are time-poor, resource-light and chaotic in their execution, due to their many other responsibilities. I’m thinking of it being similar to Top Gear flinging family-friendly hatchbacks around its test track as well as luxury sports cars.

This may well be a pipe dream, and perhaps it’s only me who is interested in truly realistic gardens. But I think I’ve reached my personal saturation point with aspirational, unobtainable spaces wholly detached from my own growing reality. There’s so much to be learned from the ingenuity and scrappiness of those who succeed – as well as fail – at creating gardens filled with flourishing crops and blooms, when their space and wallets have limits and their lives are full.

The one thing that I wouldn’t want to change, though, is how soothing Gardeners’ World can be. I know I’m not alone in finding the tone and the pace – even the ambient sound of bees buzzing past – to be a balm for the soul, and plenty of that can be attributed to Monty’s gentle screen presence. I’d wager that the upcoming generation of gardeners also have jangled nervous systems that could do with some calm – so let’s hope that whoever comes next understands the assignment and keeps the show sailing on a steady and serene trajectory.
