Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfold

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 06:00:03 GMT

The world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home

US marks 25 years since 9/11 – latest updates

As clear as that cloudless September morning, Jenna Jacobs McPartland remembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.”

A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at its Windows on the World restaurant. “I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.”

Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel, born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York, would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity, and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried.

Speaking from Fairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post-9/11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart, and you visit it.”

McPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants, and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.

McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.”

On September 10, 2001 George W Bush travelled to Florida to push education reform legislation. AOL was seeking a big stake in AT&T’s cable unit. Promising tennis player Lleyton Hewitt, 20, had just swept Pete Sampras aside to win the US Open.

America seemed unassailable. It had won the cold war and enjoyed a relatively peaceful 1990s as “the indispensable nation”, in secretary of state Madeleine Albright’s framing. From fiscal years 1998 to 2001, the federal government recorded four consecutive budget surpluses.

But what had been dubbed “the American century” came to an apocalyptic end on the next morning. Nearly 3,000 people were killed as 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania.

Among the most wrenching images were office workers leaping to their deaths from the burning twin towers. On the wall of the national September 11 museum in New York is a quotation from James Gilroy, a resident of lower Manhattan: “She had a business suit on, her hair was all askew … This woman stood there for what seemed like minutes, then she held down her skirt and then jumped off the ledge … I thought, how human, how modest, to hold down her skirt before she jumped.”

Unthinkably, both of the 110-storey towers collapsed, unleashing giant clouds of ash and dust on the streets of lower Manhattan as fragments of paper fluttered down like confetti. David Blight, a historian who advised the museum, which opened in 2014, said: “It’s the most visual event in history – so photographed, so much footage, so many documentaries. It is so shocking, so horrifying that you can’t watch it without a certain weeping. One of the things that should never stop about 9/11 is the essential grief of it. There is a sheer sense of unspeakable loss.”

At first the loss brought out America’s better angels. Firefighters and first responders displayed inspiring courage. Ordinary citizens queued to donate blood. The nation came together as rarely before and received global sympathy, with Russia pledging support, Iran holding candlelight vigils and Nato invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in its history. Bush visited Ground Zero in New York and, wielding a megaphone, declared that “the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon.”

They did. The US invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaida and topple its Taliban protectors, a war that would drag on for a record 20 years only for the Taliban to return. Bush then attacked Iraq on the false premise that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction, at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives.

The global war on terror expanded into a sprawling enterprise of military intervention, intelligence operations, detention and interrogation. Some suspects were tortured, including through waterboarding at CIA “black sites”.

A quarter of a century later, 100 million Americans are too young to remember 9/11 and only from this vantage point, perhaps, can the consequences be seen clearly.

Historians and policy experts interviewed by the Guardian suggest that the reaction to 9/11 was a profound strategic miscalculation that distracted the US from the rise of China and sowed the seeds of its own decline.

“9/11 is when things began to go wrong for the United States,” suggested Bill Galston, a former policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The United States was at the apogee of its post-cold war power on September 10 and then, through a series of missteps and misjudgments on both the foreign and domestic front, we have thrown away a great deal of not only our power but our credibility.

“In my judgment, 9/11 set off a quarter-century of misgovernment in the United States and we’ll pay the price for that for a very long time.”

Did Osama Bin Laden, the al-Qaida leader who masterminded the attacks, win after all? If the metric of victory is measured by Bin Laden’s immediate, messianic desire to establish a global caliphate and expel all western presence from the Middle East, he evidently failed. Al-Qaida was eventually hunted to near-extinction and Bin Laden himself killed in a Pakistani compound in 2011.

But if the terrorist’s success is measured by the magnitude of the self-inflicted wounds they provoke from their target, Bin Laden’s legacy is a slow, autoimmune decay within the US, it may have exceeded his darkest fantasies.

Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser under Barack Obama, said: “Bin Laden in some ways failed in his intentions. He wanted the United States out of the Middle East. He wanted to topple certain governments in the Middle East. But in other ways 9/11 is the most successful terrorist attack in history insofar as it prompted such an overreach from the United States that we hastened our own decline, division and betrayal of our own story.”

Like countless others, the course of Rhodes’ life was changed by 9/11. He was 23 and working on a city council election campaign at a polling site on the Brooklyn waterfront. He saw the second plane hit the twin towers and watched the rest of the carnage unfold. The event spurred him to move to Washington, and get involved in foreign policy.

He regards the cost of 25 years of “forever wars” as incalculable. They placed a huge burden on the Americans who fought them and had to deal with problems ranging from war wounds to the opioids crisis. They also contributed to the destruction of the rules-based order, paving the way for Russia’s Vladimir Putin and others to reject the rules and use the language of counter-terrorism to justify stringent crackdowns.

Then, there is the domestic sphere. Rhodes says the typical Fox News viewer during the Bush years was promised great victories over foreign enemies. “When nations don’t keep those types of promises, when you unleash that kind of nationalism and xenophobia and you don’t succeed on the battlefield, history tells you that people start to look for enemies within to blame,” he explained.

“My experience in the Obama years is very much that ‘the other’ that had been constructed around terrorists morphed into the Black president or the immigrants crossing the southern border or LGBT people. The segments were the same but the enemy had changed to an enemy within.”

Donald Trump launched his first bid for the presidency, a decade ago, against the backdrop of this search for blame. Promoting the lie that Obama is a Muslim, demonising immigrants, and promising to build a border wall, he cut through by railing – in a clear break from Bush and Republican orthodoxy – against political elites for waging forever wars that he claimed he would stop (he has called the invasion of Iraq “the single worst decision ever made” in US history).

“You’d never have Donald Trump as president without 9/11 because he basically stepped into that slipstream of othering people and captured the ugly xenophobia and nationalism that had been unleashed and the anger that people, particularly on the right, felt at being gaslit by the Bush administration for eight years,” said Rhodes.

“It’s no coincidence that Trump’s ascent was marked by the destruction of Jeb Bush, who symbolised all those broken promises.”

Now, Rhodes argues, the war on terror has come home. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are “basically running counter-insurgency strategies in American cities, with the same military equipment that we used to fight wars now in the hands of law enforcement”, he said. “Some of the same people have signed up to do it, and the same surveillance technologies that we use against terrorists abroad are now used against Americans. We are now living in the theatre of the war on terror and it’s obviously a source of growing discomfort to many Americans.”

As the US overextended itself abroad, the machinery of endless war also boomeranged back on to the domestic front, eroding civil liberties and legal norms it claimed to defend. The Patriot Act, which dispensed with rules that prevented the state monitoring US citizens without “probable cause”, was passed just 45 days after the attacks, radically expanding the powers of law enforcement agencies.

Jameel Jaffer, who moved to New York just weeks after the attacks before spending 14 years litigating national-security cases for the American Civil Liberties Union, saw the transition from the ground level. His early volunteer work involved visiting immigration detention centres in New York and New Jersey, where hundreds of immigrants had been rounded up in the panic after September 11.

Over the next decade and a half, Jaffer litigated major constitutional battles involving warrantless wiretapping, secret detention and targeted killings. He watched as the National Security Agency developed an enormous surveillance apparatus, much of which became public through reporting and, later, Edward Snowden’s disclosures.

Jaffer, now executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, argues that many of the surveillance authorities created after 9/11 remain in place or have become even more sweeping. “So much of what’s going on now is traceable to the institutions and authorities that were created after 9/11 and that the courts failed to limit,” he said. “The use of the material support laws to prosecute anti-ICE protesters in Texas. The use of the Espionage Act to threaten and intimidate journalists who are writing about issues that the public needs to know about.

“Even the arrests and detentions and threatened deportation of students for protesting on university campuses: that policy is built on deference that the courts extended to the executive branch 25 years after 9/11. We are absolutely living with the legacy of these decisions made and policies instituted in the years after 9/11.”

Guantánamo Bay, where 780 men and boys have been imprisoned since 9/11, became one of the most visible symbols of the era. The Iraq war produced the Abu Ghraib scandal, in which US personnel and contractors subjected detainees to abuse, humiliation and torture.

Obama tried, and failed, to shut down Guantánamo. Trump has since faced intense criticism for sending immigrants to the prison.

Jeremy Varon, a history professor at the New School in New York and leading member of Witness Against Torture, a group seeking to close Guantánamo, said: “The United States committed to a programme and policy of torture, violating international law and its own laws, and an element of gratuitous cruelty and even sadism became operationally part of the war on terror.

“People equated national strength and security with the ability to inflict harm on vulnerable others. The more violence we dish out, the stronger and the better and the safer we somehow are and a lot of that violence boomeranged and made new enemies.

“But beyond those it victimised, it destroyed any pretence that we’re a constitutional order that obeys the rule of law, that honours national treaties. It inaugurated an era of executive power operating with utter impunity and immunity. The lawlessness of Trump is an utterly predictable consequence of the contempt for the rule of law, oversight, checks and balances that the Bush administration displayed.”

For Varon, there is a clear connection between the brutal methods of the global war on terror and the excesses of ICE under Trump. He points to notorious detention centres in Texas and New Jersey where inmates routinely suffer medical neglect, and recent reports of harrowing deportation flights where migrants are flown to Africa in shackles.

“People report living in fear and filth and squalor without access to basic hygiene, to attorneys,” he said. “Families are broken up and there’s a level of the willful infliction of suffering that is staggering and wouldn’t seem to be even a necessary part of the broad immigration strategy.

“Again there’s this sick need that collectivities feel they have to dominate those that they perceive as lesser. Muslims and Arabs were the great community under suspicion and that’s been replaced to a large extent by brown-skinned migrants from other parts of the world. When you have a rhetoric that demonises people as criminal and subhuman, it invites their mistreatment.”

The collateral of this 25-year trajectory has been the evisceration of trust in US public institutions. Varon argues that this environment birthed a “post-truth condition” where empirical reality was abandoned and conspiracy theories thrive.

The official September 11 narrative was challenged by the “truther” movement, which suggested the attacks were an “inside job” orchestrated by the US government. The Bush administration’s false claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction laid the groundwork for Trump’s cynical style, which relies on the public believing that everyone is lying so they might as well vote for a demagogue who is honest about it.

Only last week it was reported that Trump has ordered the Department of Homeland Security, created in the aftermath of 9/11, to burnish his false claims of election fraud by embarking on a weeks-long search for non-citizens on US voter rolls, a move seen by watchdogs as an intimidation effort ahead of November’s midterm elections.

The president will attend a commemoration at the Pentagon on Friday while JD Vance will be at the national 9/11 memorial in New York.

Once again crowds will pause to remember the workers desperately waving clothes, sheets and tablecloths from the doomed towers, the firefighters who climbed staircases and never returned, the airline passengers who stormed the cockpit to stop United Airlines Flight 93 reaching its target in Washington.

But will they weigh what came next, what it cost the US in blood and treasure and what might have happened if the country had chosen a different path?

“Consider what we didn’t do,” said Rhodes. “I sometimes am haunted by this. The trillions of dollars spent on a forever war: what could that have been spent on? Climate change, universal healthcare, public education. There’s a real opportunity cost to how we chose to spend our time and resources.

“If you came down to Earth from another planet and you had to make sense of the fact that the United States spent several trillion dollars chasing a relatively small number of terrorists around a few countries, toppling governments and then fighting insurgencies, when it has huge problems with deindustrialisation, with its education system, with the onset of climate change, you would think this is a country that has gone insane.”

Osama bin Laden shook the world on 9/11. Today it is clear how his wider plans failed

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 05:00:02 GMT

The al-Qaida leader envisaged an economically battered US withdrawing from the Middle East – and a global Muslim uprising. Then the tide turned

On 11 September, 25 years ago, Osama bin Laden drove with a small number of al-Qaida retainers and aides to a remote location in eastern Afghanistan. His convoy of SUVs was accompanied by a minivan converted into a makeshift communications centre.

The van’s rudimentary equipment did not allow Bin Laden to watch the 19 men he had started sending to the US more than a year before fly planes into the twin towers in New York and the Pentagon near Washington DC, killing about 3,000 people. But he listened as shocked radio announcers broke the news.

Within days of the murderous assault, the then president, George W Bush, had begun framing the US response as a global “war on terror”, a clumsy, inappropriate and counterproductive strategic choice.

For those of us reporting on the ground during this period – watching US bombers over Afghan mountains and tanks in Baghdad streets, interviewing aspirant suicide bombers or the victims of attacks by extremist groups that proliferated from the UK to the Philippines – the errors and failures of this “war on terror” were glaring.

This unprecedented and indiscriminate series of campaigns would lead to invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, involve torture, renditions and alliances with dubious regimes, cost huge amounts of money, destabilise swathes of the Middle East and bring suffering to millions of people.

Was this what Bin Laden had hoped to achieve?

It is frequently suggested that Bin Laden’s aim with the 9/11 attacks was to draw the US into wars that would weaken its economy and lead to its eventual collapse, much as the Soviet Union had been fatally drained by the war in Afghanistan between 1979 and 1989. As a young militant, Bin Laden had witnessed this conflict and even participated in it, albeit in a marginal role.

But there is little evidence to back this theory up. Though Bin Laden was undoubtedly inspired by the earlier conflict, he rejected as unrealistic his aides’ warnings that the planned attack would bring US troops to Afghanistan, probably expecting little more than another barrage of ineffective missiles by way of reprisal. Certainly, he had no plan when the US troops did come. Within months of the attacks, shaken al-Qaida members described “misfortune [and] disaster”.

In reality, Bin Laden had a different strategy. He wanted to weaken the US economically and consequently force a withdrawal from the Middle East, not an invasion. In 2004, he boasted that al-Qaida was “bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy”, and that every dollar the group spent attacking the US had cost Washington a million dollars in economic fallout and military spending. This lecture in the advantages of asymmetric warfare resonates today, but was wildly optimistic.

The most costly single event to the US would have been another successful major attack. This never came – an unarguable success of US policymaking since 9/11 and a major failure for al-Qaida. And despite the obvious economic problems in the US, no one could argue that the country has suffered a similar fate to the USSR. Nor, obviously, has it withdrawn its forces from the Middle East.

A second objective of Bin Laden was to force the US to end its support for all the rulers in the region that the once-privileged, Saudi-born dissident so hated, starting with the al-Saud family.

Some of Bin Laden’s targets have been felled since 2001, but not by his actions or by anyone aligned with his vision. Muammar Gaddafi was deposed and killed by western-backed rebels, Saddam Hussein was ousted by the US, and the Assad dynasty’s rule was ended by an al-Qaida veteran who explicitly disavowed the group’s ideology and agenda.

A third aim of Bin Laden was propaganda. His theatre of terror was designed to send a bloody, spectacular and unforgettable message that would radicalise his followers, mobilise new ones and divide communities. He emphasised how attacks such as 9/11 were “just reactions to what’s happening against our children in Palestine, in Iraq, in Somalia, in southern Sudan, in Kashmir”, and called for a global uprising of Muslims against their enemies.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

While the 9/11 attacks undoubtedly focused international attention on the conflicts in which Bin Laden saw Muslims as oppressed by the west or its allies, it brought no significant improvement for the victims. The wave of support for Bin Laden and broader interest in extremist Islamism peaked only a few years after 2001, and then quickly ebbed more or less everywhere. Shortly before he was killed by US Navy Seals in Pakistan, Bin Laden was contemplating a rebrand of al-Qaida, its name tarnished by growing criticism within the Islamic world that it was responsible for killing large numbers of Muslims. His successor, the Egyptian Ayman al-Zawahiri, gave up on the uprising altogether, pivoting to a strategy prioritising the local over the global.

If in 2014, in Iraq and Syria, the Islamic State was able to capitalise on the chaos left by the US invasion, sectarian tension and much else to establish its appalling caliphate, even this was over by 2019.

Since then, such groups’ brand of extremism has been confined in large part to the periphery of the Islamic world, and to zones from which the threat to the developed world is intermittent at best. Al-Qaida and the Islamic State have expanded most effectively in sub-Saharan Africa, exploiting anarchy, failed states, demographic pressures, communal competition for scarce resources and the inattention of the west.

Some analysts add together the presumed strength of groups in Somalia or Mali that have very loose, historic links to al-Qaida, and warn that their total membership is higher than those loyal to Bin Laden in 2001. But these few thousand young men with AK-47s have little in common with the organisation Bin Laden led 25 years ago, both in aims and capabilities.

There are still appalling attacks inspired by Bin Laden’s twisted ideology, and there will undoubtedly be more. This is in part due to the polarisation brought about by his violence and the reaction to it – as was his aim.

But it is noteworthy that neither al-Qaida nor IS have prominent charismatic leaders. One reason is that any such figure will be swiftly killed by the vastly more capable US, making identification risky. But it is also because the era when such individuals could command a significant following is over.

It is often said that for an insurgent or terrorist group to win, it merely needs to survive, but there are exceptions. That al-Qaida still exists is an achievement of sorts for the group and, posthumously, for its founder. But it should not be described as any victory.

Jason Burke is the Guardian’s international security correspondent and the author of The Revolutionists: The Story of the Extremists who Hijacked the 1970s

Houthis Seize a Key Red Sea Island, Threatening Another Global Oil Route

The New York Times September 11, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The militia captured the island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a choke point for trade. Saudi Arabia also announced it had shut down a critical oil pipeline after a drone attack launched from Iraq.

By Adam RasgonShuaib AlmosawaSaeed Al-Batati and Pranav Baskar

Adam Rasgon reported from Tel Aviv, Shuaib Almosawa from Sanaa, Yemen, and Saeed Al-Batati from Al Mukalla, Yemen.

The Iranian-backed Houthi militia seized an island in a choke point of the Red Sea after days of fierce fighting, two Yemeni government officials said Friday, giving Iran and its allies sway over the two main routes for shipping oil out of the Middle East.

The capture of Perim Island came as Saudi Arabia announced that it had shut down a critical oil pipeline, a day after Houthi forces swept into the strategic port city of Mokha in Yemen. Both were major setbacks for the Saudi kingdom, which exports most of its oil through the Red Sea. The kingdom’s foreign ministry said the pipeline was hit on Thursday by drones launched from Iraq.

Perim Island sits in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow pathway at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Its seizure adds a new dimension in the war between the United States and Iran. The Islamic republic has already largely cut off the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf and leveraged that influence to demand concessions from Washington.

Now, the Houthi militia, Iran’s ally, has a foothold at a bottleneck in the Red Sea and could further disrupt shipping there.

The island’s capture came after intense ground battles in Yemen as the Houthis have staged a lightning advance against forces allied with the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has faced frequent Houthi attacks on its tankers and energy facilities, even as its leaders have tried to avoid a direct war with the group, analysts say.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia spoke to President Trump about the escalation in Yemen in calls this week, and urged the United States to take military action against the Houthis, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations. Mr. Trump told him he was not willing to do so, the officials said.

Mr. Trump, however, told the crown prince, the de facto Saudi leader, that he would continue to assist in intelligence and targeting.

Source: Critical Threats Project at the American Enterprise Institute (Houthi stronghold).

The New York Times

A senior administration official said, “The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea.” The official added, “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.”

In July, as tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis escalated, the group declared a blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea, straining oil prices.

The widening clashes in the Middle East in recent days have pushed up oil prices, which surged on Thursday above $109 a barrel for Brent crude, the international benchmark. Oil prices eased to around $104 a barrel on Friday, but are still at their highest point since July.

Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, said that the Houthi takeover of Perim Island was a “game changer,” enabling the group to more easily destabilize Red Sea shipping.

“In the past, they were creating uncertainty,” he said, but “now they’re controlling everything around Bab al-Mandab, the land and the islands.”

The Saudi government said on Friday that a strategic pipeline that carried oil across the kingdom to its Red Sea ports was also “subjected to several attacks” on Thursday and that the pipeline had been shut down “as a precautionary measure.” The kingdom’s foreign ministry said the attacks had resulted in some injuries, but did not specify any particular group responsible. Militias backed by Iran operate out of Iraq.

Satellite images obtained on Friday by The New York Times showed a plume of black smoke more than 60 miles long rising from an area close to the pipeline, which allows Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

Josh Holder/The New York Times

On Friday, Iran’s foreign ministry appeared to offer a statement supporting the Houthis.

“The Islamic Republic of Iran reiterates its principled and consistent position on the need to respect Yemen’s independence, national sovereignty, and territorial integrity,” the ministry said.

The foreign ministry spokesman told Iranian new outlets that “plans were underway” for talks in Oman between Iran and Persian Gulf states on Monday to “discuss regional issues,” including the Strait of Hormuz. Omani officials did not immediately comment.

Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, did not explicitly say whether the Houthis had taken Perim Island. But he asserted in a statement that the “Saudi enemy” — apparently referring to forces allied with the government — had been expelled from more than 5,000 square kilometers, about 2,000 square miles, of territory.

Mr. Saree also said that shipping was safe for all companies except Saudi ones.

Saudi Arabia has not commented publicly on the capture of Perim Island. On Friday, though, the Yemeni government’s forces appeared to announce an air force counteroffensive, warning civilians to avoid roads linking Taiz to Mokha and Mokha to Dhubab, which sits directly on Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The New York Times

For weeks, the Houthis have carried out intermittent attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on energy facilities. This week, the Saudi authorities said 73 civilians had been injured in Houthi attacks on the southern part of the kingdom.

On Friday, the Houthi-controlled broadcaster Al-Masirah said that Saudi Arabia had launched two rounds of airstrikes on the port of Mokha. The Saudi government’s Center for International Communication did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It was unclear exactly when the Houthis reached the island. The Yemeni officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. A spokesman for the Yemeni government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Houthis and the Yemeni government have been at war since 2014, when the militia took over the capital, Sanaa. Soon after, a Saudi-led military coalition began a bombing campaign to try to restore the government to power, plunging the impoverished nation into a devastating war.

A fragile truce, reached in 2022, has unraveled in recent months. Since fighting escalated sharply in Yemen last week, at least 46,000 people have been displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration, a U. N. body.

The pace of the Houthis’ recent blitz has been striking, analysts say. But the offensive itself was not necessarily a surprise.

The Saudi bombing campaign ultimately failed to displace the Houthis. The truce in 2022 left the militants with time and territory to prepare for a major offensive, according to analysts.

“They created new weapons," said Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen specialist at Chatham House, a research institution in London. “They restructured the military. They made a much more brutal and efficient version of the state, by raising taxation and spying on people.”

Simultaneously, calls by the Yemeni government for more munitions, anti-drone technologies, air cover and intelligence support from the world have largely gone unanswered, said Hisham Al-Omeisy, a senior Yemen adviser at the European Institute of Peace.

And a Saudi effort to consolidate Yemen’s fighting units, splintered by regional factions and rivalries, has struggled.

The Houthis “chose a time they could exploit” those fragmented forces, said Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni researcher and policy adviser. Taken together, the factors made for what Mr. Al-Omeisy called a “perfect storm.”

Reporting was contributed by Maggie Haberman, Eric Schmitt, Abu Bakr Bashir and Josh Holder.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Pranav Baskar is an international reporter at The Times, based in New York.

A Tale of Two U. S. Opens: $20,000 vs. $100 (Yacht Not Included)

The New York Times September 11, 2026

U. S. Open

Advertisement

Supported by

If money is no object, the luxury options are plentiful. But if you take the subway and don’t mind watching the match on a screen, a budget day at the finals is possible.

By Hilary Howard and David Waldstein

Photographs by Hiroko Masuike

On Tuesday night, about 100 people gathered on the lawn outside Hudson Yards to watch the U. S. Open for free on a 30-foot screen. Many New Yorkers that night complained of being priced out of the live matches at the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center in Queens.

“In sports, if I have to spend more than $200, I won’t do it,” said Maurie Keppens, 27, a Carlos Alcaraz superfan and Ph. D. candidate from Ghent, Belgium. She had hoped to watch Alcaraz, the tennis star from Spain, live, but was dispirited when she saw that the cheapest tickets were going for $500.

Despite the fact that the tennis center is on city-owned land run by a nonprofit, the U. S. Open continues to cater to the moneyed class. Over the past year it removed some 2,800 upper-level seats to make room for two new levels of luxury suites, which can accommodate up to 35 people and cost at least $29,500, all of which are booked for finals weekend. The Open gift shop is selling out of its $1,400 gold tennis necklaces and touting heavily embroidered bomber jackets for $600. With its Disney World-inspired express lines and $100 caviar chicken nuggets, the tournament seems most eager to court the wealthy.

The tennis, however, has been thrilling, and Friday night could very well be the match of the summer, when two American men, Frances Tiafoe and Ben Shelton, battle it out for a spot in the final. But it won’t be a cheap night out. Some upper-level tickets for Friday’s match at Arthur Ashe Stadium were going for more than $1,500 — more than twice their face value.

Add a burger and a beer — that’s another $50 per person. Factor in car service to and from the tournament, and the total could jump by $200 to $400, depending on surge pricing, making a middle-of-the-road, two-ticket date to the Open cost north of $3,000.

What’s left is one tournament for two different demographics: the frugal and the big spenders. “The Open doesn’t seem to be for the middle class,” said Jason Reyes, 44, of Jackson Heights, Queens.

Although he lives just a few subway stops away from the live matches, Mr. Reyes had instead opted for a lengthier commute to the lawn at Hudson Yards in Manhattan on Tuesday night. He saved money and he avoided the crowds.

Among the budget-conscious, those lucky enough to get tickets for the women’s final (Saturday) or men’s final (Sunday) will opt for the 7 Train, the cheapest and most popular way to get to the Open. For a few dollars more, there is the Long Island Railroad, which is quicker and lets passengers off closer to the stadium.

But if money is no object, why take the train when you can hire a helicopter? Or charter a boat?

The Williamsburgh Yacht Club in Flushing has a dock just steps away from Citi Field, the baseball stadium for the Mets, and a short car ride to the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center. For $1,500, Dream Boat NY, a charter boat company, will ferry a group of six passengers there from Chelsea Piers on Manhattan’s West Side, even offering a Champagne lunch ($80 per person).

For some, the wild blue yonder is the only way to go. According to the Blade helicopter company, which has been flying passengers to the U. S. Open for five years, interest in the service has, ahem, taken off this year.

“We’ve never seen it like this before,” Lee Gold, a spokesman for Blade, said. The flight from the 30th Street heliport takes 5 to 7 minutes and lands at LaGuardia Airport. From there, a Blade SUV drives you right to the grounds, which is included in the $595 helicopter ride.

Perhaps the most exclusive way to enjoy the Open this year is to buy courtside tickets affiliated with the Blue Room, a staid, clubby space in Ashe steps away from the court with a private entrance manned by security officials and well-dressed hosts who are determined to guard the privacy of their VIPs.

Earlier this week, a single front-row seat with Blue Room privileges for the men’s semifinal match was listed for more than $23,000. The night before the match, though, the asking price dropped to a more reasonable number: $12,000.

There are perks that accompany the high cost. Fans are offered prosecco upon arrival and an array of to-go snacks, including sushi, olives and chocolate-covered almonds. Customers may enjoy an open bar and a sit-down, three-course meal that includes razor-clam ceviche, blackened monkfish au poivre and crème brûlée.

The Blue Room is temporary. Next year, new “bunker suites” and clubs will offer similar levels of service.

As of Friday afternoon, Ticketmaster had courtside seats affiliated with other hospitality suites in the stadium that ranged from about $2,600 to $34,950, while seats that were close to the action without the perks went for between $1,500 and $5,800.

Before the match has even started, the big spender could have dropped more than $20,000 for two tickets.

But there are other ways to soak up the vibe. Seats in the very last rows of Ashe (we’re talking X, Y and Z) are still available for the finals, starting between $200 and $500, depending on the session. So for those who live or die by being inside the Thunderdome, it’s still possible to get there this weekend by subway, have a few snacks and cocktails and buy a pair of seats in the nosebleeds for between $600 and $1,200.

Another tactic is to buy cheap seats right before a match, especially when tournament favorites, like Coco Gauff, don’t make it to the finals. On Friday afternoon, for example, 90 minutes before the first men’s semifinals match, tickets in the top section were going for as little as $20, according to Ticketdata. com.

A more reliably affordable option is the Fan Fest Grounds Pass, which provides a kind of once-removed U. S. Open final experience. Technically, fans with a grounds pass would not witness a live event, but they would be in a stadium with other fans — even if the match they are watching is on a jumbotron. But many love it.

As of Friday, grounds passes are $30, but this is the 2026 U. S. Open, and the resale frenzy has already infected this affordable option, with some passes going for $47 for the men’s final on Sunday.

A grounds pass also provides access to the giant screen in the fountain plaza outside of Ashe as well as access to food stalls, like Salt Hank’s, which offers a $38 French dip sandwich that people line up for and influencers find irresistible.

Many U. S. Open employees and veteran fans slip out to Tommy’s Doghouse, the quintessential hot dog and burger shack that feels as if you’ve landed in the late 1980s, when Ivan Lendl and Chris Evert ruled the Open, and a hot dog costs what you might expect a hot dog to cost: $4.

All of this to say, the most affordable way to be near the action this weekend could cost under $100 for two grounds passes and some wise food budgeting.

Insiders who want to see the finalists up close know to keep an eye on the practice courts next to Ashe a few hours before the matches. Most players go there to hit and loosen up. It’s a great way for fans who wouldn’t dream of spending thousands for courtside seats to get close enough to see and hear how incredibly hard the top players hit the ball.

And then there’s Hudson Yards, on Manhattan’s West Side. The site, which has lawn chairs and food trucks nearby, has developed a devoted following since showing the Knicks during their championship run and World Cup matches earlier in the summer.

“I love the ambience here,” said Patrick Whalen, a retiree who lives in Chelsea. “They should have more of this around town.”

On Tuesday night, as two American women tennis stars, Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro, squared off in the quarterfinals in Queens, budget-minded New Yorkers settled in with drinks and bites to watch the freebie match.

“This would be $75 at the Open,” said Mr. Reyes, showing his array of ballpark food: jumbo hot dog, two bags of chips, French fries and two sodas. All for $33.

Mr. Reyes, a passionate fan, has been to the U. S. Open, the French Open and the Italian Open. In Europe, “everyone who walks in is treated well, even if you just have a grounds pass,” unlike the two-tiered system he has encountered in New York, he said. “It’s a grind just to find a seat at the Open.”

His roommate, Drew Kromm, who had joined him for the night, put it simply:

“I’m here because it’s free.”

Hilary Howard is a Times reporter covering how the New York City region is adapting to climate change and other environmental challenges.

David Waldstein is a Times reporter who writes about the New York region, with an emphasis on sports.

Hiroko Masuike is a New York-based photographer and photo editor for The Times.

Connections Coach

For five decades, the artist has made sculptures that are larger-than-life — and also singularly reflective of his own.

The artist Jeff Koons, photographed with two of his handblown gazing balls at his studio in Hell’s Kitchen on June 9, 2026, wears an Hermès jacket, hermes. com; and Bottega Veneta shirt, bottegaveneta. com. Credit... Photograph by Renee Cox. Styled by Zara Mirkin

Supported by

By Nick Haramis

ON THE FIRST page of the French writer Michel Houellebecq’s 2010 novel, “The Map and the Territory,” a fictional midcareer artist named Jed Martin is having trouble completing his new painting, “Damien Hirst and Jeff Koons Dividing Up the Art Market,” an imagined encounter between two of art’s wealthiest and most polarizing figures. Although Martin is satisfied with his portrayal of Hirst, the English artist known for his diamond-encrusted human skulls and vitrines of taxidermied animals — you could make him “a rebel artist (but rich all the same) pursuing an anguished work on death,” Houellebecq writes — he can’t quite capture the other man’s essence. Koons, the American who still holds the record for the most expensive piece ever sold at auction by a living artist, appears, according to Martin, “to have a duality, an insurmountable contradiction between the basic cunning of the technical sales rep and the exaltation of the ascetic.”

Koons the pop culture figure is often at odds with Koons the artist, causing some deep ambivalence among the art establishment. He’s at once an esoteric conceptualist and a marketing genius rivaled only by Andy Warhol and Salvador Dalí, and he’s been a recurring target for the ire of critics, who categorize his work as neo-Pop or kitsch, depending on whom you ask. Nearly a half-century after “The New,” his 1980 debut at the New Museum of Contemporary Art in downtown Manhattan, which featured unused vacuum cleaners and floor polishers displayed like plastic-wrapped sarcophagi in illuminated acrylic cases, he’s shown at practically every major museum, not to mention at Versailles, at a former slaughterhouse on the Greek island of Hydra and on the moon. In a Times review of his 2014 retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, Roberta Smith wrote that it “reek[ed] of Gilded Age excess, art star hubris and the ever-widening inequality gap that threatens this country.” (In his own review, New York Magazine’s Jerry Saltz, Smith’s husband, called the sculptures “huge, shiny baubles for billionaires,” and those were the ones he liked.)

Koons is also arguably more a part of mainstream culture than any other fine artist since Pablo Picasso. He’s been mentioned in the multiplatinum Lady Gaga song “Applause” (“One second I’m a Koons, then suddenly the Koons is me”) and on “The Simpsons.” During a battle sequence in “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” (2023), an animated version of his mirror-polished stainless-steel “Balloon Dog” sculpture is beheaded; miniature replicas of that piece are sold at Walmart. He’s participated in as many brand deals and corporate sponsorships as a rising influencer, collaborating, at one point or another, with BMW, Burton Snowboards, Dom Pérignon, Evian, Google, H&M, Illy, Kiehl’s, Louis Vuitton, Snapchat, Squarespace and Supreme.

On a hot afternoon this summer, Koons, 71, invites me to his studio in an office building in Hell’s Kitchen. In person, he’s disarmingly earnest, never breaking eye contact while describing his practice the way a cleric might talk about a higher calling. He’s not smirking when he compares “Ilona’s Asshole” — a 1991 silk-screen of him and his ex-wife, Ilona Staller, midcoitus — to the 19th-century French painter Gustave Courbet’s “The Origin of the World” (1866). He tells me he wants to encourage others to “realize the sense of the oneness of the information of a universal vocabulary.” The American artist Richard Prince, 77, his friend and contemporary, sums him up like this: “He’s either from another planet or he’s on another planet.”

NEXT TO KOONS’S desk, there’s a store-bought aluminum stepladder with a colorful mirrored-glass orb taped to every rung — a model for a “stairway-to-heaven-type thing,” he says. The work belongs to a new series that expands on his “Gazing Ball” project, which debuted in 2013 and includes blue spheres attached to white plaster casts of everyday items and classical figures (he later integrated reproductions of famous paintings by the likes of Gustav Klimt and Vincent van Gogh). Koons has said the spheres represent “the vastness of the universe and at the same time the intimacy of right here, right now.” (The new pieces will have handfuls of gazing balls in a variety of colors and, instead of just one hovering in front of a painting, anywhere from five to 10 will form clusters on the canvas or jut out in a straight line.)

It’s been a while since his last major museum exhibition — “Jeff Koons: Lost in America” at Qatar Museums in Doha closed in 2022 — but he’s never stopped working. In May, “Split-Rocker” (2000), a 37-foot-tall sculpture of parts of children’s toys covered in live flowering plants, opened to the public outside the David Geffen Galleries at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. He recently partnered with the fashion designer Stella McCartney on a small collection of tops and accessories, and this month Hublot will release a line of his watches. Art making is only part of what keeps the Koons-industrial complex running; one might say he’s the art equivalent of a musician with a Las Vegas residency, spending more time revisiting and reiterating old ideas than coming up with new ones. As he talks, he seems aware of a larger audience visible only to him: apologizing after every digression; repeating himself for impact and clarity; expressing concerns about sounding “weird”; and reassuring me that he’s not also taping the conversation. Early on he asks, although there’s no video equipment in the room, if he should incorporate my questions into his responses, as if footage from our exchange might be broadcast later.

Around 2015, when he started showing the “Gazing Ball” paintings, he sometimes had more than 100 people working around the clock, including a night shift of at least a dozen staffers dedicated to hand-copying versions of works by old masters. One former employee, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, described the studio as a “24-hour facility.” Koons, they said, “slept better knowing that work was being done continuously.” (Legend had it that he’d show up unannounced at any hour, but most of the staff assumed this was company propaganda to encourage productivity.)

Today he’s down to about 20 people, but each almost seems to have carefully rehearsed their role in our exchange. As Koons walks me through the space, explaining some of his more intricate pieces — an eight-foot-tall pink ballerina rendered from a single block of marble that took 12 years to make; a series of 125 small stainless-steel orbs, each representing a unique lunar phase and named after a cultural figure like Nefertiti or Helen Keller, which were shot into Earth’s exosphere in 2024 on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket — they’re ready with irrigation drawings and CT and photogrammetry scans to help me understand his elaborate fabrication techniques. Sitting on his office sofa, Koons explains that he has superior eyesight. “I’m somewhat humble,” he says. “I’m not saying that I shouldn’t be humble, even though I do believe that maybe I’ve been gifted biologically.” Dan, a member of the studio for more than 20 years, pops his head in. Color perception, Dan tells me, is measured in what’s called Delta E, and the average person can discern between hues with a difference of, say, at least 2 Delta E’s. “Jeff can go below 1 Delta E,” he says before disappearing.

It’s easy to see how one might question Koons’s sincerity. He emerged from a 1980s New York art community whose success relied on inventing a persona, then taking it to the extreme. That era of self-promotion was hard on its stars: Warhol died suddenly in 1987 after surgery for an infection; a year later, Jean-Michel Basquiat overdosed; the gallerist Mary Boone, who helped launch the careers of David Salle and Julian Schnabel (and did one show with Koons early on), would eventually spend more than a year in prison for tax fraud. By the fall of 1990, the art market, which had been boosted by new Wall Street money and loose regulations, started to collapse. But Koons’s career never has.

Hirst, 61, a central figure of the Young British Artists, an informal group that emerged in the late ’80s, was a student at Goldsmiths College in southeast London when he discovered Koons’s work in a magazine. “I couldn’t understand it, but I couldn’t stop thinking about it,” he says. One can’t really look at Hirst’s “Pharmacy” (1992), an eerie simulacrum of an apothecary perfectly stocked with empty pill bottles, without seeing Koons’s influence. Yet unlike Hirst, Koons has always endeavored to be as shiny as his art. “Jeff invented himself to the point where it’s not even about whether you believe him or not,” says Hirst. “It’s just a new truth.” Schnabel, 74, the American filmmaker and artist known for his Neo-Expressionist plate paintings, which involve layering pigment on top of shards of broken crockery, met Koons around 1980 and took him under his wing. When he introduced Koons to some older artists at the downtown club Max’s Kansas City, “one of them said, ‘Well, what do you do?’” Schnabel recalls. “Jeff said, ‘I present the new.’ I think they wanted to slug him.”

KOONS HAD A modest suburban upbringing. His father, Henry, worked as an interior decorator and ran a furniture store in York, Penn., a small industrial city about 80 miles west of Philadelphia, and his mother, Gloria, a seamstress, took care of Koons and his older sister, Karen. Early on, they taught him to be self-reliant. As a child, he’d go door to door selling wrapping paper, mints, bows and greeting cards. On weekends, he took private art lessons. “My sister could count further, spell better and jump higher,” he says. “I didn’t know what art was, but I could draw.”

In 1972, while attending a first-year lecture at the Maryland Institute College of Art (he’d spend his senior year at the Art Institute of Chicago), Koons, then 17, was shown an image of Édouard Manet’s “Olympia” (1863), an oil painting of a white prostitute and her Black maid. His professor drew the class’s attention to certain details and what they might have symbolized — a cat; the bouquet of flowers in the maid’s hands — and made connections to a similar piece by the Spanish artist Francisco Goya. For Koons, it was an awakening. “All of a sudden, I realized that painting was about philosophy, sociology, psychology, history and all the human disciplines. I just felt like my life … expanded. And that expansiveness, the opportunity to continue to become and transcend, I feel it every day.”

After graduating, Koons moved to New York and got a job selling memberships at the Museum of Modern Art. To stand out, he turned himself into a kind of canvas, dyeing his hair red, drawing on a Dalí-style pencil mustache and wearing paper vests decorated with fake flowers. Although his style wasn’t for everyone — to avoid offending a visiting Russian diplomat, he was asked to step away from the front information desk for a few hours — membership increased.

At the end of the ’70s, Koons was making sculptures by arranging mass-produced inflatable flowers and a rabbit in front of precut square mirrors. In 1980, he left MoMA and became licensed to sell mutual funds, stocks and bonds and, later, commodities. When he was hired by First Investors Corporation as a broker, a job he’d maintain at various investment firms for the next six years, he recalls his manager saying, “Jeff, you must realize that this is theater. It’s like opera. You need to use your voice.” It was around this time that he started talking about his practice in mystical terms — or, as Smith put it in her review, like the “truest believer in a cult of his own invention.” Over the course of our conversations, he’ll invoke the idea of transcendence at least eight times and refer to his output as “metaphysical,” “biological” and “sublime.” When I ask Koons about the challenge of making and maintaining a perfect object, he says his art is “about these ultimate states of being. In certain ways, they’re better prepared to survive than you.”

As Koons became more famous, his sculptures got bigger: His largest yet, at over 100 feet long, is “Dugong,” an inflatable sea mammal installed in 2022 at Al Masrah park in Doha. Beginning in the mid-90s, his staff started “actually applying the paint” in order for him “to be able to get the work done,” he says. He’s since issued training manuals and implemented precise systems like 3-D digital modeling, paint-by-numbers color codes and standardized lighting requirements across different facilities to ensure “that every gesture, every color, every shape is exactly the way I want it.” So much of the art that we attribute to a single genius wouldn’t exist without invisible labor, going back to the Renaissance, when painters relied on the help of anonymous apprentices. The 20th-century conceptual artist Sol LeWitt practically never executed his wall drawings; younger painters now openly outsource to China. Schnabel suggests that Koons’s art is about the “lack of human touch.”

In 2011, he established his own stonecutting operation in Pennsylvania. He uses foundries in California, upstate New York and rural Germany to cast his stainless-steel sculptures, and some of his marble pieces are fabricated by master carvers in Carrara, Italy, and nearby Pietrasanta. He went to northern Italy to supervise the production of “Banality” (1988), a series of large, mostly porcelain and wood sculptures, many of them depicting mass-culture symbols — Michael Jackson and his pet chimpanzee, Bubbles; the Pink Panther embracing a topless woman; Buster Keaton on a donkey — that he would exhibit at New York’s Sonnabend Gallery. To viewers, these are perhaps his most difficult works; Koons seemed to be trivializing the notion of fine art, testing his audience’s patience. One sculpture, titled “Ushering in Banality,” made of polychrome wood and looking like something out of a Precious Moments catalog, depicts a young boy and two angels pushing a pig. Koons saw himself as the pig. “I was trying to call myself one before anybody else could,” he says. “I thought, ‘If you’re going to judge me, fine, because I can only go up from here.’”

To communicate specific flesh tones to the Italian ceramists, he’d show them censored clippings from pornographic magazines. In one, he came across Staller, the Hungarian model known as Cicciolina. “I was captured by her beauty,” he says. “But I was also captivated by an Eastern European fantasy, how she posed in front of painted backdrops of serpents or ocean waves that were quite surreal.” While he was working on “Banality,” he also saw a different photo of Staller — a member of Italy’s Parliament by then — leaving a party at the prime minister’s house. “I’d kind of become an art star,” Koons says, but he wanted to be something more. In 1989, when the Whitney invited him to design a New York billboard, he knew just what to do. “I’d been thinking about participating in society in a vaster way, so I thought, ‘I’ll be a film star.’ And in my mind, the easiest way to be a film star would be to make porn.”

Koons reached out to Staller and asked her to take pictures with him. What they shot together — “simple nude photos” at first, Staller says, that progressed to scenes “with penetration” — became Koons’s most grotesque series, “Made in Heaven” (1989-91). “I was trying to remove all guilt and shame in any form,” he says. In 1991, Koons and Staller got married and, a year later, their son, Ludwig, was born. The couple separated shortly after, at least in part because Staller had continued her career in the adult entertainment business. Their subsequent divorce and yearslong custody battle — which, according to legal records, “involved both parents removing their child to foreign jurisdictions against explicit court orders” — was financially ruinous. (“We made some mistakes,” Staller admits. “He’s an artist, I’m an artist — two strong characters. Maybe that’s why it didn’t work out. But we had two and a half very good years.”)

To cover his legal fees, Koons says, he “liquidated everything,” selling off his art collection and his own proofs. During this period, he also reconnected with his first child, Shannon, now 51, who had been put up for adoption by Koons’s college girlfriend. Coincidentally, she’d been raised about 20 miles from where Koons grew up in Pennsylvania, swimming in the same rivers and going to the same ice cream shop. (Koons visited his son during his childhood in Italy; now 33, Ludwig lives in New York and the two are close.)

What was arguably the low point of Koons’s life was also a turning point in his career, during which he produced his most impressive and enduring projects. Each was a gleaming shrine to childlike innocence and wonder. “I was trying to make art that my son could look on in the future and would realize I was thinking about him very much during these times,” he told The Guardian in 2009. There was “Puppy” (1992), a massive dog-shaped topiary that can house up to 60,000 flowering plants (“It’s about fertility and giving up control”) and “Celebration” (1994-2019), a series that includes a giant bouquet of mirror-polished stainless-steel tulips (as well as a balloon dog, party hat, hanging heart and Easter egg). He also began construction on a nearly 11,000-pound heap of Play-Doh, made of polychrome aluminum, that would cost a small fortune and take him almost two decades to finish. This kind of risky investment boosted Koons’s public profile and started a conversation that has persisted ever since about his fortune — the making and losing of it, and the making of it again — which has been indelibly linked to his art, as if to render it simultaneously more and less worthy of our attention. Whatever desperation kick-started this conversation, Koons can’t help but perpetuate it. One doesn’t unintentionally design the packaging for a $20,000 bottle of Champagne, after all.

Koons says he thinks of his success as a “double-edged sword,” though, then compares himself to several Renaissance and Baroque painters. “Michelangelo, Leonardo, Raphael, Rubens, Rembrandt — they were all extremely wealthy,” he tells me. “The idea that artists are supposed to suffer is new.”

However much these works have become symbols of capitalistic hedonism (his orange “Balloon Dog” sold for roughly $58.5 million at a Christie’s sale in New York in 2013), the irony is that Koons did indeed suffer to make them. Prince compares it to an apocalyptic scene from the 1959 sci-fi movie “On the Beach,” in which, after a nuclear war has destroyed most of the planet, some survivors detect a Morse code-like radio signal and believe that it means there are others. “Of course, there’s no one sending the signal — the device got caught in the wind,” Prince says. “The signal just represents hope. Jeff’s work is the signal.”

A MONTH AFTER our first meeting, I return to Koons’s studio. I suggested we meet at his conjoined Upper East Side townhouses or take a fitness class together (he had a gym built in his former studio, where he’d train five days a week), but he’d rather stick to the office. When I arrive, his assistant hands me a Dunkin’ coffee.

Koons greets me in a pair of white chinos and a blue button-up shirt. He looks rested, although he’s just returned from a 10-day work trip to Germany, Italy and Greece, and the following week he’ll attend an annual ideas summit for industry leaders, celebrities and politicians at a private club in rural Montana. “We usually don’t speak too much about these conferences publicly, but there are hosts who bring people together from different areas of life to discuss subjects that are interesting today, whether it’s biology, A. I. or politics,” he says. In 2014, Koons invited Gaga to attend.

When he’s at home in New York, he and his wife of 24 years, Justine, 54, a painter and sculptor and Koons’s former sculpture assistant, like to shoot pool with some of their younger children. In total, Koons has eight, six of them, ranging in age from 14 to 25, with Justine. To transport everyone from the city to their family farm in Pennsylvania — it once belonged to Koons’s maternal grandparents, who used the property as a weekend getaway — they usually ride in what he calls the Koonsmobile, a customized stretch van with individual captain’s chairs.

The studio is quieter than normal. In a fluorescent-lit room, an employee is polishing a gazing ball. Elsewhere, men on motorized lifts are following his paint-by-numbers system to create photorealistic depictions of waterfalls and the cosmos. Koons directs my attention to a nearly finished canvas. Its base layer, a rendering of a volcano, took at least two years for an assistant to complete. During the process, Koons himself applied a few colorful brushstrokes on top — “gestures,” as he refers to them. “It takes like 10 seconds.”

On my way out, Koons says he wants to show me something else. We return to his office to look at his reproduction of the Flemish artist Peter Paul Rubens’s “The Drunken Silenus,” an early 17th-century painting depicting an intoxicated Silenus, the companion and tutor of the Greek god Bacchus, encircled by satyrs, a tiger and a breastfeeding mother. A blue gazing ball seems to float in front of the scene. Standing side by side, we stare at the orb. In it, we can perceive the painting it’s attached to, the room in the background and ourselves. He looks at me through the rounded mirror and says, “See?” We stay like that for a while, until he breaks the silence. “Everything’s dependent on us,” he tells me. “We’re affirmed.”

Art hasn’t just motivated him; he’s committed himself to turning each milestone — his move to New York; his stint as a broker; his first marriage; his fatherhood — into part of the lifelong practice of becoming Jeff Koons. His personal history has only made the persona seem more exaggerated. Prince says, “I understand why people would ask themselves, ‘Can I believe what he just told me?’”

As I prepare to say goodbye, I’m not sure. It’s now impossible to distinguish the showman from the artist, and trying to separate the man from either of those characters does them all a disservice. “The only thing we ever have,” Koons says, “is just who we are.”

Grooming by Inna Shats. Photo assistants: Richard Rose, Kyle Aaron Lacy. Grooming assistant: Micka Omura. Stylist’s assistant: Jesa Chiro

I’ve long been fascinated by Jeff Koons. Not only for his sculptures, which have become emblems of American art — maybe even the American Dream — but also for the critical response to them. Perhaps no living artist has been as celebrated and derided. His work sits so squarely between art and commerce that it’s difficult to even know *how* to engage with it.

Nick Haramis is the editor at large of T Magazine.

For the 25th Time, New York Marks the Shattering Loss of 9/11

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Sept. 11

Advertisement

Supported by

At a ceremony in Lower Manhattan, elected officials and loved ones of those killed in the 2001 terror attacks gathered in solemn remembrance.

By Michael Wilson

Gordon M. Aamoth Jr.

Edelmiro Abad.

Marie Rose Abad.

A quarter-century after the terrorist attacks that shook New York City and the world — an ashen morning followed by years of grief and repair, rebuilding and war — dignitaries and mourners gathered once again in Lower Manhattan to read aloud the names of those killed when hijackers crashed airplanes into the World Trade Center and sent the twin towers crumbling to the ground.

Milton G. Bustillo. Thomas M. Butler. Patrick Dennis Byrne.

The ceremony on Friday took place beneath a canopy of swamp white oak trees between the two memorial pools where the towers once stood. The pools were designed to appear bottomless, and their cascading waters lent a whispering backdrop to the morning. Relatives held aloft photos of the dead, forever young, as children on the podium spoke directly to grandparents, aunts and uncles they had never met.

“My dad always talks about how wonderful you were,” one girl said after naming a lost relative. She is among the 100 million Americans born since that day.

Some people used their turns at the microphone to criticize the federal government for continuing to work with Saudi Arabia in the years since the Sept. 11 attacks. Family members of those who died have sought to hold the kingdom responsible in federal court, claiming that its government provided support for the hijackers.

Among them was Terry Strada, an official with 9/11 Families United, whose husband was killed in the attack. Her organization has tried for years to pursue legal action against the Saudi government. The kingdom has denied involvement.

“It has been one betrayal after another,” Ms. Strada said from the podium. She urged the assembled elected officials to “stand with survivors, stand with Americans.”

Later, a nephew of Lisa Marie Terry, who died in the attack, accused “the deep state” of hiding the truth. He called on President Trump to “release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia, while what’s left of the victims’ families are still alive to see it.”

Four living former presidents, from Bill Clinton to Joseph R. Biden Jr., stood silently nearby. Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, was also in attendance, despite a petition signed by thousands of people, including victims’ family members, urging him to stay away. He was joined by former Mayors Bill de Blasio, Michael R. Bloomberg and — awkwardly — Rudolph W. Giuliani, who was in office on Sept. 11 and earlier this week said that Mr. Mamdani’s presence at the ceremony “offends me.”

Mr. Mamdani nonetheless approached Mr. Giuliani at the ceremony. The two men shook hands, and Mr. Giuliani’s position seemed to have softened. Cameras captured him apparently telling Mr. Mamdani: “I’ll pray for you. It’s a really hard job.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul was there, as was Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and former Gov. George E. Pataki of New York, who had also called on Mr. Mamdani to skip the event.

Vice President JD Vance stood in for Mr. Trump, who instead attended a ceremony at the Pentagon. In his remarks, the president talked about how Sept. 11 had changed America.

“Twenty-five years after the attacks, we know the world will never return to the way it was at that dawn on that beautiful, peaceful Tuesday morning, 2001,” Mr. Trump said, “before the towers fell, before the Pentagon was hit, before the specter of evil, and this horrible, horrible evil came crashing into our lives.”

In New York, as is custom, there were no speeches from elected officials, putting all the focus on the families. The names of the victims read on Friday included the six killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

Uniformed firefighters present and past — many older now, grayer — gathered at the ceremony, at churches and, later, in the city’s barrooms, to raise glasses to their 343 fallen brothers.

The effects of Sept. 11 played out for months, years. The Fire Department would go on to be further gutted by mass retirements of high-ranking officers. The Police Department lost 23 officers that day, and was reshaped by the introduction of new tactics, units and equipment to fight terrorism.

On Friday, there were the traditional six moments of silence, marked with the tolling of a bell: one for each of the towers struck, one for each building’s collapse and two for the plane crashes at the Pentagon and in Shanksville, Pa.

A seventh moment of silence was added this year to commemorate those who had died of Sept. 11-related illnesses. Mr. Mamdani’s administration this week released more than 170,000 pages of previously withheld city records about the air quality around ground zero after the attacks. The documents seem to suggest that New Yorkers were encouraged to return to the area before it was safe to do so.

The mournful wail of bagpipes — a fixture at hundreds of Sept. 11 funerals — rang out at the start of the memorial. Elsewhere in the plaza, Yo-Yo Ma played his cello softly behind the reading of the names.

Robert William O’Shea. Elsy Carolina Osorio Oliva. James R. Ostrowski.

Some relatives reached for levity, thanking their lost family member for whatever role they played in pulling off “Knicks in five.”

One of the relatives reading names sought to describe the importance, for him, of returning to this event every year.

The man, Jim Giaccone, spoke of his older brother Joseph Giaccone, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald’s offices in the north tower. His brother loved a glass of good wine while his Bolognese sauce cooked on the stove on Sundays for his family, The New York Times wrote in 2002.

“This ceremony is essential,” Mr. Giaccone said on Friday, choking up. “At the very least, I get to come here one day a year and speak my brother’s name, Joseph Michael Giaccone, out loud, and you hear it. And he is here, and he is present, and he is never forgotten.”

Four hours and 2,983 names later, the ceremony drew to a close, and the spouses, siblings, children and grandchildren of the men and women killed at work or while rescuing others that day turned away from the site and back toward the lives they’ve built. It was Sept. 11, 2026.

Reporting was contributed by Andy Newman, Liam Stack, Jeffery C. Mays, Maggie Haberman and Shawn McCreesh.

Michael Wilson, who covers New York City, has been a Times reporter for more than two decades.
