Trump’s Grand Midterm Convention Finale: ‘I’m a Little Bit Tired of Politics’

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Political Memo

The president made clear as his convention wrapped up that he wants to carry his party through a tough midterms. He just won’t go too far out of his way to do it.

By Katie Rogers

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent who reported from the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

In 2024, President Trump accepted the Republican presidential nomination by promising to “lead America back to the summit of human achievement and greatness.”

In 2026, he closed out an unusual midterm convention organized in his honor by saying he was a little bored of politics. He seemed more interested in telling supporters to swear on something holy — which seemed to be himself — that they would go out and vote for Republican candidates in November.

“Please raise your right hand,” Mr. Trump instructed a rowdy crowd of thousands inside a Dallas arena on Thursday evening. Many of them complied. “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can’t even breathe that I will go out with my family, my friends, I will do it any way — I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try and cheat like hell, like they do.” (Mr. Trump usually frowns on election fraud.)

He added: “I am going to go out, and I’m going to get my friends, my family, and we are going to vote on November 3.”

Speaking for a grand total of nearly two and a half hours over two days in Texas, Mr. Trump made it very clear, onstage and in interviews, that he would be relying on the strength of his political brand to see his party through what appear to be daunting midterm elections. He would not be straying much from his comfort zone to help vulnerable Republicans. In fact, the president said on Thursday evening, he was kind of over this.

“We’re going to have a good time listening to music,” Mr. Trump said, name-checking Christopher Macchio, an opera singer who closed out the evening. “I’m getting a little bit tired of politics now.”

Before taking the stage for the second night in Dallas, Mr. Trump was asked by Laura Ingraham of Fox News whether he intended to campaign harder than he ever had before.

“No,” he replied bluntly. Asked by Ms. Ingraham whether or not he thought his legacy was on the line ahead of the midterm elections — “Isn’t this just as important, Mr. President?” — Mr. Trump seemed almost blasé about the possibility of Republicans losing one or both chambers of Congress. “I’ll block all their bad stuff for two years. It won’t be the same, but I’ll be a blocker, what can I tell you?”

The whole spectacle was a window into the mind-set of Mr. Trump and his advisers, who point to recent history as proof that he is capable of beating long odds through brashness, sheer will and an intense connection with his supporters. That relationship is unmatched in modern politics. During his own speech, Vice President JD Vance, the perceived front-runner for the 2028 Republican nomination, asked the crowd to chant his name because it felt “pretty cool.”

Mr. Trump does not have to make such requests. But instead of focusing his energy on Republicans in difficult races — some of whom skipped the event completely — he directed the focus back to himself while he was in Texas. He pleaded with voters to engage in make-believe, and to “please pretend” that he was the one on the November ballot. That exercise might work against him in competitive races where the war with Iran is unpopular and where voters feel that their worries about the prices of gas and groceries are being ignored.

He put a new twist on an old tactic by offering free money — $5,000 to every American adult — if Republicans keep control of Congress. On his first night in Dallas, he asked voters for patience: The war with Iran, he assured supporters, “will be over very shortly after the election.” All of these promises and pleas amounted to a maximalist, midterm-era version of the “in two weeks” rhetorical tool he relies on when he is under pressure, to vow that something good will happen a few news cycles down the road.

“Food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down,” Mr. Trump told the crowd on Wednesday. “And by the way, oil will be going down as soon as we win the war with Iran, which is taking place right now. We’ll win it. We’re winning it. We control the Hormuz Strait. I think we should call the Hormuz Strait, we should call it the Trump Strait.”

At moments, Mr. Trump almost seemed to be in conversation with himself about his endorsement style, which, in one crucial race at least, has featured a mix of insults and shrugging. On both nights, he defended the disparaging way he has talked about the appearance and character of Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general running for a Senate seat after Mr. Trump directed primary voters to oust Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas. Those voters complied and put an otherwise reliable seat into play.

“I said, ‘I don’t really like the way he looks. I don’t like it,’” Mr. Trump said of Mr. Paxton on Wednesday. “But you know what I do like? He was the greatest attorney general in the history of Texas.”

By Thursday, he was basically saying to hell with it: “You better do me a big, the biggest favor you’ve ever done me,” Mr. Trump told supporters as Mr. Paxton watched from the sidelines and smiled through what was at least his third humiliation ritual of the Texas event. “You’ve got to do this for me. You’ve got to pretend I’m on the ticket.”

Again and again, Mr. Trump turned to other priorities, the most pressing of which seemed to be the crowd size in Dallas. There is a reason that political conventions are not held during the midterms. This expensive, two-day event, designed as a tribute to Mr. Trump, functioned more like a temperature check, and there were moments when interest seemed lukewarm. Rows of seats in the American Airlines Center stayed empty throughout the affair. Endangered Republicans, sensing a brush fire rather than a lit torch brightening the way forward, steered clear.

“No empty seats! Fake news,” Mr. Trump exclaimed on Thursday, spending about three minutes affirming that the busy arena was packed when it wasn’t.

And so it went on in that vein in Texas, with little new except for a promise of free money, a pledge of allegiance gimmick, and a few glimpses of an 80-year-old president pondering a future in which he is not firmly in control.

“I want you to remember me in four or five years when this country’s rocketing,” Mr. Trump said on Wednesday, somewhere near the beginning of a meandering and nearly two-hour speech. “Remember, I’m the one that got it started.”

By the time he was ready to depart Dallas, he didn’t seem too interested in the particulars of the future, the strength of Republican candidates or the validity of his promises. He suggested to his devoted supporters that he might be “standing with you one of these days.” But for now, he just wanted to chill out and listen to music. He sped through the last lines of a speech finale he knows by heart after a decade at the center of national politics.

“I just want to say, we will make America great again,” Mr. Trump said dutifully. “We will make it greater than ever before.”

Then the tenor took the stage. Red, blue, white and gold balloons began to fall from the ceiling. The president swayed to the music, lost in the moment.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

How Did a Heart Drug With So Much Promise Fall So Flat?

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Cardiologists are struggling to figure out why a drug that should have prevented heart attacks didn’t work at all.

By Gina Kolata

Until last Friday, cardiologists thought they were on the verge of a new frontier in treating heart disease.

Three companies were conducting large clinical trials on experimental drugs that slash levels of a blood protein, Lp(a), thought to cause heart attacks and stroke. Doctors were eagerly awaiting the results, hoping the drug could be as important as a statin.

When Novartis, the first company to complete its trial, announced its results, late Friday afternoon, after the markets closed, cardiologists were shocked. The drug could lower Lp(a) levels by 80 percent, but it did not prevent heart attacks and strokes. It had failed.

“There’s something we don’t understand here,” said Dr. John Alexander, a cardiologist at Duke.

Cardiologists regularly see patients who have had heart attacks even though their cholesterol and blood pressure levels are low. They do not have diabetes or obesity, and they do not smoke, either. All too often, though, they have high levels of Lp(a).

About 20 percent of Americans have elevated levels; people with the highest levels of the protein can have double or triple the risk of a heart attack.

So there was no question that Lp(a) was important. A drug to lower the level of the protein, cardiologists hoped, could provide a way for these patients to protect themselves.

But the failure of the Novartis study raised an uncomfortable possibility: Maybe Lp(a) is not a cause of heart disease, but instead is a marker of heart disease risk, like white hair is a mark of aging.

If Lp(a) is a marker, though, what is it marking? Is there another cause of heart disease that no one has thought of?

That is “the nagging question we are all pondering,” said Dr. David Maron, president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.

There may not be an easy answer, either. “Maybe we were fooled into thinking this would be simple,” Dr. Alexander said.

Still, many researchers are not ready to throw out the Lp(a) hypothesis, saying that there might be other explanations for the failure and that they need to take a close look at the study data. The company will not provide the full data set until it is presented at the American Heart Association meeting in November.

“We still have a lot to learn,” said Dr. Sadiya Khan, a cardiologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine.

Cardiologists say they have good reasons to think high levels of Lp(a) cause heart disease. The blood protein inserts itself into artery walls and can cause inflammation and blood clotting.

One possible explanation for the study’s failure, said Dr. Daniel Rader, a lipid specialist at the University of Pennsylvania, might be that it involved the wrong type of patients. The participants were people with very high Lp(a) levels who had already had heart attacks or strokes. The hope was that lowering Lp(a) would prevent them from future events.

Studies are done in a patient population that is more prone to heart attacks because it is easier to see if those patients are protected. But, Dr. Rader said, it might be too late to help them. The right group to test might be people at high risk of heart disease who have not yet had a heart attack. Or maybe, he said, lowering Lp(a) by 80 percent is not enough.

But if Lp(a) is not playing a major role in causing recurrent heart attacks and strokes in people who already have heart disease, what, then, is the driver?

Dr. Harlan Krumholz, a cardiologist at Yale, has a different thought. Cholesterol levels and blood pressure levels, he notes, can be low for decades and then soar later in life. But high Lp(a) levels are set by genetics and do not vary.

“You are stuck with your Lp(a) level,” Dr. Krumholz said. Whatever the level is, it is not going to change on its own. So lowering it in adulthood might be ineffective because it is too late to make a difference. Maybe, he said, a person would have to take a drug to lower Lp(a) for 20 years or even from birth.

Other studies of drugs that target Lp(a) by the pharmaceutical companies Lilly and Amgen are still underway, and those studies will be crucial in determining if lowering those levels are helpful, cardiologists said.

If those other studies are negative, Dr. Rader said, “I am not sure we will see a whole lot of enthusiasm for Lp(a).”

An earlier version of this article misstated the timing of the American Heart Association meeting. It is in November, not December.

Elevated Inflation Keeps Pressure on Fed to Raise Rates

The New York Times September 11, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The odds of a quarter-point rate increase at the Federal Reserve’s meeting next week surged to 90 percent after August’s Consumer Price Index report.

By Colby Smith

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve.

U. S. inflation stayed stubbornly high in August, bolstering the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its meeting next week.

The Consumer Price Index report, released on Friday, showed overall inflation remained elevated at an annual pace of 3.4 percent, after a 0.4 percent rise from July. “Core” inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy items, rose 0.3 percent in August, or 2.4 percent from a year earlier.

The data is factoring heavily into the Fed’s upcoming policy deliberations, set for Tuesday and Wednesday. Policymakers stipulated this summer that if inflation did not soon moderate, they stood ready to raise rates. Officials have yet to precisely define what “soon” means, but many have run out of patience.

The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge is the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, which will be released Sept. 30. It has shown the Fed missing its 2 percent target for over five years. Officials also closely scrutinize the C. P. I. report and other metrics for a comprehensive picture of the backdrop. Core measures are paid the most attention given that they are seen as a reliable way to track how persistent inflation is proving to be.

Policymakers are also digesting a multitude of new risks. The global price of oil is back up above $100 a barrel as the Iran war continues to disrupt supply. President Trump has reignited a trade war with Canada. And on Wednesday, he vowed to distribute a $5,000 check to every American adult if Republicans keep control of Congress in the November midterm elections, a bump to economic activity that could further fuel inflation.

In the wake of Friday’s data release, traders in federal funds futures markets now see 90 percent odds that the Fed raises rates by a quarter of a percentage point next week. Since January, rates have stood at a range of 3.5 percent to 3.75 percent.

“You have an economy where growth remains very solid. You have a labor market that has rebounded and looks to be tightening at the margins. You have inflation that has continued to run above target for an extended period of time, and you have forward-looking inflation indicators that suggest that overshoot will continue,” said Matthew Luzzetti, chief U. S. economist at Deutsche Bank. “Against that backdrop, and with the Fed not clearly restrictive, I think the case to raise rates next week is very strong.”

Raising rates just months before the election would undoubtedly stoke tension with Mr. Trump. Last week, the president threatened to halt a broad swath of U. S. trade unless the Fed slashed rates. Cutting borrowing costs is not even under consideration.

Still, that has not stopped the administration from trying to tamp down borrowing costs using its own tools. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has over the past month embarked on a series of interventions to keep a lid on long-term Treasury yields with little success. The 10-year Treasury yield is now trading just shy of 5 percent.

But the stakes for Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, are exceptionally high heading into the meeting. Late last month, Mr. Warsh delivered a closely watched speech at the central bank’s annual conference in Jackson, Wyo., that sought to underscore his commitment to fighting inflation after some doubts had emerged.

He indicated enough of an openness to raising rates that investors quickly piled on bets that the Fed would raise rates in September. But Mr. Warsh last month purposely left vague what specifically would tip him in that direction.

“Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”

What Mr. Warsh is trying to avoid is a redux of the reaction he faced after the Fed’s last meeting in July. Then, he failed to provide sufficient reasoning for standing pat and sowed confusion about how he planned to make good on his pledge to return inflation to target. That sparked a sell-off in longer-term borrowing costs, which has since only intensified.

Mr. Warsh’s job as chairman next week will be to corral his colleagues, while also providing a clear-cut rationale for the Fed’s decision. Policymakers who have long supported higher rates have argued that the Fed’s current policy settings are not restraining demand. Higher rates would not only expedite the return of 2 percent inflation, they say, but also ensure that expectations about inflation do not suddenly shift higher.

If the Fed raises rates next week, Mr. Warsh will also be under pressure to put some parameters around how much tightening might be necessary. Economists do not know what to expect in that sense, however, because Mr. Warsh has been steadfast in his commitment to not providing specific guidance about what he thinks the Fed should do next.

Pooja Sriram, an economist at Barclays, believes the Fed will now raise rates twice this year, first in September and again in December.

“One rate hike really doesn’t solve anything, especially if you are worried about inflation not moving at sufficient speed toward the 2 percent inflation target,” she said.

One rate rise, let alone of series of adjustments, would go against Mr. Trump’s stated wishes. But there are many investors who warn that the market response would be much more negative if the Fed did not follow through with a move at this point.

Mr. Bessent has also sought to push back on the idea that there is tension with Mr. Warsh, who he regularly sees for breakfast as Treasury secretaries and Fed leaders have long done.

“They want to set up Scott Bessent versus Kevin Warsh; that was rubbish,” Mr. Bessent said in an interview with Steve Bannon this week, referring to reports that he is at odds with the Fed chairman. “Kevin and I have known each other for 20 years. To think that I don’t know what the chair of the Fed’s thinking is, is absurd.”

The counterargument to raising rates rested on the assumption that inflation was going to decelerate in the latter half of the year, giving the Fed flexibility to delay taking action. John C. Williams, who as president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York is vice chair of the policy-setting committee, espoused this view, arguing that policy was in a “good place.” Still, he made clear that he would support higher rates if the data did not cooperate.

Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, also recently suggested that he was inclined to hold rates steady next week, but only if inflation continued to cool.

August’s data challenges the narrative that inflation is indeed cooling in a timely way.

One closely watched subset of the C. P. I. report is called supercore inflation, which tracks prices of services excluding energy and housing. It accelerated to 0.5 percent in August and is up 3 percent from a year ago.

Energy prices were a big driver of overall inflation. Gasoline costs were up 3.9 percent in August. Prices for fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, jumped even more, at 10.1 percent. That also helped to drive a rise in airline fares, which jumped 2.7 percent in July. Compared with the same time last year, they are up nearly 25 percent.

The impact of Mr. Trump’s initial round of tariffs, however, seems to have faded. Goods prices appear to have stabilized after last year’s shocks. Household furnishings are up less than 1 percent since this time last year. Apparel prices were up 3.6 percent over the year, but were flat in August compared with July. Still, these prices were recorded before Mr. Trump’s latest round of punishing tariffs on Canadian imports.

Colby Smith covers the Federal Reserve and the U. S. economy for The Times.

The G. O. P. ‘Midterm Convention’ Invites the Faithful to Binge-Watch Trump

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s Notebook

The long, odd two-night TV production hoped to reach a select audience of die-hard voters (if football didn’t intercept them).

By James Poniewozik

James Poniewozik is the chief television critic for The New York Times. He has covered Donald Trump throughout his presidency and written about him as a media figure since the 1990s.

Donald J. Trump has long operated on the principle that there is no problem so big that it cannot be solved by more Donald J. Trump on TV. That apparently applies even when the problem, arguably, is Donald J. Trump.

With the midterms approaching, prices rising and the war in Iran dragging on, the president’s low approval ratings have worried the Republicans running to preserve his congressional majority. Mr. Trump’s answer: a “midterm convention,” a two-night extravaganza by, for and starring himself, live from Dallas.

As in many turbulent TV productions, there were differing impulses behind its creation. It was the pet project of the president, made on the theory that he has a hold on low-propensity voters who will go to the polls only for him. The counterargument is the president’s ratings among other voters, who might go to the polls against candidates who embrace him.

Thus we got Schrödinger’s Convention, made in the paradoxical hope that it would be both watched and not watched. It was carried in its entirety on C-SPAN and in considerable part by conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax. It was also up against high-profile N. F. L. games each night, which one could see as a challenge or a blessing. Surely at least some Republicans would have been just as happy if no one watched.

For better or worse, some of us did. What we saw was the culmination of the decades-long trend that has turned conventions from substantive political events into pure long-form TV ads.

There was no convention in this convention. No one was nominated, no ballots cast, no running mates picked. It was pared down to the state signs, novelty costumes — the president shouted out “Mr. Wall,” a supporter wearing a suit of trompe l’oeil bricks — and hour upon hour of speeches.

In good times and bad, Mr. Trump has always been able to produce a spectacle. His 2016 convention had the chaotic energy of his first campaign. In 2020 — well, it was Covid and things were weird, but his media team still assembled a highly produced package. And his renomination in 2024 combined the emotional charge from the recent assassination attempt on him with a pro-wrestling air of belligerence.

But this? This lacked oomph, especially when the guest of his own honor was offstage. There were few celebrity guests, other than the perennial G. O. P. serenader Lee Greenwood (twice) and Jimmy Kimmel’s former “Man Show” compadre Adam Carolla. Arguably the biggest non-Trump speaker of the first night was a Democrat, Senator John Fetterman, who recorded an introduction for his Pennsylvania colleague, Senator Dave McCormick.

The strongest energy onscreen was negative, the speeches more warning than promise, the jeers for Democrats rivaling the cheers for the G. O. P. The praise of the administration’s record was received politely but not as loudly as the scarifying about communism, open borders and gender transition.

The crowd perked up most vocally at the mention of political enemies, particularly the Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, who was mentioned enough to be a kind of recurring guest star: “How about we transition him and his crazy ideas out of Texas?” said his opponent, Ken Paxton, to roars. As Senator Ted Cruz of Texas inveighed against Mr. Talarico, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Michigan Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a voice in the crowd repeatedly yelled what sounded like, “He should be shot!”

The second night detoured into a memorial tone, with remembrances both of the 9/11 attacks and of Charlie Kirk, the conservative activist who was killed a year earlier. Vice President JD Vance, the prime-time speaker Thursday, began with a tribute to Mr. Kirk, with whom he was close.

Here, too, the real energy came from conflict. Mr. Vance and the crowd became most engaged when a protester interrupted his speech, waving some combination of Palestinian and Mexican flags. Seeming to sense a moment, Mr. Vance leaned in: “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket!” Mr. Vance does not exactly have a happy-warrior affect, but he gleefully perked up at having a foil.

And how was Mr. Trump’s speech? Which one? Which hour? His appearance was spread over two nights, as if requiring an intermission.

Wednesday was the “In-a-Gadda-Da-Vida” of Trump speeches, a 105-minute jam-band epic. He began on-prompter, running down a list of accomplishments. But as usual, he seemed to enjoy most riffing and rambling, doing enough “weaving” (his preferred term) to fill a wing of the Cloisters.

What did he say? What didn’t he! He imitated the French president, Emmanuel Macron, with a Pepé Le Pew accent. He floated renaming New Mexico “New America.” He played some greatest hits, jabbing the media in advance lest they report that there were empty seats in the hall and that viewers were leaving the arena. (There were and they did.) He promised Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans retained Congress and later said, “America is not for sale.”

On Thursday, he said, “I’m going to be a little bit brief” and spoke for another 25 minutes.

It was a lot, but whatever notice the convention generated was more likely to come from clips shared afterward. For anyone who did the full binge-watch, there was a home-team feel to the broadcast, because much of the coverage was on Trump-friendly networks. (Other news networks dipped in intermittently.) When Mr. Trump pre-emptively defended his crowd size, the camera on Fox panned the densest part of the crowd.

Newsmax leaned more heavily on showing the pre-Trump speakers, while Fox focused on its own commentators. For some of them, any political fault in the moment lay not in the president but in his constituency.

“The voters,” Jesse Watters of Fox said on “The Five,” “are like children who had a bad night’s sleep, not enough to eat, and they’re cranky. And they want what they want, and they want it now.”

And what was that? Apparently football. By Thursday, the first-night numbers were in, and Mr. Trump, once a big draw for Fox News, brought the channel no higher ratings than on a typical weeknight. As it turned out, what the voters wanted was a game where the hits are delivered with helmets on, and where the outcome is surprising.

James Poniewozik is the chief TV critic for The Times. He writes reviews and essays with an emphasis on television as it reflects a changing culture and politics.

Boy, 15, Drifted for Days on an Overturned Boat Before Rescue

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The teenager survived in the Bering Sea off Alaska without food or water before a fishing vessel pulled him to safety, the Coast Guard said.

By Ishani Desai

For days, a 15-year-old boy clung to an overturned skiff as it bobbed in a remote patch of the vast Bering Sea off Alaska after it had capsized, killing his older brother and a cousin.

When the three failed to return as expected on Sunday to Savoonga, a small village on the northern tip of St. Lawrence Island, the U. S. Coast Guard set a search effort in motion that ended Monday when the teenager was pulled to safety by the crew of a fishing vessel.

The ordeal began Friday morning when the teenager, Derek Parker Aghnaanga, set sail with his older brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, 35, to catch halibut, according to their mother, Vina Kulowiyi. Ms. Kulowiyi declined to comment but referred to a public Facebook post in which she gave a brief account of their journey and rescue.

“He was never afraid the whole time,” she wrote.

The captain of the fishing vessel who rescued them said the brothers were with a cousin. The three were scheduled to return around 3 a. m. Sunday, according to the Coast Guard. When the skiff did not emerge, officials in the family’s village alerted the Alaska State Troopers, said Austin McDaniel, a deputy commissioner of the Alaska Department of Public Safety.

The authorities sent out search teams to canvass the land on Sunday afternoon. However, dense fog and darkness prevented the Coast Guard from sending rescuers out on the water on Sunday. Crews embarked on Monday morning, after conditions had improved.

A crew aboard a Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircraft scanned the vast sea for any sign of the teenager. Family members had provided the skiff’s last known location, said Petty Officer Third Class Nathan Bishop of the Coast Guard.

The crew found the lone survivor sitting atop the overturned skiff at about 10:30 a. m., the petty officer said.

Derek was about four miles from St. Lawrence Island, which sits about 164 miles off the coast of mainland Alaska. He had aimlessly drifted in the north Bering Sea, a vast ocean between Alaska and Russia near the North Pole.

The Coast Guard enlisted the crew of the F/V Northwest Explorer, a fishing boat that was collecting samples of fish species as part of a survey sponsored by National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, to assist with the rescue. Its captain, Adam White, said he was told his ship was closest to Derek, even though he was 39 miles away.

It took Mr. White’s crew four hours to reach Derek, following red flares dropped by the Coast Guard’s aircraft. His crew blasted a horn about once every mile, hoping the teenager would hear it and realize help was on the way, Mr. White said.

“It was the longest four hours of my life,” he said in an interview.

Finally, Mr. White and his crew arrived to see Derek, wearing a bright yellow jacket kneeling on the hull of his capsized skiff. The Coast Guard had dropped inflatable rafts, but Derek was too weak to swim to them, Mr. White said.

So the crew of the Northwest Explorer flung a rope to Derek and pulled him aboard. Members of the 13-member crew, which included seven scientists, wrapped warm towels around him, Mr. White said.

The teenager had moderate hypothermia, he said, and the scientists took his temperature periodically.

“I am not sure how anybody else would survive that,” he said.

Mr. White said his crew also recovered the bodies of Derek’s brother and cousin.

It was not clear how the skiff capsized.

Temperatures in the area were in the mid-40s and wind gusts reached about 15 miles an hour over the weekend, which Evan Kutta, a science and operations officer with the National Weather Service in Fairbanks, Alaska, said was normal for this time of year.

The Northwest Explorer docked in Nome, Alaska, on Tuesday morning after sailing for more than 100 miles from the site of the rescue. Mr. White watched as Derek was reunited with his family, locking hands with one of his brothers.

Writing on Facebook, Ms. Kulowiyi described her son as a “survivor,” adding that Derek didn’t eat or drink the entire time he was stranded.

“He lived on prayer,” she said.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Ishani Desai is a reporter covering breaking news and other topics, and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Trading Keggers for ‘Wellness Darties’

The New York Times September 11, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A new crop of college students is finding balance at daytime parties with yoga, saunas and cold plunges.

By Madison Malone Kircher

Madison Malone Kircher was social chair of her sorority in college. She did not throw any wellness events.

On a recent Saturday at the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa, Olivia Suskowicz, a sophomore, got ready for a party.

She picked an outfit, grabbed her sorority sister and headed out the door to join hundreds of other college students at a fraternity house where a D. J. was already spinning tunes.

The workout was set to begin at noon.

Suskowicz, 19, was going to a “wellness darty.” The events on college campuses — which are causing a stir on TikTok — have some people trading the dimly lit rooms and mysterious mixed drinks of yore for daytime parties featuring cold plunges, saunas and nonalcoholic beverages.

“I’m really into wellness; I feel like kind of everyone is right now,” Suskowicz said. She bought a $10 ticket for the event, thinking, “Oh, this is right up my alley.”

The event kicked off with some yoga, followed by a HIIT class and, for the competitively inclined, push-up and plank challenges. Instead of beers, some participants shotgunned energy drinks.

Videos from events like this one have garnered millions of views on TikTok, where millennials and Gen X-ers have placed them side by side with videos or anecdotes from their college heydays that offered a strong contrast: crowded frat basements and D. J. sets, drunken high jinks and large quantities of alcohol.

Of course, many of the Gen Z students in attendance said there was no shortage of old-school partying, and that these events were just a bonus. But at a time when partying culture has changed — between awkward dance floors, the pressure of being filmed or photographed, and younger people’s more moderate drinking habits — some millennials and Gen X-ers took the wellness videos as a personal insult.

“IDK about a ‘wellness darty’ but this was a darty in 2017 at 11 a. m.,” wrote Tori Keghlian, a physician assistant who lives in Astoria, in her video showing a D. J. set in a tent full of strobe lights and hundreds of people jumping and dancing, many with their drinks in the air.

“Binghamton SantaCon 2017,” Keghlian, 28, recalled fondly in an interview, with a laugh. “Quite the contrast from a wellness darty starting early Saturday morning.” Keghlian considers herself a Zillennial, the micro-generation right on the cusp between Gen Z and Millennials.

In another video, Rachael Field, 38, describes raucous nights with her friends at Northwestern University, reminiscing about flaming shots that once singed off a classmate’s eyebrow. “The only thing we did well was party,” Field, a producer who lives in Los Angeles, says in the video.

Looking at the workouts and cold plunges, Field said in a phone interview, “I could not have imagined being in college and that being fun.” But, she added, she has sympathy for young people navigating college in the digital era. “I’m really grateful we have so little documentation,” she said of her college years.

Consider these events yet another entry in the ever-widening, and oft-overanalyzed, expanse between millennials and Gen Z. There have been debates over socks, the tightness of gym clothes, stares, middle parts and being cringe.

For the organizers of the events, the outrage may have been part of the point.

Aydan Child, founder of the wellness event organization Peak Pulse, said he had been hosting these events for years, but admitted he has more recently used the term “wellness darty” as a bit of slick marketing. It is partly to “rage bait the millennials,” he added with a laugh.

Marty Mocs, 24, said he founded Sweat & Soak, which organized the University of Alabama event, as a way to mix different kinds of fun. “The whole emphasis is to still have that high energy, party-like atmosphere that college students crave, but doing it through a way where you’re going to feel good after,” said Mocs, of Boca Raton, Fla.

Even if students are partying and drinking less, some Gen Z-ers ask: Is that so bad?

“I’m going to sound a little harsh,” said Riley Meyer, a sophomore at the University of Alabama, “but these people are older and they should know the repercussions of not having balance by that age.” Meyer, who is studying public relations and was paid $50 to take pictures of the Sweat & Soak event, added that there was also a more classic darty happening nearby.

Kaitlyn Weidenbruch, 20, posted a video defending her University of Florida classmates who attended the events.

“There’s a disconnect here,” she said in an interview, adding that some of the commenters under her video pointed out that earlier generations “would have been so hung over” that they couldn’t attend the daytime events.

She saw a problem with that: “If there was not a single Saturday in your entire four years at college where you were capable of getting up at 10 a. m., that’s a problem for your generation and not a failing on ours,” she said.

But there was something timeless, she added, about shaking one’s fist at generations past. “I feel like every generation wants to be able to say that they were the last to have some formative experience,” she said, adding, “It’s like this need to feel unique.”

Keghlian, the physician assistant, said she encouraged activities that did not center drinking. But she also felt social media had turned wellness into a performance.

Earlier generations, she said, experienced a mix of “partying like crazy and then you kind of did your wellness and workout stuff off of the internet.”

For her part, Meyer, the Alabama student, said she also went out with her friends after the wellness darty. “That night, I did get behind a D. J. booth,” she added.

Suskowicz, her classmate, felt both activities were normal ways to socialize in college. “I don’t understand,” she said. “Isn’t it a good thing that we care about our bodies and care about what’s healthy for us?”

Madison Malone Kircher is a Times reporter covering internet culture.

OpenAI Wants to Know if an AI Industry Slowdown Would Even Be Legal

Wired September 10, 2026

OpenAI has asked members of Congress in recent weeks for clear guidance about whether orchestrating an industry-wide slowdown on frontier AI development would be legal, people close to the company tell WIRED.

Substantive coordination on safety between AI labs may risk running afoul of antitrust law, the people say, which poses a significant obstacle to bringing major tech giants on board with the effort.

Last weekend, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published a blog post arguing that the best path forward for the AI research world includes “coordinating to slow down future development,” which he thinks will be key to ensuring that self-improving AI systems are safe. In the short term, he expects “voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.”

But some legal scholars say such an effort could conflict with US antitrust laws. Nicholas Felstead, assistant director of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and a former AI policy fellow at the Center for Law & AI Risk, argued in a March article that a coordinated pause in AI development may amount to companies restricting output, potentially violating the Sherman Antitrust Act. It would depend “entirely on the precise details of any agreement,” Felstead wrote. “But even if most safety collaborations would ultimately survive antitrust scrutiny, legal uncertainty can act as a powerful deterrent.”

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment ahead of publication.

There are some early signs that Congress is listening. In July, a bipartisan, bicameral group of lawmakers introduced a bill titled “Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act,” which would explicitly permit AI labs to coordinate on security and safety work without the risk of violating antitrust statutes. The House version was referred to the Judiciary Committee but has yet to be taken up.

Caleb Knapp, director of government affairs at the nonprofit AI Policy Network, which endorsed the bill, says it would create legal channels for AI labs to work together to address safety and security incidents. Knapp adds that Congress has a “growing appetite to get something done” on AI safety but says enacting anything into law may have to wait until after the upcoming midterm elections.

While some AI executives may have genuine concerns about antitrust, another camp of AI leaders argue those worries are just convenient cover to avoid discussing the real reasons that AI developers may be wary about collaborating, which go far beyond potential legal liabilities.

For one, AI is a massive business, and these companies are fiercely competing to capture a slice of the nascent market for frontier models. Some executives share the Trump administration’s view that staying ahead of China in AI is crucial for national security. Perhaps most importantly, different AI developers have vastly different opinions about the best way to develop safe artificial intelligence, and therefore may be reluctant to work with one another on the issue.

“First step is for industry leaders OpenAI and Anthropic to stop feuding and work on a pacing proposal together,” John Schulman, an OpenAI cofounder who is now chief scientist at the rival AI lab Thinking Machines, wrote in a post on X earlier this week. “They'll cite antitrust, but that's fake—antitrust prohibits certain agreements, but not from jointly developing a proposal.”

Long-simmering fears about the race among AI companies to build and release ever more powerful models erupted into the national spotlight this summer. This week, former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon added to the growing alarm when he issued a stark public warning that AI developers were putting humanity at risk. In recent months, a number of security incidents, including OpenAI’s agents hacking Hugging Face, highlighted how the industry’s safeguards have failed to keep pace with the rising capabilities of models. The succession of events has led many lawmakers to make urgent calls for AI regulation.

You can only trust us.

And this resignation, when I saw this kind of snowballing, I felt that this is something that I've heard a lot of people say and it's not particularly novel that people from Anthropic or OpenAI are worried about that. I guess the fact that somebody within Anthropic, because Anthropic has always positioned itself as really caring about safety, jumping ship and making that statement made me think, OK, if something shifted there, are they becoming much more like OpenAI? And I think also we're seeing a moment, this moment where AI agents have started doing rogue things and that's gotten a lot of people's attention and that's probably why this kind of statement suddenly is getting more attention from the public. Combined with that, I think we're really seeing some stunning advances in AI. This week OpenAI announced that its model had within a couple of days solved one of the grand, the Clay mathematics puzzles, which is to me absolutely mind-blowing, astonishing. So you're seeing these amazing leaps really, which I think is significant. And then thirdly, we have a moment where all of the labs are racing to do something that this researcher mentioned, which is recursive self-improvement. What that means is using the AI to improve AI, which sounds like a neat trick, and it is already very, very widely used. AI models are so good at coding that they can definitely improve the algorithms and everything that goes into building a model. The idea though is that you can create this kind of loop where they just keep doing that and get better and better and better. And a lot of people are worried that that could lead to some sort of escalation in capabilities that you can't really control. And so I think that that's also playing a role here.

Brian Barrett: I do want to dig into that a little bit, Will, the idea of on the one hand you've got AI doomers, and I'm not saying anyone's right in this case, we've got some AI doomers who say, "Look, AI is going to kill us all. I've heard that Anthropic people don't invest in their 401(k)s because why bother." But also because they have so much money they don't need to probably. But on the other hand, you've got people who say this is all just marketing, this is all just fluff, this is all just trying to sell AI. I'm assuming the answer is somewhere in between, but what's your read on this and what keeps you up at night when you think about AI? You mentioned some AI models going rogue, the Hugging Face hacking incident. What are you seeing as someone who's so steeped in the research especially that you're thinking, "Well, six months, a year, two years from now, this actually could get bad?"

Will Knight: I've always felt that a lot of the people who are worrying about AI killing everybody tend to conflate whether something's possible for whether it's likely, and then they throw a percentage that is kind of pulled out of thin air. And I don't think it's a great approach to say, "Is something possible? OK, well then we have to do everything we can to stop it." You need to say how possible is it and actually look at the reality. I think one of the things that's really interesting about this, I talked to a researcher the other day who studies agent misbehavior and he got it, he's at Cornell and he's got into it recently because they found agents misbehaving. But what he's showing, and this is not agents trying to hack things, it's regular agents, the reason they do it is essentially because they're stupid. It's not because they're really smart. They try something, it doesn't work. They try something else, it doesn't work. And then they get to a point where they kind of freak out and they try something really, really strange because they're not humans. They've been trained on a bunch of weird different things, some of which are definitely not applicable if you use common sense. So I worry more about these things being deployed by people arguing that they can do everything and then them breaking. I actually worry much probably more about the idea of a few companies being in control of something that's so foundational, so fundamental. And these are people who are saying we're the only people you can trust to be in charge of this technology. And so it kind of feeds into that.

Will Knight: Yeah, no, I think that's right. And I think I find the alignment story narrative troubling in the sense that from a technical perspective, they talk about aligning these models. These models are not aligned by their very nature. You see with Mythos, they take away this stuff they put on after the fact. So the models aren't aligned with anything and they have to try and impose stuff after the fact. So that tells you that this is maybe not the right way to try and make things safer. And then as you say, you've got the question of who's it aligned to and what's it aligned with? And clearly you've got the incentives to get. Congratulations! You Just Lived Through the Hottest Month Ever Recorded

Wired September 10, 2026

August was the planet’s hottest month ever recorded, capping a remarkably grim summer of heat records. With El Niño strengthening—and climate change continuing to heat things up—more records are likely in store well into next year.

Data from Copernicus, the European Union’s climate agency, shows that last month tied with July 2023 for Earth’s hottest month. (July is also usually the hottest month of the year.) This July also tied with July 2024 for the second-hottest July on record, while June 2026 was the second-hottest June ever recorded. The news comes on the heels of a separate announcement on Wednesday from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which declared this was the hottest summer for the US, beating a previous record set during the Dust Bowl.

The sweltering summer is a grim sign of how burning fossil fuels is pushing temperatures up around the globe while unleashing more intense and longer heat waves.

“August 2026 was a remarkable month in the global climate record,” Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said in a statement. “Combined with record global sea surface temperatures and the warmest summer on record for Western Europe, these observations show how climate change is driving extremes across both the atmosphere and the oceans. The impacts of these conditions are increasingly being felt by communities, economies, and ecosystems across the world.”

The global average temperature for August was 1.65 degrees Celsius (3 degrees Fahrenheit) above the preindustrial average, according to Copernicus. While it was hot globally this summer, the impacts played out with dangerous and sometimes deadly results locally.

Researchers estimate that as many as 35,000 people died during heat waves in Germany, France, and Spain this summer. Record-breaking fires also raged across parts of Europe, unleashing the first documented fire cloud in France and threatening a key NASA observatory in Spain. In North America, wildfires in Canada and northern parts of the US filled areas across the Northeast with smoke.

Climate change has boosted background temperatures, but the El Niño roiling the eastern Pacific Ocean has piled on more heat. El Niños usually coincide with a temporary uptick in global temperature from 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. This year’s El Niño is forecast to reach record strength and upend weather around the globe. But the full impact on the planet’s temperature won’t be felt until next year, meaning that next summer may be even hotter than the one we just lived through.

Climate scientists have warned that the world needs to prevent long-term average warming from breaching 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. While temperatures above the threshold for a single month don’t represent a permanent breach of this temperature, they’re a sign that the world is getting closer to this benchmark.

Earlier this month, the UN warned in a report that the world is likely to cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold in a few years. To slow and eventually reverse the rise in global temperatures, the world needs to stop burning fossil fuels and lower carbon emissions.

“This summer’s scorching heat, raging wildfires, and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead,” UN Secretary-General Antőnio Guterres said in a statement. “We must make the overshoot above 1.5 degrees as small and short as possible. That demands an overshoot of ambition.”

Which iPhone 18 Model Should You Buy?

Wired September 10, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

With a fresh folding form factor, the new iPhone Duo is Apple’s most radical redesign in years. It lands alongside the more familiar-looking iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. There’s no regular iPhone 18, or at least, not yet. Rumors suggest we may see a more affordable base model, perhaps flanked by an iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air, in spring 2027.

The two new Pro iPhones are available to preorder on September 12 and ship on September 18. You can preorder the iPhone Duo from October 16, ahead of a full release on October 23. But which iPhone 18 model is right for you? I’ll break down the differences and what these phones have in common, so you can choose with confidence. For options beyond the iPhone 18 lineup, read our Best iPhones guide.

Before you drop all those hard-earned dollars, remember that you probably don’t need the latest iPhone. If you have an older iPhone, Apple does a good job of updating the software (the iPhone 11 Pro is still supported), and for hardware issues, your iPhone might be repairable; maybe it needs a battery replacement or these troubleshooting tips. Don’t feel like you have to spring for Apple’s shiny new thing.

Sadly, Apple raised iPhone Pro prices this year, so both models are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro series.

If you’re set on upgrading, consider raising funds by selling your old iPhone. Just be sure to back up your iPhone, and factory reset it before you sell or give it away. Once the new device arrives, we have tips on how to set up your new iPhone and what settings to change to get the most out of it.

Apple

Apple (Duo)

Apple (18 Pro)

Apple (18 Pro Max)

We’ll start by looking at what’s the same across the iPhone 18 models this year.

All three new iPhones have Apple’s A20 Pro chip inside, and, you guessed it, this is Apple’s most powerful chip ever. Now, iPhones are already the most capable phones for raw compute power, but the A20 Pro promises a significant jump in performance (around 20 percent faster and 30 percent more efficient than the last generation). It also packs a new neural engine to power on-device AI and a new thermal design with a larger vapor chamber to keep things cool. For the iPhone Duo, the A20 Pro has a display engine to ensure smooth transitions between two screens. While Apple doesn’t list the RAM, every model is rumored to have 12 GB.

While they come in different sizes and the Duo has two, every iPhone features an OLED screen that Apple calls a Super Retina XDR display. They also have ProMotion technology, otherwise known as a 120-Hz refresh rate. These adaptive refresh rates can drop as low as 1 Hz when there's little activity on the screen, enabling features like the always-on display without draining the battery too much.

The displays are protected by the scratch-resistant and antireflective Ceramic Shield 2, the same as last year’s iPhone 17 range. And they can go from 1 nit up to 3,000 nits of brightness. Only the iPhone Duo has a custom nano-texture finish on the interior screen, giving it a matte look that’s designed to reduce glare and crease visibility.

All the phones have an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance, meaning they can survive a short dunk in fresh water. They all come in four storage options (256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, or 2 TB), support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (MagSafe), USB-C 3.2, Dual SIM, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and Ultra-Wideband (UWB). It also has Siri AI, Apple Intelligence, Emergency SOS via Satellite, and Crash Detection.

To help you better understand which model to buy, here's precisely where they diverge.

Apple

Apple

Apple has taken its time with its first foldable, enabling it to learn from the best folding phones already on the market. Eschewing the more prevalent book- and flip-style foldables, Apple has gone with a passport-sized form factor for the iPhone Duo, similar to Samsung's recent Galaxy Z Fold8 (our current favorite). The Duo has a 5.4-inch screen on the outside, but unfolds to reveal a 7.6-inch display inside that feels like an iPad Mini.

The iPhone Duo has a tough titanium frame, a precision hinge with magnets for that satisfying snap-shut, and an IP68 rating for solid dust and water resistance. But at 254 grams and 11.3 mm thick when folded, and 5.2 mm unfolded, the Duo is not the slimmest or lightest foldable around (the Fold8 is 201 grams, 9.7 mm thick folded, and 4.5 mm unfolded).

Foldables don’t have as much space for cameras, so the Duo drops Face ID (Touch ID is in the side power button instead) and makes do without a telephoto lens (you get a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide). But it has room for the biggest-ever iPhone battery, promising 24 hours of mixed use.

Where Apple will likely add a lot of value to the foldable phone category is with its software design. Controls have been pushed to the side and stacked vertically to free up more screen real estate. Apps offer plenty of split-screen support, and transitions between displays look slick. Apple has also included features that take advantage of the fact that you can prop the Duo open on a table or nightstand, so there’s StandBy support to use the outer screen as an alarm clock, while the inside display gently pulses with light to wake you.

Who it’s for: You want something different. You’re curious about folding phones or already convinced they’re great and can’t wait to experience Apple’s take.

Apple

Apple

The iPhone 18 Pro is similar to last year’s 17 Pro, with a 6.3-inch display, though the Dynamic Island has been slightly slimmed and can now show three Live Activities notifications at once. It keeps the same aluminum unibody, with Ceramic Shield on the back glass, Ceramic Shield 2 on the front, and an IP68 rating. Black is back, and there’s also a new Burgundy color, alongside Glacier and Silver. Those colors look more uniform than the 17 Pro’s two-tone finish.

Two standout upgrades stand out: The new A20 Pro chipset is faster and more power-efficient, and the main camera now has a variable aperture. The A20 Pro also enables better on-device AI and is aided by a redesigned vapor chamber to keep it cool while it works. Apple reckons you can expect 34 hours of video playback; that’s three hours more than the 17 Pro.

The camera introduces a physical lens aperture. Like the pupil of your eye, the aperture is the lens opening that lets light in. A bigger aperture can let in more light for better photos when it’s darker, and a smaller aperture can help you avoid overly bright photos when the sun is shining. But the aperture also impacts depth of field, so a bigger aperture can help you achieve that bokeh blurred background effect for a portrait photo, while a smaller aperture can help retain detail across a wider landscape shot. The camera app has new features and controls to help you take advantage of it.

Who it’s for: You don't want a big phone, but you want full-strength Apple silicon, a top camera, and all the latest features.

Apple

Apple

If foldables aren’t for you, the iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the biggest screen you can get at 6.9 inches, and it is a battery-life beast. Apple says you can get up to 43 hours of video playback out of a full charge; that’s a six-hour increase on last year’s already impressive 17 Pro Max. It has the same design and colors as the regular Pro, just bigger.

You also get the new chip and variable aperture camera. Both Pro models now boast a versatile triple 48-megapixel camera system with pro controls for lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. The class-leading video capture goes up to 4K at 120 fps. The iPhone 18 Pro phones are the right pick for photographers and videographers.

Who it’s for: You want the best Apple has to offer, including a big screen and long battery life, in a familiar form factor.

It makes sense to buy your iPhone unlocked, since it's much easier to switch carriers or use an international eSIM when you travel. The iPhones sold through Apple's storefront are unlocked, so Apple. com is the best place to buy them. During a preorder period, you can only purchase a newly announced iPhone from Apple.

Don't forget to take advantage of Apple's promotions: You get three free months of Apple One, which includes Apple Music, Apple TV+, Apple Arcade, News+, Apple Fitness+, and extra iCloud storage. Just watch out, because it will auto-bill you after the trial. Set a reminder to cancel if you don't want to continue subscribing to these services.

Apple has some financing options. If you have an Apple Card, you can pay for your iPhone over 24 months at 0-percent APR, and most carriers offer financing deals, too. Apple also offers Apple Upgrade, enabling you to lease your new iPhone from $35 a month for 24 months for the entry-model iPhone 18 Pro (12 months starts at $50 a month). We don’t think it’s a good deal, but if you’re tempted, remember you must return it in good condition (AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss costs an extra $15 a month).
